# Gateways

# Overview

A Gateway is really a configuration for the purchase process. For example, they tell what payment types are available to the user if this gateway is selected. They also tell the user which processing currency would be used.

We select a gateway when we build the Cart because clients need to know the available payment types to propose them to the user (e.g. adyen, spreedly, undostres…). The gateway can be changed during the checkout process.

The `PaymentPlatform` is used so we can find a Gateway by a “name” (e.g. the gateways configured for IOU payments).

## Different types of gateways

Bookie currently uses a terminology to differentiate different types of gateways. These are defined here:

### Explicit gateways

- Mainly used for PMD sources where the purchases are paid directly to bus companies and we must charge users in the currency of the sources.
- Example of a PMD source: Metro Turizm (Turkey).
- In grand-central database, the `gateway_id` is never null for PMD sources.
- In bookie, we use the `gateway_id` from the source to [find the appropriate gateway](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/11b1599514c127342fd3ebc72ad880edbfc37249/apps/bookie/components/cart/related-models.ts#L93-L94) for a payment.
- In bookie database, we set `external_charge` to true for PMD gateways.

### Automatic gateways

- Used for non-PMD sources and they don’t have a `gateway_id` configured in GC database.
- In that case, bookie must figure out which gateway to use for the payment. It is done in [findByCurrency](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/28d5126a7ac6ad1a2d3f36ef7e6f9054641354f0/apps/bookie/models/db/gateways.js#L171-L172), where we select the gateway based on various factors including available payment platform (e.g. Adyen, Spreedly), billing country, user currency, etc…
- We have a few restrictions:
    1. Interconnected trips are restricted to Spreedly gateways. In bookie db, we look up for gateways where `payment_platform` is set to `spreedly`.
    2. If users want to be charged in Argentinian pesos (ARS), they can do that as long as the sources are from Argentina (e.g. `source.currency` is ARS).
    3. Moka (integrated via Spreedly) and Iyzico (integrated via Adyen) gateways (where `gateway.currency` is TRY) can only be used in neredennereye.com.
- In bookie database, we set `external_charge` to false for non-PMD sources.

### Non-PMD sources with explicit gateways

- These are non-PMD sources with an explicit gateway (e.g. `source.gateway_id` is not null and `gateway.external_charge` is false).
- Gateway examples: SprinterBus USA ePay, Greyhound PMD - USD and - DC2NY USA ePay
- These are the remaining active gateways as of January 2021.

### NN gateways

Gateway selection for NN is still [a hardcoded thing](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/11b1599514c127342fd3ebc72ad880edbfc37249/apps/bookie/models/db/gateway-restrictions.ts#L5).

# The gateway selection process

For this section, you should have a look at the contents of the `gateways` table in the Bookie database.

It’s also a good idea to look at the functions in [the Gateway model file](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/11b1599514c127342fd3ebc72ad880edbfc37249/apps/bookie/models/db/gateways.js#L15) where the last bit of logic for obtaining proper gateways is contained. They’re rather complex SQL queries.

One thing that is important to understand about the following elements is the order of importance that they occupy in the gateway selection logic and the fact that we do not have active gateways in the database to cover every possible scenario, so there might be holes where we are not able to provide the expected gateway. In such cases, we try some fallbacks, but the logic here is complicated. It’s possible to encounter odd or hard to understand behaviours from the resulting combination of all these configuration knobs.

Example of holes:

- Requesting a gateway for a currency we do not process. We’ll fallback using `processing_currencies` or the default USD fallback, if possible.
- Requesting a gateway for a billing country we do not process (e.g. Israel). We’ll fallback using user country or the default USD fallback, if possible.
- Requesting a gateway for Installments payments in a currency where no gateway has `installments_supported` set to `true`. Installments will not be presented as an option for that currency choice.
- Requesting a gateway for a currency + payment platform combo for which no active gateway exists and no fallback mechanism (e.g. `processing_currencies`) has been defined. This will result in an error.

Here’s an example where a fallback is not possible: https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/9443

Roughly speaking, the order of importance of these elements is:

1. payment_platform
2. currency
3. installments flag
4. billing country (processing_countries)
5. processing_currencies
6. weight
7. As a last resort, FALLBACK_CURRENCY = `USD`

## processing_countries

Can be used to limit which billing countries can make use of the gateway entry. Assigning a country code value, **for a country code that we do not process directly**, to this column for a particular Gateway entry indicates that we would like to use that gateway for that country.

For example, we have an user whose billing address is in Israel. There’s no gateway to process Israeli New Shekel. Adding `ISR` to BusbudEurope gateway means that we want to use that gateway and the user would be charged in EUR.

## processing_currencies

This one can be tricky to understand. Assigning a currency value, **for a currency that we do not process directly**, to this column for a particular Gateway entry indicates that we would like to use that gateway for that currency.

For example, here we have configured the Gateway of **Adyen** platform and `BusbudEurope` merchant account, which captures payments in `EUR` only, to be the gateway of choice when the user is browsing in currencies like `DKK`.

![cart-processing-currencies-sql.png](Gateways/cart-processing-currencies-sql.png)

The result in Pubweb:

![cart-processing-currencies.png](Gateways/cart-processing-currencies.png)

Note that this is meant as a sort of safety net mechanism with the goal of optimizing billing currencies (lower transaction processing costs). As such, it makes sense to establish `EUR` as the billing currency for someone who’d otherwise want to use DKK.

You may have noticed that we also have **MXN**, **SEK** and **PEN** in there too. But, we actually have active Spreedly gateways for those:

![cart-processing-currencies-spreedly-sql.png](Gateways/cart-processing-currencies-spreedly-sql.png)

So you’d expect to see the Spreedly form being shown and the Cart Summary charges appear in SEK, right? Well, yes, **if** there is no not-Sweden Billing Country selected and none of the other more important params interfere with the selection:

![cart-processing-currencies-spreedly.png](Gateways/cart-processing-currencies-spreedly.png)

## installments_supported

Simple flag that will be used for filtering while fetching the most appropriate gateway when a payment using installments is being requested.

## adyen_merchant_account

Relevant if the gateway is of type `adyen` only. These names MUST map exactly to one of our active Adyen Merchant Accounts (e.g. `BusbudEurope`). See the active accounts by logging in the Adyen console.

## spreedly_gateway_type

Relevant if the gateway is of type `spreedly` only. There is [logic in place](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/40345344d22f9ab7542e204651c1f741717e5d77/apps/bookie/lib/payment-methods/spreedly-gateway-specific-fields.ts) to send “gateway specific fields” to certain payment providers that we use via our Spreedly integration. This column helps identify the provider to achieve this functionality.

## weight

If all else is equal in the gateway selection logic and many gateways are eligible, the `weight` column can help in choosing a winner.

However, it’s important to realize that `weight` acts as a distribution mechanism (similar to Pubweb XP mechanism) rather than a pure decision mechanism. For example, for 1000 gateway selections between equally eligible Gateway A having a weight of 950 and Gateway B having a weight of 50, the result will be:

- Gateway A picked approximately 950 times
- Gateway B picked approximately 50 times

If a gateway should never be used, deactivate it (`active` = false).

## payment_types

List of payment types that a gateway can support. If we were to introduce a new payment method, then it should be added to that column.

## active

If you do not want a gateway to be used, then it should be set to `false`.

## external charge

It is set to `true` for PMD sources.

## description

This column defines the gateway. It is decided by the finance team.

## charge_description

The value of this column will appear on the user’s credit card statements.

# Pubweb Checkout Pages

# Introduction

Pubweb’s checkout pages are a two-step checkout process. In the first step, called passenger step, we ask the users for their contact information and to fill out passenger questions. In the second step, called payment step, we ask the users to enter their billing address and payment details.

# The Payment Form

We use the Adyen DropIn form when possible. Some gateways may use the Spreedly form. Ideally, we should only use the Adyen DropIn component. That makes it easier to integrate with new payment methods and to keep up-to-date with their upgrades.

The main downside is that we can’t access payment information that would be useful for derisk if that needs to happen before we authorize, which is the case with payment methods that capture the money right after authorization (e.g. BusbudTurkey merchant account).

### Adyen’s Web Drop-in

We use Adyen’s [Drop-in solution](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/prebuilt-ui#drop-in) to integration payments UI in checkout for web, iOS and Android. The payments squad owes the web SDK and the mobile squad is responsible for both iOS and Android SDK.

The payment methods we currently offer include:

- Cards, including credit card, debit card, 3DSecure versions 1.0 and 2.0
- Apple Pay for some of the merchant accounts, such as BusbudCanada and BusbudSouthAfrica
- Google Pay for some of the merchant accounts, such as BusbudCanada and BusbudUSA

We also support these payment methods, but they have been disabled due to [technical issues](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/7526):

- Sofort
- Klarna
- iDeal
- Trustly
- Interac
- Bancontact
- WeChat

### Spreedly

We use this payment form for the following scenarios:

1. neredennereye, which uses Moka because it is integrated via Spreedly’s API
2. For users being charged in the following currencies: Argentinian pesos ARS, Mexican pesos MXN, and Peruvian sol PEN (dLocal and ebanx gateways)
3. For PMD gateways (e.g. Metro Turizm)
4. For interconnections because [we removed Adyen support](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/docs/adrs/0006-make-interconnections-use-spreedly.md).
5. If Adyen goes down, then we would fallback to Spreedly. This would be an extremely rare scenario.

### Billing Address

1. We ask for the billing address information from all users, except Neredennereye’s users. This is because Turkish customers don’t have proper billing addresses that can be confirmed in Turkey. Therefore, we won’t be able to provide it to fraud derisk partners when we derisk.
2. Moreover, we offer the option to pay in Google Pay or Apple Pay on the first step (aka passenger step) of checkout as a way to complete checkout faster. For the users who opt to checkout from the passenger step (see screenshot below), we don’t get their billing address because we ask for that information on the payment step. [This would need to be addressed at some point](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/7424) as not getting the billing address impacts how we analyze point of sale per country.

![checkout-passenger-step.png](Pubweb%20Checkout%20Pages/checkout-passenger-step.png)

1. The billing address is also used to determine which currency to charge the user in (aka gateway selection). If a user were to enter Canada as their billing country, then the user would be charged in CAD.

### Google Pay

The button is not translated based on the website language, but using the browser locale. For example, if my browser is in French:

![google-pay-button-fr.png](Pubweb%20Checkout%20Pages/google-pay-button-fr.png)

This is not super ideal because I could use Busbud in French but see “Pay with GPay” because my browser is in English.

But we think it’s ok since:

1. It’s not trivial to solve, this is Google doing his thing and we’d need to hijack that
2. It’s OK since the user should be familiar with their browser locale
3. It can be fixed with this [SDK version 4.1.0](https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/release-notes?integration_type=web#releaseNote=2021-03-09-web-componentsdrop-in-4.1.0), where you can specify the button locale in the configuration.

# Demand Partners

**Demand Partners** are resellers of Busbud’s inventory. They connect to our API and either sell content directly on their site, or deeplink to ours inside of the search flow somewhere.

# Creation

To create a new demand partner:

- Go to the [Partners](https://backoffice.busbud-int.com/dashboard/partners) screen in Backoffice and click the “Create Partner” button next to the word “Partners”
- Fill out the minimum information required based on what Global Ops has provided: name (slug), display name, technical contact email, URL, currency code and feeds language. If the “Deal Type” is referral, set `no` payments Type, otherwise if the deal type is Booking set Payments Type to “Allow Some” and select `iou` only. Set `BoB` or `BoX` depending on what kind of integration they are doing. Make sure the “Deal Type” is set to the correct value – this should never really be “N/A” unless you know what you’re doing. When done, click Save.
- Send the partner name to Global Ops and request they fill out the rest of the information on the page.
- By default, partners only have access to a subset of our supply. Depending on the deal type, they might be entitled to more. For example, referral partners aren’t resellers and have access to more supply than resellers like Trainline. You should ask Global Ops whether we should grant this partner access to more supply using [Supply Rules](https://backoffice.busbud-int.com/dashboard/bus-company/supply-rules).
- Create a public and private token for both preview and production. Note these down. Don’t worry about sending production tokens already – they will not work until the partner is activated, and they will need the production private token to access the cities/locations/routes data feeds.
    - Preview tokens and production private token will work even though the partner is set as inactive
    - If you are creating preview tokens before the preview DB sync, you’ll need to also create the same partner on backoffice preview
        - If the partner ID does not match with production, run a DB update on the preview DB to align the IDs
- In the Github repo for the [documentation site](https://github.com/busbud/docs/), run `yarn do:create-partner <partner-name>` and note the resulting username/password generated. Commit changes and push to the main branch. Once done, run `yarn deploy:partnerdocs`y so the changes will take effect.
- Send all four tokens and the documentation username/password/URL to the partner, or to Global Ops so they can pass them. The documentation URL for partners is [https://partner-docs.busbud.net](https://partner-docs.busbud.net/).
- Inform the partner that they should contact us via partner-support@busbud.com if they need any help during the onboarding process, if they do not have a Slack Connect integration with us or if they are not using WhatsApp.

# Validation

Once the partner has completed their integration and are ready to go live in production, we invite them to a validation meeting where they make a **live presentation of search and booking functionality** and we examine the logs on our side to make sure all requests and responses look correct. This is notably a good time to ensure they are:

- creating a search and polling properly
- not merely a frontend integration (i.e. they aren’t hardcoding our API tokens in a way that others can intercept and rip off)
- not making excessive or repeated calls to details/selection endpoints like `GET /trips/:id/stops`
- not creating useless carts just to get extra data
- submitting passenger questions and other important values in the proper format
- submitting the customer’s email for the `purchaser` correctly (we do not want the partner’s support email in `purchaser`)

To do this, during the live demo an engineer will typically keep BigQuery’s NAPI preview dataset open ([`departure-archive.fastly_logs_mtl.napi_preview_logs`](https://console.cloud.google.com/bigquery?project=departure-archive&d=fastly_logs&p=departure-archive&t=napi_preview_logs&page=table)), and run queries for a specific partner ID and timespan (ordered by time) after each user action. Example:

```sql

SELECT
  timestamp, method, status, url
FROM
  `departure-archive.fastly_logs_mtl.napi_preview_logs`
WHERE
  (TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(timestamp, DAY) = TIMESTAMP("2023-09-27") OR timestamp IS NULL)
  AND partner_id = "999"
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
```

If you’d like to see Search logs in real time, you can use the following:

```jsx
bb logs -f -a poll-service-preview | grep express | grep -E '(PARTNER_PUBLIC_KEY|PARTNER_PRIVATE_KEY)' | jq -rc '"\(.time / 1000 | strflocaltime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")) \(.request.method) \(.request.url)"'
```

If needed, you can collect request IDs from this set and check to ensure properly-formatted requests were passed along to Poll Service, Bookie or the adapters. If you’re confident though, you can skip this and only use BigQuery and the Busbud Support tool with the purchase IDs.

This is a good time to also validate the purchase line items in Busbud Support Tool (prices, currencies and partner commission). Partner commission and partner currency adjustments are made within the partner’s configuration page in Backoffice/Busplatform.

If any anomalies are observed in the partner’s requests, don’t hesitate to point these out and ask that they fix them before going live. We will not activate them for production use unless any show-stopping bugs are corrected. In this case, you can schedule another validation demo once they’ve corrected the problems.

# Setting Up Demand Partner Payments (Referral)

Referral partners get a commission on every purchase that was attributed to them. At the end of each month, the finance team runs the Demand Partner Report (in the [analytics api](https://github.com/busbud/analytics-api) repository) which generates the list of purchases attributed to each demand partner and the amount that we owe them.

The payout currency and the commission amount of a demand partner are hardcode in the `scripts/demand_partners.py` Python script. To make sure a referral partner is paid in the correct currency and gets their commission, you will need to update the code with the partner-specific details.

```python
self.default_cpa = 0.5
self.custom_cpas = {"buscaonibus": 0.3, "kelbillet": 0.6, "checkmybus": 0.55}
self.default_currency = "EUR"
self.custom_currencies = {"buscaonibus": "BRL", "transatca": "CAD", "checkmybus": "USD", "lacomuna": "USD"}
self.repository_service = repository_service
self.cur = cur
```

# Go Live

When a new demand partner is ready to go live, after having passed validation:

- send a message to Accounting informing them of the imminent switch to production, including the partner ID and name, currency and business email contact
    - Make sure you reference the proper terminology for the type of deal they have so they set it up properly - Finance calls **referral** partners “demand merchant partners”, and **direct booking** partners are “distribution partners”
- inform the partner that, in case of problems with user purchases, they should reach out to CX at support@busbud.com; technical problems can be directed to us on Slack (if they have a Slack Connect integration with us), WhatsApp or partner-support@busbud.com
- once Accounting has acknowledged the message, and Global Ops has given the OK, click the “Activate Partner” button on the partner page in Backoffice

# Deploying a new adapter to an existing source

Some deployments require a switchover from the existing adapter to a new adapter. In this case the following must be checked off in addition to the deployment procedures.

## Update Source slugs

Go into grand central database and update the `booking_settings` field with the new adapter endpoints. Replacing the base_url with the new one generated from the adapter. If there are multiple sources update all of them.

```json
{
  "method": "busbud-adapter",
  "development": {
    "source_slug": "existingsource",
    "base_url": "https://old-adapter/existingsource"
  },
  "production": {
    "source_slug": "existingsource",
    "base_url":  "https://old-adapter/existingsource"
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "method": "busbud-adapter",
  "development": {
    "source_slug": "existingsource",
    "base_url": "https://new-adapter/existingsource"
  },
  "production": {
    "source_slug": "existingsource",
    "base_url":  "https://new-adapter/existingsource"
  }
}
```

## Reload the Source for `inventory-service`

Once the source has the new adapter configuration setup in the database, reload the source for inventory-service (both for the US and EU instances) using the `/reload` endpoint. ✨
Here’s how to do it:

```bash
# For inventory-service US instance
curl -X POST 'https://inventory-service-production-us.busbud-int.com/reload'\
	-H "x-busbud-token: $(vault read -field="NAPI_TOKEN" secret/grand-central-production)"\
	-H "Content-Type: application/json"\
	-d '{"source_name":"<source_name>"}'

# For inventory-service EU instance
curl -X POST 'https://inventory-service-production-eu.busbud-int.com/reload'\
	-H "x-busbud-token: $(vault read -field="NAPI_TOKEN" secret/grand-central-production)"\
	-H "Content-Type: application/json"\
	-d '{"source_name":"<source_name>"}'
```

## Clear cached trips

In addition, you can go ahead and clear out all the trips from the old source. Make sure to clone inventory service and run the following in your command line.

```bash
cd inventory-service
bb as tools -- node tools/cache-cleaner/index.js "<sourceid>"
```

## Getting rid of the old adapter

Has your new adapter been running nicely for many days/weeks and the team has given you green light to proceed with this? (if not, get out of here)

So CD into the **OLD** adapter folder and use the following command:

```bash
terraform destroy
```

At the step it asks for the "Commit hash to be used as the image tag”, use `latest`.

If you have never used terraform at the old integration folder, you may need to use the following command before (it will advise it during the first command if it's needed):

```bash
terraform init
```

# Deploying to Preview

You can deploy to preview any time during the development workflow. This can help you:

- Ensure operators, sources and mappings show appropriately.
- Perform live searches in the preview environment.
- Identify UI issues with large datasets (like Banff Airporter’s departures).

<aside>
⚠️ The preview environment is restored every week. Any mapping will then be erased. Ensure to either script / backup your changes OR not do any costly manual work.

</aside>

In this section we will describe the full flow that you will need to employ to deploy your integration to the preview environment.

- Configure the integration
- Deploy to Kubernetes
- Run the import

## Configuring for Preview

You should have a configuration available by running `bb config -a "myintegration-dev"`.

Setting your source config there for preview is a must, for example, you can run:

```bash
bb config:set -a "myintegration-dev" SOURCE_CONFIG_myintegration='{"key": "secret_api_key", "client_id":"busbud"}';
```

<aside>
💡 A cool thing about setting your config in the vault is that scratch can reuse it! You need to deploy again after each configuration change.

</aside>

## Deploying the dev adapter

Deploying to the preview environment is equally easy with the help of the `bb` tool.

```bash
cd myintegration # the folder where your integration is located
bb deploy dev # note, dev here, very important!
```

Once the process is done, you can check the state of the deployed pods:

```bash
kubectl --namespace myintegration-dev get pods

> NAME                                 READY     STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
> myintegration-dev-769f8c5b96-mrgb5   1/1       Running   0          5m
```

The above command shows a successfully running pod, ready to receive traffic.

<aside>
❓ Do you not see your pod in the above list?

It is possible that your pod is not deployed in your currently configured context. Integrations are deployed to the cluster the closest to the partner's server, in US `busbud-int-us` and europe `busbud-int-eu`.

You can find the context for a particular integration running `bb context myintegration`. As you see, you shall not append the `-dev` suffix. All the contexts should be configured, and you can toggle the context using: `kubectl config use-context CONTEXT` where `CONTEXT` would be the result of the previous command.

You will now be able to read the logs with:

```bash
bb logs -a myintegration-dev -f
```

</aside>

## Setting up the import

Remember to set up the cron so the import will run automatically. 

In the importer database, table source, you have the import_schedule column. Take examples with others integrations or ask chatgpt to generate the correct schedule value. 
If your integration takes a lot of time, don’t trigger it every day !

## Running an import

Now that your integration is configured and deployed appropriately, you can run the import. The import process extracts all locations and routes info from your adapter and puts it in a temporary database.

Before you can run the import you will need to:

- Ensure the source exists on the **NAPI preview** and **NAPI production** databases in the `sources` table.
- Ensure the source exists on the `busbud-int-importer` database in the `sources` table.

## Create the source in NAPI

You can create the source in the napi production database and wait a week for preview to be up to date. As we are deploying a development adapter we can also create the source directly in the preview database.

In order to create the source, you should have in your integration’s README a series of SQL commands that will create the source.

Execute those commands against the **preview** *and* **production** databases.

## Create the source in the Importer

To create the source in the importer you can use the following command, **from the [integration-importer](https://github.com/busbud/integration-importer) project folder**:

```bash
echo "INSERT INTO sources (slug, env) VALUES ('myintegration', 'development');" | psql `yarn -s db:get-url`
```

### Importing locations and routes

<aside>
💡 Keep the logs open as described above, this will let you follow the entire process.

</aside>

Then you’ll need to run the import itself:

```bash
curl 'https://importer-cg.busbud-int.com/start/development/<source_name>?force=true' -H "x-busbud-token: $(vault read -field="NAPI_TOKEN" secret/grand-central-preview)"
```

After the import is done, you will need to transfer the location and route data from the int-importer database to the NAPI database.

<aside>
💡 This step is done automatically on production imports (without -dev) so you do not need to run it in production.

</aside>

Importing the data to the **NAPI preview** database is done through a Grunt task: Change ‘myIntegration’ by yours.

```bash
//if you are not in the correct context
kubectl config use-context busbud-us-east4-1

//do the import
kubectl exec -it -n grand-central-preview $(kubectl get pods -n grand-central-preview | grep 'grand-central-preview' | head -n 1 | awk '{print $1}') -- bash -c 'BUSBUD_ENV=development yarn grunt import:full:<source_name>'
```

# Deploying to Production

You’re ready to deploy the production version of the integration once you get the production credentials from the partner. We **never** use development credentials in production, even for something like imports as we can not trust partner data to stay up to date or consistent between environments.

You can deploy the integration in dark launch mode for testing on Busbud.com before going live. This means only signed-in users with `@busbud.com` emails will be able to see results from the integration. **If it’s an integration rewrite, you’ll have to deploy it to review instead.**

**In order to QA either of those scenarios and ensure everything works, you should follow the [Connectivity procedure](https://docs.google.com/document/d/16XHD4uJb-knXNxJx3WxZF_pAvEz1Z2A9GGT0PktHd9Y).**

If you encounter the following error when using the Heroku CLI, run `heroku join -t busbud -a APP_NAME` and try executing the command again.

> ▸ You do not have permission to view dynos on example-app. You need to have the view permission on this app.
> 

## Environment Variables

Environment variables are currently stored within Vault with the naming convention `int_NAME_ENV`. Terraform will automatically pull down the latest from Vault every time `terraform apply` or `bb deploy` is used. The starterpack takes care of adding the initial variables, which likely won’t have to be changed to get your integration up and running.

To modify environment variables use `bb config`:

```bash
bb config -a your-adapter
bb config:get -a your-adapter SOME_ENV_VAR SOME_OTHER_ENV_VAR
bb config:set -a your-adapter SOME_ENV_VAR=a SOME_OTHER_ENV_VAR=b
bb config:unset -a your-adapter
```

Alternatively, you can also use the [Vault UI](https://github.com/djenriquez/vault-ui), or the Vault commandline to [`read`](https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/commands/read.html) and [`write`](https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/commands/write.html). However, be careful if you choose to go with the Vault command line because if you only specify one variable when using `write` it will overwrite **all** pre-existing variables of that secret with the one you just passed. A known work around at this moment can be found [in this issue](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/182#issuecomment-158203842).

Don’t forget to `bb deploy` or `bb deploy dev` in your adapter after updating the environment variables.

## Build and deploy

Docker is currently used to build our integrations images, and Terraform to deploy to our Kubernetes cluster. You can find what our Terraform module looks like in [terraform-modules](https://github.com/busbud/integrations/terraform-modules/tree/master/integration). We wrap these together in our `bb` command line.

There are two Kubernetes cluster we work with, one in the US and the other in Europe. The starterpack automatically assigns a region for your integration when you first create it based on latency to the partners servers from each cluster, and selecting the fastest.

We can build and deploy the container with the following:

```bash
cd my-integration # This is significant.
bb deploy # Uses the current working directory to determine the application name
```

<aside>
💡 Use `bb deploy dev` if you want to deploy to the **Preview** environment.

</aside>

If you get an issue with missing image, you need to manually pull the base images used in your Dockerfile, e.g.:

```bash
docker pull eu.gcr.io/busbud-integrations/node:6.11.2-builder
```

## Mass deploy

```bash
bb adapters | bb mass-deploy
```

<aside>
⚠️ Please make sure not to change branches while you are in the middle of a mass deploy because the script uses the files in your current active branch. If you need to change branches, please use `git worktree` to manage multiple branches ([How to use git worktree](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cRunWRC8ye0)).

</aside>

`bb adapters` lists all adapters of the integrations repository in alphabetical order, and `bb mass-deploy` runs `bb deploy` in every directory in `stdin`.

If it crashes, you can resume the deploy at a given adapter (usually the one it crashed on) after fixing the issue, e.g. if it crashed at `movelia`:

```bash
bb adapters | bb mass-deploy-resume movelia
```

If you want to do a partial mass deploy (like only TypeScript integrations), you can use a custom command instead of `bb adapters` to list only the adapter directories that you care about. The following deploys only TypeScript integrations:

```bash
echo */tsconfig.json | xargs -n1 dirname | sort | bb mass-deploy
```

And same thing to resume after an error:

```bash
echo */tsconfig.json | xargs -n1 dirname | sort | bb mass-deploy-resume perubus
```

# Documentation Review

# Introduction

Before an integration reaches the execution queue to be started by a developer, the documentation is reviewed so we can get obvious questions answered first before wasting development time. These are typically added to the sprint board as they come in, to give the business side quick feedback on expectations for the integration.

One of the key tips when reviewing docs is picturing how you’d write [each method](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html), and what information may be missing. Here you’ll find a checklist for each stage of an integration when reviewing, and the questions you should be asking yourself.

## Types of Doc Review

There are two types of documentation review:

- Pre-signing: This is simply a scan of their API docs to confirm that it is possible for us to integrate with the supplier. At this phase it is rare we have a set of test credentials as the contract isn’t signed, but the review is still required based on their documentation.
- Post-signing: This is to confirm their API does what their documentation says it does, and do a run through of the test environment to make sure it is ready to go. Resources for integration are also more accurately estimated.

There are also two different types of integration to do a doc review for:

- BoB: Buy on Busbud. These require the full review
- BoX: Buy on External. These only require the review up to and including `getTrips`

# Before starting a review

Before starting to review docs, make sure you have the following details. If they’re not available, ask for them before starting.

- Docs in the form of a PDF, website, or anything else readable that describes the API
- An endpoint for the API
- Authentication (if required) for the API.

# Account Credit & Credentials

If their development environment requires account credit for booking tests, make sure that’s added before we mark the integration as ready to go. Also, we should ask for the API endpoint/credentials for **production** as well as **development** environments if the partner is ok with sharing prod credentials before the integration is complete (some won’t be). Even though the production info is not required for writing the integration, it will make the transition to live easier later.

# Test the API

- Does the API actually work? Provide a cURL, Postman, JavaScript, or TypeScript ([Gist](https://gist.github.com/) links accepted) example when reviewing.
- Besides that, you should run a quick test for timeouts. A suggested way to do that is to connect to their API endpoint 20 times in a row and see if any timeout error occurs. See example below. Since we’ll be hitting the `getTrips` endpoint the most, use that for your tests.

```bash
 for i in $(seq 0 20); do curl ...; done;
```

# How to write a review

You can copy/paste the following template and fill in the blanks when writing up your review on Github. Again if you need reference to what each method does and what it requires, see [ImportAdapter](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.importadapter.html), [SearchAdapter](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html) and [BookingAdapter](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html) depending on the type of integration you’re evaluating. For further details about each sub-section, go past the template to the `Explanation` section of this doc.

- *General* section is a checklist of overall things to look for.
- *Methods* are to describe which methods you picture are available and which are not. The fields that are required should be challenged against the partner to find a solution. Without them, the integration doesn’t go live.
    - If a method is not supported, you can remove the `endpoints to use` and `implementation details` portions, and leave `supported` unchecked
    - Each method has a checklist of things to look for. Check them off if they’re applicable.
    - **Features** for a method add complexity to the eventual implementation, but are not blockers to a doc review
    - **Blockers Check** is a list of specific things to check for to make sure we won’t be blocked. In other words, a list of pain points someone had once upon a time stumbled upon, and we don’t want to be making the same mistake of not checking
    - `Endpoints to use` : list off the endpoints that fulfill the method requirements
    - `Implementation Details` : any additional context on how to implement that would be appreciated by the developer who integrates it. Anything you find out of the ordinary.
- *Documentation Rating* give a rating to the potential integration. Used for planning purposes
- *Further Questions* is the list of questions we still have for the BizDev team. They are separated by blocking and non-blocking, with the former blocking further progression. Take inspiration from the things that were left unchecked.
- *Example Request* is used to provide a working example of any method against the partners provided API/credentials with either cURL, Postman, JavaScript, or TypeScript ([Gist](https://gist.github.com/) links accepted). Usually, we test out the `locations` method to verify we get a proper response.

# Explanation

## General

These are all the overall things to look out for during the documentation review:

- **HTTPS production**: we require a production HTTPS connection. Devs will block the integration if we can’t securely send information to the partner’s API (especially considering passenger info)
- **Method of communication with partner**: Highlight how the integration dev will communicate with the partner’s dev team. A direct connection like slack/whatsapp is preferred over email. Can ask BizDev if it is possible, if they haven’t communicated around this issue.
- **Error codes described**: How robust is our error handling going to be in the beginning of this integration? If they don’t have error codes in their docs then they don’t. This is just a sanity check
- **ChatGPT Link if docs aren't in english**: If your documentation is not in English, please create a chatGPT on Busbud’s business account for it that the team can use. This is helpful for quick explanations of methods, and typing out responses with JSDocs.

## Import

On import our main concerns revolve around data quality:

- Either getLocations + getRoutes is required OR getLocationsAndRoutes is required. The latter is used when the data is bundled together on the partner’s API.
- Does their location method return address or latlon? If not, will they provide a dump? How are we getting location data?
- Do they actually have a route method? Are we going to have to xprod? Would it be smart to xprod if they have a small amount of locations (less than 50)?
- If location data doesn’t look sufficient for a person to map, have the BizDev team reach out to see if we can get more information

## GetTrips

Confirm that we can take 2 of their location IDs, a date, and a number of passengers to create a search, then respond with results with pricing and departure times

One-way support is required. Roundtrip and interconnection support dependent on if it can all be booked in a single API call.

Potential Features:

- **Passenger Categories:** List the passenger categories that are supported by the integration
- **Passenger Discounts supported**: List the passenger discounts that are supported by the integration. Currently applicable values are `military` , `student` and `teacher`
- **Optional seat selection supported**: We have optional seat selection on the frontend. Check off if users can select their seats. If seat selection is required and every seat has a price, highlight that in `implementation details` as we’d need to adjust the code to add the lowest seat price difference into the trip’s base price (so that the cheapest seat is free)
- **Passenger Questions Required**: list the required questions we need to ask the passenger. this may also be derived from the request we need to send them during booking
- **Fees on search**: Canada requires that all fees be displayed at the time of search. If Canadian, add how we would do this in `implementation details`. For other countries just check if applicable.
- **Different origin/destination XIDs than on search:** Some integrations use city-to-city routes for searching and return stop-to-stop on search. If these stops aren’t added during import, add to `implementation details` how we get the location data (lat/lon, name etc) for these stops
- **Contains additional T&Cs information**: For now, this is just a tracking field. Some integrations return long strings of the full T&C of the trip that we currently have no way to return in the response. Check if this is the case.
- **Ticket Type Selection**: This is just a tracking field. some partners allow the user to select their desired ticket type from a list of options (for the oldies that want printed tickets I guess).  Check if this is the case.

Blockers check:

- **No unsupported passenger questions:** All passenger questions that we need must already be supported by busbud, or can be dummified so we don’t actually ask the user. If there are new questions required, add to `implementation details`
- **All trips are bookable:** We can only book trips that are instant-confirmation, ie when we hit the booking endpoint, the user is confirmed and can expect to get on their bus. If the trip requires “operator confirmation in the next 24hours”, then we cannot support it. If we can filter these out, add to `implementation details` .

## TripRefresh

Required as either getTripDetails OR one of getVehicleLayout and getPrices. If both getVehicleLayout and getPrices need implementation, use getTripDetails

Potential Features:

- **Vehicle Layout added:** (required for `getVehicleLayout`) check if a seat layout that wasn’t available on getTrips is now available
- **Prices guaranteed to change:** (required for `getPrices`) check if there is a price update. Typically in the form of adding taxes or fees
- **Passenger question list added:** The partner has a dynamic list of passenger questions, and we only find out the list by selecting the trip on the API. If this is checked, then `getTripDetails` is required
- **Trip Stops added:** The partner has an endpoint to get all the stops the vehicle will stop at. If this is checked, then `getTripDetails` is required
- **Authentication updated for specific user:** Sometimes a partner requires a unique token for a user for booking, but the token is created during search. The other common use-case is when we have separate credentials in Argentina for Argentinian users vs international users. This is where the correct credentials is solidified.

## Book

Required. 

Problems that sometimes happens:

- **They want us to pass a credit card**: **Short answer is “not happening”.** If they want us to pass credit cards, align with BizDev to see what the next steps are. While we do have existing examples of passing credit cards, it is generally not preferred as we will no longer be able to refund our customers. Any existing examples are because we either are desperate for its supply (viarail and amtrak), or its a relic of the past that still exists (sprinterbus)
- **Account credit required for booking**: sometimes the partner wants us to prepay them and deducts from the payment when booking tickets.
    - If this is required on dev, make sure we have a proper portal that we can “fund” (on dev typically no money is actually passed through)
    - If this is required on prod, align with BizDev and Finance to make sure we want to move forward with this partner
- Check if the response has a URL for tickets, a barcode or alike. If not, it’s probably a sign we will run into problems in getTickets (see method below for more info)

## GetTickets

GetTickets required, or acceptance of our Hodor tickets required

Note: this is the most common blocker. We will not move forward until the requirement is fulfilled.

## Cancel

**Voucher-only cancellation**: We now allow T&Cs to indicate if users can cancel and be refunded in the form of a voucher (instead of money). Check if this is supported. 

**CFAR cancellation**: CFAR passes in `refund_type: "none"` which means we’re just looking to release the seat so the operator can have someone else book it, but we acknowledge we are not expecting a refund

## Other

- Is the environment provided production or development? If prod, mark it in **BIG BOLD LETTERS** stating we should have a dev environment to work on, or that the proper rules are in place to make purchases against prod (e.g we don’t want to pay for them).

## Difficulty Rating

How good are the docs?

- General rating on how understandable the documentation was. 1 if 1 being if they’re in Klingon using SOAP where the XML response body contains only one field that’s an URL-encoded representation of the response where some fields can themselves be XML-encoded, and where the bus layout is described as a list of x/y pixel coordinates on a canvas. And 10 being the integration practically writes itself.

How easy is the implementation?

- Easy (i.e.: only one-ways available, well-written API and documentation)
- Medium (i.e.: only one-ways available, not so bad API and bad documentation)
- Hard (i.e.: roundtrip or interconnections available, or badly implemented API)
- Super Hard (i.e.: 4 calls to API to getTrips, with roundtrip or interconnections, badly written API and terrible documentation)

## Further Questions

- Blocking Questions: These are questions that are blocking progression on the integration. Development will not start until the questions are answered. Examples:
    - No ticket file available, will they accept our ticket?
    - Partner has 10000 locations and no routes. We aren’t going to do a cross-product on that many locations. We need a list of routes.
- Non-blocking Questions: These are questions that will effect the quality of the result, but development is not blocked. Examples:
    - Do I really need this huge list of passenger questions for *every* trip?
    - Can I have some lat/lons? Pretty please?

# QA

Before deploying, check that you understand how QA will happen to test your changes.

# The case of a new integration

If the partner has a dev environment, it’s a good idea to deploy and test it in the Preview environment first.

If not, or when you’re ready to move to production, deploy the integration in dark launch mode.

Then, pass it over to the Connectivity team.

# The case of an integration rewrite

The integration already exists in production. Thus, passing it into dark launch mode may not be an option.

Just like the case of a new integration: if the partner has a dev environment, it could be a good idea to test it in preview first. Or we could accept to take the risk of deploying and testing in production. Just sync yourself with the Connectivity team to agree on a QA plan (e.g. where & when to deploy?).

# The other cases

If you’re adding new features or fixing bugs of an existing integration, testing strategy will depend on the nature of you change.

Previous advices are still relevant. The key idea is to sync up with the Connectivity team to understand how this should be tested. How do you know that your changes are working? You need to answer that.

# Rewriting Integrations

# Setup

Before you get started, you’ll need a development config for your integration, consisting of the following:

- [ ]  a development module in your `main.tf`
- [ ]  a development secret in `vault`

If you’ve got all this, great! If not, see below.

## 1. `main.tf`:

```
module "development" {
  env         = "development"   // changed from "production"
  replicas    = 1               // changed from 2
  // everything else stays the same
}
```

## 2. Development secret:

Not sure if you have one? Check if this command returns anything:

```bash
vault read --format=json secret/int_{your-int-name}_development
```

If you don’t have one, get the example template, and create a config based off it:

```bash
vault read --format=json secret/int_example_development | jq .data > config.json
```

In your new config file, change ‘example’ in `ADAPTER_NAME` and `BASE_URL` to your integration’s name.

Also in `SOURCE_CONFIG_example`, replace `example` by the name of the source, and put the development configuration JSON as a value.

Then write the config:

```bash
vault write secret/int_{your-int-name}_development @config.json
```

You’re ready to QA!

# QA

## 1. Update NAPI preview config.

At a minimum, you want to set darklaunch so only @busbud.com users see the integration while we’re testing.

```bash
heroku pg:psql -a napi-grand-central-preview-us
// Check what state is set to first, change it back to that in cleanup.
BEGIN;
update sources set state='darklaunch' where name='{your-int-name}';
COMMIT;

// Restart db
heroku restart -a napi-grand-central-preview-us
```

## 2. Set config to use prod credentials

n.b. **You’re about to configure the integration to charge Busbud for any transactions**. This is the time to warn the engineering @team.

```bash
bb config:set -a your-int-name-dev SOURCE_CONFIG_your_source_name='{...prod-config...}'
```

## 3. Deploy!

```bash
cd path/to/integrations/{your-int-name}
bb deploy dev
```

You may have to do this twice if you get a `CreateContainerConfigError` the first time.

n.b. If you have `method interactive` in your `.netrc`, you’ll have to delete that line.

Check: `https://int-{your_int_name}-dev.busbud-int.com`—if it’s up, you’re good to try some test purchases.

# Cleanup

1. Reconfigure dev env not to use prod:

```
bb config:set -a your-int-name-dev SOURCE_CONFIG_your_source_name='{...dev-config...}'
```

1. Set replicas to 0 in your terraform dev configuration.
2. Change state in napi-grand-central-preview-us back to `active` (or whatever it was pre-testing).
3. Re-deploy integration.

# Setting up infrastructure resources

# Number of pods

All integrations by default have a replicas at 2 and a max_replicas at 8 for production.
For preview and test, it’s only 1 for both.

![Screenshot 2024-05-06 at 12.06.54 PM.png](Setting%20up%20infrastructure%20resources/Screenshot_2024-05-06_at_12.06.54_PM.png)

That means the adapter will have 2 pods by default running and can scale up to 8.

<aside>
💡 The main goal is too have a low number of pods, a steady number of them running and avoid scaling up and down too much.
The reason is the adapters rely on in-memory cache, so too many of them or scaling up/down will mess up this cache.

</aside>

# CPU and memory

It’s a developer job and it’s important to correctly set the amount of CPU and memory the adapter will have.

For the CPU, it’ll change how fast the number of pods will scale up and down.
For the memory, it’ll prevent to have inconsistent out of memory issues.

For both, it’s important to test and see how the system reacts to adjust.

Values are set in the [main.tf](http://main.tf) file of the adapter.

## Dashboard

The dashboard is located [here](https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/awt-3cz-2ui/integrations-system-metrics?fromUser=false&refresh_mode=sliding&view=spans&from_ts=1715007424425&to_ts=1715011024425&live=true).

You can select your integration on top. It has to be live in production to display values (can be darklaunch).

<aside>
💡 When reading values, the timestamp windows has to be 1h (or less). If you are reading values from the past month, it’ll erase the outliers.

Example :
From the past month, you can read memory has a max of 800M, so you set up the memory to 1000M.
Because you have an average with a time window of a month, you can miss that regurlarly the memory goes up to 1200M and so you’ll have a lot of Out Of Memory.

</aside>

## CPU

There are 3 dashboards that you have to read :

- CPU usage - Max over all pods
- CPU usage - Average over all pods
- Replicas Running

The average will help you define what the cpu_request should be (as a first attempt)

The replicas running to see the impact of the CPU. You want a low steady number

The max to understand why the number of pods is going up

<aside>
💡 You don’t want to have a big cpu_request to have a low steady number of pods.
This has a money cost and it’ll be wasted resources. 
You want to test to find the lowest-ish value that will allow this.

</aside>

Change the cpu_request and see the result in production

<aside>
💡 cpu_limit has to be at 0, never put a different value here.

</aside>

Put lowest value for development env.

## Memory

For the memory, you want to avoid Out Of Memory issues (OOM) but as the same time, putting a high memory value will have a money and performance cost.

As long as the adapter is doing the import, take this into account because imports need more memory.

The dashboard to follow is Mem usage - Max by pod (yes max) and Restard counts.

If you see restarts, check the reason but OOM has a big change to be the issue.

The values to set are mem_request and mem_limit. 

<aside>
💡 Both mem_request and mem_limit have to have the exact same value.

</aside>

Put lowest value for development env but take care you don’t have OOM (even more true if the adapter does the import).

# Flow of an integration

## Glossary

- **Adapter**: An adapter is the code component that allows Busbud’s infrastructure to communicate with a 3rd party API or website to get information about departures, tickets, locations, etc.
- **Source**: A source is usually the partner Busbud has a contract with. It can be a bus company or an aggregator. It is possible that many sources can use the same adapter if they share the same backend infrastructure.
- **Operator**: An operator is the bus company that provides specific departures. A source can have multiple operators.
- **Location**: For Busbud, a location can be a city or a stop. It will depend on what the partner’s API provides. It is possible that both concepts are used. There are 2 methods where Busbud will expect locations and store them if they don’t exist, explicitly in `getRoutes` and implicitly in `getDepartures`. You can read more about both methods below and in the schemas.
- **Route**: The route between two locations. Whether the route will be between cities or stops will also depend on the partner’s API. The rule of thumb is that the route combination must contain the same location IDs that will be used for searching.

## Importing

Importing takes care of retrieving locations and routes data daily through [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes). These methods are called at the same time at the time of importing. It’s good to keep that in mind in case a partners API has a single call to get both routes and locations. It’s suggested to keep a cache of the single request in memory to later be parsed by [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes).

The core purpose for these methods is to keep an up to date cache of a partners active locations and routes. For example two [xid](/tsdocs/modules/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.html#xid) from [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) are used for a route in [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes), which gets passed as the [origin_xid](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_departure.departure.html#origin_xid) and [destination_xid](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_departure.departure.html#destination_xid) to [getDepartures](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getdepartures). Our consuming API keeps these cached in order to reduce time finding known locations, and prevent making useless searches to the partners API.

<aside>
💡 For partners who don’t have the ability to run supply known routes through [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes), we have a tool called Dora that will take all known locations from [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and make calls to [getDepartures](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getdepartures), marking a route as valid if departures are returned. We try to leave this as a last resort, but if you are stuck using it be sure to return an empty array in [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes) and disable its tests.

</aside>

# getDepartureDetails

This method has multiple responsibilities:

- Fetch additional details on a departure from our partner’s api (if they exist).
- Check the information for a departure hasn’t changed. This is really important as the `departure` param it is passed will likely come from cache, so even if `departure` contains all the info you need, you still have to make a fresh request to the api for the details.
- **Double-check** the information for a departure hasn’t changed. NAPI doesn’t just call this method when a user wants to see info on a departure, it also calls it just before trying to process a reservation (to double-check we have no price/availability changes).

Departures are cached by route, passengers counts, outbound date, and return date (which may or may not exist). This is important to remember when reasoning about what information you can reliably expect to find on a departure object.

## Example 1

Say you’re trying to track a user’s session from search -> booking, so you try to generate a unique id in `getDepartures` and store it in each result you return.

This approach will not work, as the departure passed to `getDepartureDetails` will probably come from cache instead of from a user’s search (we have millions of users and, more often than not, someone else will have searched for the same route, dates, and passengers quite recently).

The departure received by `getDepartureDetails` will therefore not contain an id unique to the user who requested the details.

## Example 2

Say a departure was returned from a search as the outbound half of a roundtrip, and you want to store the return date requested in the search on the departure.

You *can* store this info on a departure and count on it being correct when passed to `getDepartureDetails`, as the departure will only ever be returned from cache when a user searches for the same roundtrip with the same outbound and return dates.

# getRoundtripDetails

This is not called *instead of* `getDepartureDetails`, it is called *as well as* `getDepartureDetails` as seen in the roundtrip calls diagram.

Its first two params, `outbound_departure` and `return_departure`, are the result of calling `getDepartureDetails` on one departure each from the arrays returned by `getRoundtripDepartures`, and its third param, `roundtrip`, will be one of the objects from the `roundtrips` array.

NAPI will pass the same params, via the same process, both before a user requests to see details, *and* before a user attempts a reservation.

This is the only method in an integration that sometimes requires no partner API call.

# File structure

The [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) is a tool that creates a full integration directory with methods, imports, and basic error handling preset for you.

```
┌── Dockerfile
├── README.md
├── package.json
├── scratch
│   ├── index.ts
│   ├── scratch.ts
│   └── testgen.ts
├── src
│   ├── adapter
│   │   ├── api.ts
│   │   ├── index.ts
│   │   └── interfaces
│   │       ├── index.ts
│   │       ├── request.ts
│   │       └── response.ts
│   └── index.ts
├── test
│   └── index.ts
├── tsconfig.json
└── yarn.lock
```

The files that concern you the most live inside `src/adapter`.

**api.ts** is where all the logic for communicating with the partner API lives. It handles preparing the outbound request bodies, making the request, and converting the responses to something that can be easily processed, and then returning it to `index.ts`.

**interfaces/request.ts** is where your interfaces for your outbound requests to the partners API live.

**interfaces/response.ts** is where your interfaces for your responses from the partner API live.

**index.ts** is where the logic lives that calls the individual methods in `api.ts`, and converts the response data to Busbud formats.

# Throwing Errors

## Busbud Error vs Adapter API/HTTP Super Error

`src/adapter/api.ts` is the file from where we send requests to the partner’s API. This file should only throw API and HTTP SuperErrors. Example: **BlablacarHTTPError** or **BlablacarAPIError** for the Blablacar integration.

- An **AdapterHTTPError** should be used when a communication with the partner failed due to an HTTP problem (timeout, connection failure, DNS, etc).
- An **AdapterAPIError** should be used when the partner API returned an error state with a message we can decode and record.

`src/adapter/index.ts` is the file where the adapter’s methods are implemented. The methods should catch any error thrown by methods of `api.js` and throw a proper [BusbudError](https://github.com/busbud/busbud-errors) instead when it contains a comparable error type. Each adapter’s method signature is available in the [TypeScript docs](https://docs.busbud-int.com/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getdepartures) including a non-exhaustive list of BusbudErrors each method can throw.

# Writing an integration

Before jumping directly in to coding your integration, it’s best to evaluate the documentation from the partners API and plan for what methods they have the potential to support. For example, if they provide a bus layout, you’d want to include that while writing [getDepartureDetails](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getdeparturedetails). Or if you see they have the ability to reserve individual seats, you’d want to plan to include the [reserve](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#reserve) method.

The general way to write an integration from start it finish is to write the methods in order they are defined. Starting with the importer, then search, then booking.

**Steps:**

- Evaluate documentation.
- Consider the format of the partners API. JSON, XML, SOAP, etc.
- Consider what methods the partners API will be able to support.
- Run the [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) with `bb starterpack` to generate an integration folder with all the necessary dependencies and templating.
- Use the provided `scratch/scratch.ts` to start playing with adapter methods and get to coding!

Your scratch file is where you can develop and test against your integration. It comes pre-filled with all the available methods, and a place for your to pass your config to your adapter. It can then easily be executed with `ts-node ./scratch`.

You’ll find more details on the methods and their requirements in the [schema docs](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html).

# Testing an integration

While developing your integration, you need to write tests for each adapter method using our test framework to make sure the responses matches the schemas and catch common mistakes. Tests will ensure there’s no regression when modifying the integration later on.

The way we test an integration is by writing different test cases for each adapter method. A test case is made of two parts:

- A list of calls that are expected to be made to the partner website for which we match the URL and map a static response. We call those `fixpoints` (made-up word).
- A `parameters` object, that contains the parameters for the function call and the result fixture (what the method is expected to return).

## Generating tests from real calls

We provide a tool to generate test cases from real calls to the partner API. By utilizing the function calls you make in `scratch/scratch.ts`, it’ll log all the calls you make on the adapter, all the HTTP requests to the partner API, and write the responses and results to disk together with the parameters you used, in the format of our test framework.

Run `ts-node scratch/testgen.ts`, and it will create a `test` directory with all the required parameters and fixtures. Unfortunately sometimes the responses from partners API’s can be quite large (especially when related to locations or routes), and this isn’t something we wish to be committed in to git. It’s recommended to reduce the size of the response fixtures by hand so that the minimal amount of data is used in order to verify your tests work correctly.

## Linking generated tests

Then in your `test/index.ts` you can load those generated tests like:

```tsx
const { fixpoints, parameters } = bats.helpers.loadTests(__dirname);
```

This is just for a better understanding, the [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) is taking care of this for you already.

## Playing the integration tests from testgen

Basically, it just requires you to run `yarn test`. But as `testgen` creates tests using the scratch file and configuration, `test` command will use its own. So it’s possible to have some mismatches in the results by running `testgen` followed by `test` in a row.

Below are some explanations on how this works and how you may have to adapt some configuration in order to have `yarn test` result in a success.

### Index Configuration

The test folder of an integration has an entry point `/index.ts`. This file contains the configuration of the tests; such as the name of the source, the url (faked), and an instance of the adapter. A valid format of the `adapter_config` will have to be provided as it is the one that will be used when launching `yarn test`.

!!! note Depending on the parameters in your config, results may be different if the scratch config is different than the test folder’s `adapter_config`.

The suite_config also contains a field `disabled` that corresponds to a list of methods to be tested or not; remove the lines of the methods that are to be tested.

### Fixpoints Configuration

Each tested method will result in a test folder of its name, and will contain:

- the fixtures
- the parameters
- an `index.js` binding the parameters to the results.

Here are some explanations of configuration parameters, in case you need to update them:

- `response_code` when the API is expected to return another code than `200`, you can specify it here.
- `parameters.params` make a habit of using the previous tests results as entry parameters for the next tests instead of having a raw object here, in case testgen did not do it. For instance, for a `departure_details`, the `departure` parameter could be `departure: require('../departures_0/results.json')[0],`. Besides enhancing readability, it sometimes helps to avoid some characters escaping issues.
- `fat:true` can be set on the fixpoint level or in the result one.

!!! warning `fat: true` is to be used with caution! Only use it when the size is not too much above the limit and when reducing the response payload is complex for some reason.

### Add unit tests

You can create unit tests files if you want / need to in the test folder. As `test/index.js` is the entry point, you’ll just have to import it anywhere using `require('./unit-test-file');`. Then the tests contained in the required files will be played automatically along the integration tests.

# UDMv4 FAQ

All frequently asked questions for integrating supply with UDMv4

# General

## Why are my testgen-generated tests failing?

Your BATS config (ie your `suite_config`) in `test/index.ts` takes in an optional parameter called `adapter_version` . This defaults to v2. Set it to `v4` to run the test suite for v4

# UDMv4 Prices

## How many items should I have in my PriceGroupv4 array?

Similar to other UDM versions, a price group should represent a single bookable entity in the trip. In v4 terms, this means that you should only ever have one item in your PriceGroupv4 array being returned from the integration.

If you cannot book a roundtrip in one API call (ie need one set of calls for booking the outbound, and one set of calls for booking the return leg), you do not need to support roundtrips in your integration. Simply throw `BusbudErrors.NotImplemented()` when you see more than one LegSearchParam.

## What is a group option?

A group option is a group of potential ticket possibilities that the passengers can choose for their booking. Passengers must all choose one of their ticket options from the same group. In practice (in the integration), this usually means that each group option has a single `fare_xid` associated, and a trip can have multiple group options, one for each possible fare type.

## What is a ticket option?

A ticket option is a choice the passenger has for their purchase. For example they can either book a fancy, business class seat (one ticket option), or a economy seat with less leg room (another ticket option).

When there are multiple segments (ie buses) in the trip, the price of the ticket option is the combined price of the multiple segments, if the user chose all the corresponding classes in the ticket option’s `classes` mapping.

Note that different passengers can choose different respective ticket options within the same group option (one passenger can choose a business class seat, while their friend chooses an economy seat).

## How do I restrict my passengers so that they must choose the same class within the same segment?

Since every booking must select a single group option, you can restrict your passengers by creating multiple group options, one for each possible class.

### What happens if I have multiple segments and multiple classes?

Suppose you have 2 segments, each with classA and classB, with different respective prices per segment. If we create group options per above, we’d have one group option with `segment1: classA, segment2: classB` and another with `segment1: classB, segment2: classA`. However they’d both be represented in `groupOption.class_xids` as `[classA, classB]` . There is no identifiable difference for clients between these two group options. The integration is advised to discard these group options, and only return group options where the class between the segments are the same.

# Wallet Tickets

# How it works

If you want to generate wallet tickets for a booking, add a `ticket_fields` object to your [PassengerBooking](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/blob/a8e258e52d23651d060e47f463a286a3e75eee49/packages/integration-schemas/schemas/booking/book-response.d.ts). You’ll need to fill out the information that you want to display on the ticket as defined in the [TicketFields schema](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/blob/master/packages/integration-schemas/schemas/ticket-fields.ts). Hodor will then read that object and generate everything for you.

<aside>
❗ **Important!** You also need to update the source entry on Bookie’s and Grand Central’s database with the default `pkpass_template`:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE sources SET pkpass_template='default' WHERE id=<SOURCE_ID>;
COMMIT;
```

</aside>

# What to show on the tickets

## Already included

These are automatically included, so there’s no need to add them yourself:

- Passenger name
- Departure date
- Departure / arrival time
- Origin / destination cities
- Origin / destination station addresses (w/ maps links)
- Purchase ID
- Link to PDF ticket
- Link to full T&Cs
- Link to help page

## Defined fields

We’ve included support for the most common fields (e.g. seat #, booking reference, etc.) in the [TicketFields schema](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/blob/master/packages/integration-schemas/schemas/ticket_fields.d.ts). All fields are optional, it’s up to you to determine which ones need to appear on the ticket. Take a look at what’s on the PDF ticket, put yourself in the customer’s shoes and ask yourself which info is necessary. Space on the tickets is limited, so fields may overflow to the back (they’ll still be available by tapping **···**, but they’ll be harder to find).

<aside>
⚠️

Make sure that the price matches the one on the PDF ticket. Careful, operators may behave differently when it comes to including taxes and/or fees.

</aside>

## Barcode

Probably the most important feature of wallet tickets. Apple Wallet supports 4 different formats: QR, Aztec, PDF417, and Code128.

<aside>
⚠️ Please be extra thoughtful when choosing what goes in `barcode.alt_text`. It will be displayed just under the barcode itself, so it needs to be relevant to the customer in that context. Look at what the operator shows on their own tickets.

</aside>

```jsx
{
  barcode: {
    format: 'qr',
    message: ticket.barCode,
    alt_text: `${ticket.carrierCode}${ticket.scheduleNumber}`
  }
}
```
