# Writing an Integration

# Introduction

The guide gives you all the information to setup yourself up for integrations. This includes making sure your local system is configured correctly, how write, test, deploy, and maintain your integrations.

The goal of an integration is to convert data to and from a bus partners API in order to complete searches and bookings of bus tickets in a single format. Writing an integration involves converting the locations, routes, search results, and booking data, fitting it in the predefined methods for consuming APIs to call. The biggest consumer is of course [Busbud.com](https://busbud.com/), where users can easily search, discover, and book bus tickets across the planet.

# Adapter lifecycle (from Deal to Live)

1. A deal is signed.
2. [Documentation needs to be reviewed](docs-review.md).
3. It is prioritized in the sprint. Its complexity estimated based on the doc review.
4. Development starts. It usually takes 1 or 2 weeks of dev time + variable time you spent blocked, waiting for information from the partner.
5. PR is reviewed. It usually takes a couple of more days.
6. Adapter is [deployed in darklaunch mode](deployment.md).
7. Adapter is tested using [our QA guidelines](qa.md) to ensure it works.
8. Finally, we switch the adapter to active in BusPlatform.

# Flow of an integration

An integration has several functions that can be read about in the [schema documentation](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html). These docs however will explain the flow of calls made depending on the user interaction on the frontend and the processing on our consuming API’s backend, and find links to the specific method, parameters, and response docs generated from our Typescript interfaces. They contain plenty of information specific to each method and variable. You’ll also find links to videos on how each method interacts with users on [Busbud.com](https://busbud.com/).

You’ll notice that not all methods are required as some partner APIs do not support all the features available, but should be written if the partners API supports it.

We split up an integration in to three different “flows”, you’ll find a quick overview of where each function falls under which flow. You’ll read more about these functions and flows later in the docs!

**Import:**

- [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations)
- [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes)

**Search:**

- [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips)
- [getSegmentStops](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getsegmentstops)
- [getPrices](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getprices)
- [getVehicleLayout](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getvehiclelayout)
- [getTripDetails](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettripdetails)

**Book:**

- [selectTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#selecttrip)
- [reserveTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#reservetrip)
- [releaseTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#releasetrip)
- [bookTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#booktrip)
- [cancelTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#canceltrip)
- [getTickets](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#gettickets)

# Glossary

- **Adapter**: An adapter is the code component that allows Busbud’s infrastructure to communicate with a 3rd party API or website to get information about departures, tickets, locations, etc.
- **Source**: A source is usually the partner Busbud has a contract with. It can be a bus company or an aggregator. It is possible that many sources can use the same adapter if they share the same backend infrastructure.
- **Operator**: An operator is the bus company that provides specific departures. A source can have multiple operators.
- **Location**: For Busbud, a location can be a city or a stop. It will depend on what the partner’s API provides. It is possible that both concepts are used. There are 2 methods where Busbud will expect locations and store them if they don’t exist, explicitly in `getRoutes` and implicitly in `getTrips`. You can read more about both methods below and in the schemas.
- **Route**: The route between two locations. Whether the route will be between cities or stops will also depend on the partner’s API. The rule of thumb is that the route combination must contain the same location IDs that will be used for searching.
- **Trip**: The composition of all data for a user’s journey, from point A to point B (and possibly back), including full pricing context, regardless of supplier. A Trip is composed of one or more Segments, one or more Trip Legs, and one or more Price Groups.
- **Trip Leg**: A set of references to trip segments, that when put together represent a logical “part” of a trip (usually outbound vs return).
- **Trip Segment**: One continuous journey in a (bus | train | whatever), from point A to point B, with no transfers in between.
- **Price Group**: Price details for a set of segments that must be booked together. Includes single trip legs with transfers (and so are represented as multiple trip segments) or “roundtrips”.

# Importing

Importing takes care of retrieving locations and routes data daily through [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes). These methods are called at the same time at the time of importing. It’s good to keep that in mind in case a partners API has a single call to get both routes and locations. It’s suggested to keep a cache of the single request in memory to later be parsed by [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes).

The core purpose for these methods is to keep an up to date cache of a partners active locations and routes. For example two [xid](/tsdocs/modules/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.html#xid) from [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) are used for a route in [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes), which gets passed as the [origin_xid](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_schemas_search_get_trips_request.segmentsearchparams.html#origin_xid) and [destination_xid](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_schemas_search_get_trips_request.segmentsearchparams.html#destination_xid) to [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips) search params. Our consuming API keeps these cached in order to reduce time finding known locations, and prevent making useless searches to the partners API.

<aside>
💡 For partners who don’t have the ability to run supply known routes through [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes), we have a tool called **Dora** that will take all known locations from [getLocations](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getlocations) and make calls to [getDepartures], marking a route as valid if departures are returned. We try to leave this as a last resort, but if you are stuck using it be sure to return an empty array in [getRoutes](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getroutes) and disable its tests.

</aside>

# Search

The [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips) method is responsible for searching the partner’s API inventory for a given day on a given route and for a given number of passengers. It will return a Trip for each possible distinct trip combination available.

When a user is searching for a one-way departure (origin to destination on a single date), the [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips) method will return trips that have only one trip leg, one segment (or set of segments) that correspond to the outbound leg of the trip, and one price group representing the one-way trip leg. In the case of a roundtrip, this is doubled: there are two trip legs returned, each containing segment XIDs pointing to the segments that make up the outbound and return trip legs respectively. This is one of the reasons why getTrips can return multiple trip legs, segments and price groups.

How do we distinguish what is a one-way trip search and what is a roundtrip (or open-jaw) trip search in [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips)? The method takes an array of LegSearchParam. One-ways will only receive one LegSearchParam here, whereas roundtrips will receive two. Always check that the origin of the first LegSearchParam is equal to the second LegSearchParam destination.

You may receive multiple LegSearchParam. The example can be the trips A>B B>C. If this is bookable in “1 call” with the supplier (so it’s one order/request/book), you should implement it (hence the origin/destination check for a roundtrip) if not, a NotImplemented exception should be raised.

Since there is an array of possible LegSearchParam, getTrips should be implemented in a way that it executes a search for every parameter received. It should return as many trips as there are combinations between the origin and destination. For a roundtrip, you may have multiple trips with the same 'way' to go to the destination but with different 'ways' to return to the origin.

## Roundtrips

A Price Group must represent all logical parts of a trip that **must be booked together at the same time and from the same supplier.** This distinction is important, as some suppliers support booking multiple legs of a trip at the same time as to benefit from “roundtrip” pricing. (In other places you’ll see this referred to as a “real roundtrip”.)

A partner API that supports this should therefore return roundtrip Trips with single Price Groups keyed to all relevant segments. If the partner’s API does not support this, and trip legs must instead be purchased and booked separately, our frontend still has the capability to represent this to the customer as a roundtrip. This is what we call a “fake roundtrip”: that is, a roundtrip with two logical, independent “one-way” trip legs that can be booked together on Busbud but separately registered on the partner API. In these cases, there must be separate Price Groups keyed to the segments of each individual trip leg. In your reservation, booking and tickets methods, you can then make as many partner API calls as you need to to coincide with the number of separate “orders” (number of Price Groups) you’re receiving, in effect.

The [getTrips](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettrips) will be called two times, one for each “one-way” 

# Trip Detail and Selection Methods

There are several methods that can be implemented to obtain more information about a trip after the initial trip search (analogous to a GET /trips/:id method in a RESTful API.)

- [**getSegmentStops**](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getsegmentstops) - responsible for asynchronously fetching a list of intermediate trip stops that occur along the segment journey. This is an optional method, only necessary if the partner’s API requires a separate call to obtain this list and it was not available on `getTrips`. Used to populate the segment’s `stops` property by the Busbud search APIs.
- [**getPrices**](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getprices) - responsible for asynchronously fetching the up-to-date price groups for a Trip. This is an optional method, only necessary if the partner’s API requires a separate call to confirm current prices for a single Trip.
- [**getVehicleLayout**](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getvehiclelayout) - responsible for asynchronously fetching the current seat layout for a Trip Segment. This is an optional method, only necessary if the partner’s API requires a separate call to get the seat layout information and it was not available on `getTrips`.
- [**getTripDetails**](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettripdetails) - in many cases, partner APIs will not have an endpoint to get more information about a specific Trip, OR will not have separate endpoints to do so (one to get prices and another to get the seat layout). In either of these cases, we can implement `getTripDetails` as a sort of “catch-all” method to refresh all possible details about a single Trip that is passed as a parameter in one go.
- [**selectTrip**](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#selecttrip) - called after selecting a Trip from the results page. This is an optional method. Some partners have additional logic that is required to “create a cart” on their API before progressing through the checkout process AND before reserving seats. If the partner API has this requirement, this method should be implemented.

The [getTripDetails](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettripdetails) method has multiple responsibilities:

- Fetch additional details on a Trip from our partner’s API (if they exist).
- Check that the information of a Trip or part of a Trip hasn’t changed. This is really important as the `trip` param will likely come from cache, so even if `trip` contains all the info you need, you still have to make a fresh request to the API for the details. Note that if a trip has multiple Legs (for example in a roundtrip), `getTripDetails` will be called multiple times: once for each Leg, then once for the entire Trip. You should implement the `getTripDetails` method with that in mind.
- **Double-check** the information for a Trip hasn’t changed. Busbud doesn’t just call this method when a user wants to see info on a Trip, it also calls it just before trying to process a reservation (to double-check we have no price/availability changes) if [selectTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#selecttrip) is not implemented.

Departures are cached by route, passengers counts, outbound date, and return date (which may or may not exist). This is important to remember when reasoning about what information you can reliably expect to find on a departure object.

## Example 1

Say you’re trying to track a user’s session from search -> booking, so you try to generate a unique ID in `getTrips` and store it in each result you return.

This approach will not work, as the trip passed to `getTripDetails` will probably come from cache instead of from a user’s search (we have millions of users and, more often than not, someone else will have searched for the same route, dates, and passengers quite recently).

The trip received by `getTripDetails` will therefore not contain an ID unique to the user who requested the details.

## Example 2

Say a trip was returned from a search as the outbound half of a roundtrip, and you want to store the return date requested in the search on the departure.

You *can* store this info on a trip and count on it being correct when passed to `getTripDetails`, as the trip will only ever be returned from cache when a user searches for the same roundtrip with the same outbound and return dates.

# File structure

The [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) is a tool that creates a full integration directory with methods, imports, and basic error handling preset for you.

```
┌── Dockerfile
├── README.md
├── package.json
├── scratch
│   ├── index.ts
│   ├── scratch.ts
│   └── testgen.ts
├── src
│   ├── adapter
│   │   ├── api.ts
│   │   ├── index.ts
│   │   └── interfaces
│   │       ├── index.ts
│   │       ├── request.ts
│   │       └── response.ts
│   └── index.ts
├── test
│   └── index.ts
├── tsconfig.json
└── yarn.lock
```

The files that concern you the most live inside `src/adapter`.

**api.ts** is where all the logic for communicating with the partner API lives. It handles preparing the outbound request bodies, making the request, and converting the responses to something that can be easily processed, and then returning it to `index.ts`.

**interfaces/request.ts** is where your interfaces for your outbound requests to the partners API live.

**interfaces/response.ts** is where your interfaces for your responses from the partner API live.

**index.ts** is where the logic lives that calls the individual methods in `api.ts`, and converts the response data to Busbud formats.

# Throwing Errors

## Busbud Error vs Adapter API/HTTP Super Error

`src/adapter/api.ts` is the file from where we send requests to the partner’s API. This file should only throw API and HTTP SuperErrors. Example: **BlablacarHTTPError** or **BlablacarAPIError** for the Blablacar integration.

- An **AdapterHTTPError** should be used when a communication with the partner failed due to an HTTP problem (timeout, connection failure, DNS, etc).
- An **AdapterAPIError** should be used when the partner API returned an error state with a message we can decode and record.

`src/adapter/index.ts` is the file where the adapter’s methods are implemented. The methods should catch any error thrown by methods of `api.ts` and throw a proper [BusbudError](https://github.com/busbud/busbud-errors) instead when it contains a comparable error type. Each adapter’s method signature is available in the [TypeScript docs](https://docs.busbud-int.com/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html#getdepartures) including a non-exhaustive list of BusbudErrors each method can throw.

# Writing an integration

Before jumping directly in to coding your integration, it’s best to evaluate the documentation from the partners API and plan for what methods they have the potential to support. For example, if they provide a bus layout, you’d want to include that while writing [getVehicleLayout](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#getvehiclelayout) or [getTripDetails](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.searchadapter.html#gettripdetails). Or if you see they have the ability to reserve individual seats, you’d want to plan to include the [reserveTrip](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_udm_adapter.bookingadapter.html#reservetrip) method.

The general way to write an integration from start it finish is to write the methods in order they are defined. Starting with the importer, then search, then booking.

**Steps:**

- Evaluate documentation.
- Consider the format of the partners API. JSON, XML, SOAP, etc.
- Consider what methods the partners API will be able to support.
- Run the [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) with `bb starterpack` to generate an integration folder with all the necessary dependencies and templating.
- Use the provided `scratch/scratch.ts` to start playing with adapter methods and get to coding!

Your scratch file is where you can develop and test against your integration. It comes pre-filled with all the available methods, and a place for your to pass your config to your adapter. It can then easily be executed with `ts-node ./scratch`.

You’ll find more details on the methods and their requirements in the [schema docs](/tsdocs/interfaces/_busbud_int_schemas_schemas_adapter.genericadapter.html).

# Testing an integration

While developing your integration, you need to write tests for each adapter method using our test framework to make sure the responses matches the schemas and catch common mistakes. Tests will ensure there’s no regression when modifying the integration later on.

The way we test an integration is by writing different test cases for each adapter method. A test case is made of two parts:

- A list of calls that are expected to be made to the partner website for which we match the URL and map a static response. We call those `fixpoints` (made-up word).
- A `parameters` object, that contains the parameters for the function call and the result fixture (what the method is expected to return).

## Generating tests from real calls

We provide a tool to generate test cases from real calls to the partner API. By utilizing the function calls you make in `scratch/scratch.ts`, it’ll log all the calls you make on the adapter, all the HTTP requests to the partner API, and write the responses and results to disk together with the parameters you used, in the format of our test framework.

Run `ts-node scratch/testgen.ts`, and it will create a `test` directory with all the required parameters and fixtures. Unfortunately sometimes the responses from partners API’s can be quite large (especially when related to locations or routes), and this isn’t something we wish to be committed in to git. It’s recommended to reduce the size of the response fixtures by hand so that the minimal amount of data is used in order to verify your tests work correctly.

## Linking generated tests

Then in your `test/index.ts` you can load those generated tests like:

```tsx
const { fixpoints, parameters } = bats.helpers.loadTests(__dirname);
```

This is just for a better understanding, the [starterpack](/busbud-modules.md#starterpack) is taking care of this for you already.

## Playing the integration tests from testgen

Basically, it just requires you to run `yarn test`. But as `testgen` creates tests using the scratch file and configuration, `test` command will use its own. So it’s possible to have some mismatches in the results by running `testgen` followed by `test` in a row.

Below are some explanations on how this works and how you may have to adapt some configuration in order to have `yarn test` result in a success.

### Index Configuration

The test folder of an integration has an entry point `/index.ts`. This file contains the configuration of the tests; such as the name of the source, the url (faked), and an instance of the adapter. A valid format of the `adapter_config` will have to be provided as it is the one that will be used when launching `yarn test`.

<aside>
💡 Depending on the parameters in your config, results may be different if the scratch config is different than the test folder’s `adapter_config`.

</aside>

The suite_config also contains a field `disabled` that corresponds to a list of methods to be tested or not; remove the lines of the methods that are to be tested.

### Fixpoints Configuration

Each tested method will result in a test folder of its name, and will contain:

- the fixtures
- the parameters
- an `index.js` binding the parameters to the results.

Here are some explanations of configuration parameters, in case you need to update them:

- `response_code` when the API is expected to return another code than `200`, you can specify it here.
- `parameters.params` make a habit of using the previous tests results as entry parameters for the next tests instead of having a raw object here, in case testgen did not do it. For instance, for a `departure_details`, the `departure` parameter could be `departure: require('../departures_0/results.json')[0],`. Besides enhancing readability, it sometimes helps to avoid some characters escaping issues.
- `fat:true` can be set on the fixpoint level or in the result one.

<aside>
⚠️ `fat: true` is to be used with caution! Only use it when the size is not too much above the limit and when reducing the response payload is complex for some reason.

</aside>

### Add unit tests

You can create unit tests files if you want / need to in the test folder. As `test/index.js` is the entry point, you’ll just have to import it anywhere using `require('./unit-test-file');`. Then the tests contained in the required files will be played automatically along the integration tests.

# Building an integration

## Dockerfiles

When deploying an integration as the [deployment docs](deployment.md) instruct, bb will package it up into a Docker container, upload and reference this in a new Kubernetes deployment that will expose it to our search and booking services. bb is configured to do this all on its own, and by default an integration doesn’t need a Dockerfile in its directory to do this.

In some cases however, you will need to include special steps or extra dependencies when the Docker container is being built so that everything will install properly. An example of this is for an integration that requires image manipulation libraries in order to generate its ticket files: you may need some special system libraries installed so that Node can reference them when installing a given NPM package. In these cases, you can include a Dockerfile manually in your integration folder, and it will be picked up and used by bb when making new deployments.

There are two ways to do this:

1. if you only need to specify extra system dependencies, you can write a Dockerfile stub ([example](https://github.com/busbud/integrations/blob/87488312d7b3c6fe29e976a7ea83c733455874e3/transdevnew/Dockerfile)). The steps included in this stub will run at the end of the build process but before dependencies are copied into the final runtime image. Don’t forget to use that `# syntax` line up top as it is required to tell Buildkit that this is to be included on top of our default builder/runtime.
2. if your steps are a bit more complicated, you can still [write a Dockerfile from scratch](https://github.com/busbud/integrations/blob/87488312d7b3c6fe29e976a7ea83c733455874e3/peterpan/Dockerfile) and avoid using the default builder/runtime altogether; bb will see that a Dockerfile is present and use that to build instead.

# Fraud and Chargebacks

# Overview

The gist of the fraud protection challenge is:

> Prevent fraudulent transactions from going through, without blocking legitimate ones.
> 

The tricky part is to correctly distinct fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. To do so, we delegate the work to a partner.

We did an open-mic on Fraud at Busbud on May 2020:

- [Video of the talk](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-5Wkcmy65tgnXAKtI7w9DYo_G6vQ-jZ_/view)
- [Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1uT6bEPJVI5FU23QtVOQPAffunpsieKzfqnLXo60GfAo/edit?ts=5ecc21c6#slide=id.g84bb484a22_0_10)

Today, our sole Fraud Risk Assessment Provider (FRAP) is [Forter](https://www.forter.com/).

# How Forter derisks our transactions

When users click “Pay” they start the purchase process. One of the steps is `derisk`: this is when we ask Forter what they think about this transaction.

To do so, we send them a maximum of data points about this transaction. These include:

1. **Transaction details** like departure information, purchaser email, payment method, credit card details, and many more…
2. **User behaviour** like the pages they visited, how long did they take to click, etc. We have installed a Forter script on our website/app so they can track every action taken by the user. They identify the user with an ID and we send this ID during the transaction so they can determine what the user did before

We send all of this to Forter `Validate` API and they reply with a decision. They typically have 3 decisions:

1. **Approve** which means they think this transaction is legit. In this case, we proceed to the next step of the purchase process.
2. **Decline** which means they think this transaction is fraudulent. In this case, we fail the purchase process because it’s likely a fraudster.
3. **Not Reviewed** which means they can’t evaluate this transaction. We call that state `challenged` and we fail the purchase because it can’t be derisked. This should not happen anymore now that Forter has been calibrated though. If it does, we need to get it sorted with Forter.

Finally, in case of a chargeback (= someone claimed this transaction was fraudulent), we tell Forter about it using their `Claims` API, so they can improve their system.

Overall, Forter does a great job at detecting actual fraudsters from legitimate users.

👉 [Read more about Forter in their docs](https://portal.forter.com/overview/introduction) (you need access to their portal)

Use [lt-reporting/tree/master/reports/2019-09-fraud](https://github.com/busbud/lt-reporting/tree/master/reports/2019-09-fraud) to generate fraud reports.

## Derisking our pre-authorized transactions

Ideally we want all transactions to be post-authorized before sending them to Forter to derisk. Transactions that are post-authorized have been approved by the bank and we get transaction-related details from them, such as card details, and this information is sent to Forter.

Another thing about derisk is that we want to do it before we capture the money. In the case of manual capture flow, we derisk a transaction after it is authorized and before it is captured.

For payments that use immediate capture flow, the transactions are authorized and captured at the same time. In other words, we don’t do those operations in two separate steps. These are called pre-authorized transactions because we derisk them before we make a request to a bank. And we derisk these transactions without providing transaction-related details to Forter as we don’t have them at that point.

# Trying out new partners

We have changed our FRAP a couple of times in our history.

To make the process easier, we’ve set up the machinery to make it easy to add a new partner in our system.

We can even use that machinery to have multiple partners running in parallel. This can be useful if it turns out a partner would work better in some specific conditions (e.g. an expert in Brazil fraud).

If the partner is being tested but we don’t use their decisions, we create them as “passive handlers”. If they have a say in the final decision, we create them as “deciders”. All deciders are composed in a `CompositeDeriskHandler` that will consolidate all decisions.

Because we may have multiple FRAPs running, we need to take a final decision. To identify it, we use the `is_final_decision` attribute in the `fraud_risk_decisions` we store.

## Multiple deciders

Roughly what we do is to ask to all partners to derisk a transaction. Then, based on all responses, we take a final decision. These decisions are all stored in our `fraud_derisk_decisions` table.

Here’s an example with Sift and Forter being both deciders. We have the freedom to compute a final decision based on both of their responses:

![Example with Sift and Forter being deciders](Fraud%20and%20Chargebacks/fraud-multiple-handlers.png)

Example with Sift and Forter being deciders

## Passive handlers

Finally, we have the notion of “passive handlers”.

These are partners to which we ask to derisk, but we don’t wait nor use their actual answer. We simply record it so we can compare with the partners we trust. It’s handy when we’re integrating a brand new partner and they need some time to calibrate their answers.

Here’s an example with *Forter* being a passive handler while *Sift Science* is the decider. Notice how we `capture()` the money right after Sift decision:

# Chargebacks

When a customer issues a chargeback to dispute a Busbud transaction on their credit card, two main things happen on our side:

- We want to be aware of this event, save relevant info about it, and notify our fraud assessment providers (Sift Science) about it to block further transaction attempts from this person.
- We send information about the transaction to Chargehound to auto-dispute this chargeback in order to mitigate some of the money loss due to fraud.

Both of these things are managed in the same project: [chargeback-reporting](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting)

## Reporting

We have one small chargeback reporting “integration” or “adapter” per payment system we use.

There used to be a lot more in the past (stripe, braintree…) but as of the time of writing, only the following are still used:

- Adyen
- dLocal

The different adapters and how they work are well documented in the project [README](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting#chargeback-reporting).

The job of these adapters is to interpret the data we receive from the payment system, build out and then send a payload suitable for Bookie’s /[chargebacks](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/routes/chargebacks/index.js#L29) endpoint.

The rest of the logic is implemented inside Bookie:

1. Saving the chargeback info to the database
2. Notifying our fraud partners about this chargeback

## Disputing (Chargehound)

We use [Chargehound](https://www.chargehound.com/) to automatically dispute chargebacks to reduce our losses. It only works with Adyen.

Our integration is [here](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting/blob/master/src/adapters/chargehound.js) and rather straightforward:

- Chargehound sends us a notification about a new chargeback event.
- We fetch Purchase data from Bookie related to this chargeback.
- We also fetch email events saved in Il Postino related to the purchase to prove that the customer opened and/or generated click events inside the Ticket confirmation email that we sent him.
- We build out the payload of information that Chargehound expects to be able to dispute.
- We send the information to Chargehound.

Additionally, the integration sends small event payloads to Sift Science to notify them about chargeback/dispute states:

- Chargeback Disputed (i.e. we dispute it via Chargehound)
- Chargeback Won (Chargehound tells us we won a dispute)
- Chargeback Lost (Chargehound tells us we lost a dispute)

We win 15-30% of chargebacks with Chargehound.

## The cost of chargebacks

When we receive a chargeback, we **loose** this amount of money:

```
GMV - Revenue + Chargeback fee
```

Revenue is typically commission + busbud fee. It’s stored under the `commission_cad` column in `an_purchases` table of ADB.

### Chargeback fees per payment provider

- D-local = 15 USD
- Checkout = 15 GBP
- Adyen = 12.50 USD

### We lose all of the GMV in the case of chargebacks

Why can’t we say to suppliers ‘sorry, chargeback!’?

We’re liable for what we sell on our website. If we sell something to a fraudster the operator doesn’t legally care, they still sold something and are owed money (especially that we’ll probably receive the chargeback after the departure date).

We could try to cancel the tickets though if it’s in the future, but we don’t do it today.

# History

[Payments and Fraud prevention](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HMAtVIEJ8NzaZNwbzr5f0CYkciZr7H6w5J-_NomjKrg) outlines the historical vision of Busbud on payments (back in 2017).

## Riskified (until 2017)

Riskified, a provider we had previously used a request/callback pattern, requiring the availability of a callback endpoint. Until that endpoint was called with the appropriate decision data, the step would implement a spin/wait pattern with a timeout. Once the decision was received, or the timeout reached, the step would be marked as complete and the decision saved to the `fraud_risk_decisions` table.

[We decided to move to Sift Science](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EJzdDNzVb-80uHD6C909otlePLHdlCvG5K4PmFYn6qY) in 2017 to reduce cost, as Sift’s model was pay per use.

## Sift Science (2017-2020)

Sift provides their decision in a request/response pattern, so it is obtained in the response of the call made to their API within a matter of milliseconds.

[We decided to move to Forter](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/issues/8950) in 2020 because Sift wasn’t performant enough in some countries like Brazil, or during events like COVID-19 lockdown.

Furthermore, Sift’s model required us to do a lot of manual work on top of their algorithm.

- [2019-08-11 Sift score analysis](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1_rjxWGi9pRDV3RLwCz8BAj4b9j-ArPbwB_3leW8xPU0)

### Renew the Merchant Identity certificate

This process is involves updating certificates on Apple's website, and Pubweb. Adyen is not involved. Note that you must
be using MacOS in order to complete the following steps.

**1. Create a new certificate**

Go in the [Busbud Adyen Prod](https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/identifiers/merchant/edit/S87US2RY79/merchant.com.adyen.Busbud) merchant ID page.

Here, click on **Create Certificate** for the *Apple Pay Merchant Identity Certificate*. [Follow the instructions from Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/account/create-certificates/create-a-certificate-signing-request) to learn how to create a certificate (it involves your keychain). As you generate the certificate, you can use the following details:

- Email: Use your Busbud email.
- Name: `Busbud`

Upload the certificate signing request file and download the generated certificate. Once saved to disk, double-click the CER file to import it in to your Apple Keychain.

**2. Generate a pem from the certificate**

1. In Apply Keychain, click on the "My Certificates".
2. In the search box in the top right corner, type in `adyen`
3. You should have a single certificate show up. Click on the little drop down toggle on the left side.
4. Right click on the `Busbud` entry, and click export.

![merchant-renewal-1.png](Payment%20Methods/merchant-renewal-1.png)

1. Export the key as `.p12` file.

![merchant-renewal-2.png](Payment%20Methods/merchant-renewal-2.png)

1. Use the following command to convert the `.p12` file to a `.pem` file.

```bash
openssl pkcs12 -in merchant.p12 -out apple-pay-cert.pem -nodes -clcerts -legacy
```

**3. Update Apple Pay certificate on Pubweb**

In Vault, look for the `APPLE_PAY_MERCHANT_CERT` env variable on Pubweb Prod.

Open your `.pem` file and copy its content. Update the value of the certificate in Vault. Remember to do it for both US, EU and BR. Store the most recent value that you are overwriting as a `BACKUP_` config var.

Finally, [deploy the config vars changes you did on Pubweb](https://docs.busbud-int.com/pubweb/Deployments/).

# Adding a New Payment Method

At the time of writing the only payment provider that allow us to add payment methods is Adyen thus the following guide is specific to Adyen.
If you're looking to add a payment method that is not provided by Adyen it's highly likely that you need to make a direct integration which starts by [adding the payment provider](notion://www.notion.so/payments/for-devs/new-payment-provider)

### 1. Add a gateway or modify the current one

Payment methods vary upon the billed currency and possibly the billing country.

If you want to enable a payment method that is available for PLN, we'll need to [get Adyen's payment methods](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/components/cart/application/service/get-adyen-payment-methods.ts#L37) with the right params

```jsx
{
  amount: { currency: 'PLN', value: 1959 },
  channel: 'Web',
  countryCode: 'PL',
  merchantAccount: 'BusbudEurope',
  shopperLocale: 'en-us',
  splitCardFundingSources: false
}
```

The currency we send, references the `currency` property of the selected gateway. This means that if we are using a generic european gateway to process european countries, we'll be sending EUR and thus we won't get the payment methods we want.

So the first step is to check if our current gateway complies the payment method constraints. If not we can add a new one, just for Polish people in this case. See [Adding a new Gateway](notion://www.notion.so/thebusbudgroup/new-gateway.md)

If you using an exisiting gateway, what you're missing only is to push the payment method to `gateways.payment_types`

### 2. Enable the payment method in Adyen

1. Login to [Adyen's dashboard](https://ca-test.adyen.com/ca/).
2. Navigate to Settings -> Payment methods
3. Select the Merchant Account you'll enable the method for

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5630976/155442487-32aa586d-4705-4da5-b474-713186eb0900.png)

1. Click on "Request payment method"

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5630976/155442519-e85c701d-ecbb-4bea-9ad9-f31e1f3ee9fc.png)

1. Search your payment method and hit submit

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5630976/155442497-0b699269-61b3-4f79-91af-034345f47139.png)

1. Verify it's been added by going to Settings -> Checkout settings and select a shopper country

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5630976/155442539-c864f41f-fbe1-4c1c-a75e-3f3d0fc10a4f.png)

<aside>
💡 **Going live -** For the live environment, the request doesn't get approved instantaneously. Requesting a payment method will open a ticket and they might ask us as few questions about our integration. It can take up to two business days.

</aside>

### 3. Map the payment method

Internally, we use different identifiers for payment methods than the ones provided by Adyen.

e.g. Adyen refers to Google Pay as `paywithgoogle` and we refer to it as `google-pay`

Thus, we need to map what we get to from Adyen and what we send to Adyen, this includes pubweb.

<aside>
💡 We are the ones who pick the internal identifiers, and sometimes they match Adyen's. There's no rule other than keeping a consistent naming strategy internally
On bookie, the starting point is [`DbModels.PaymentType`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/types/db-models.d.ts#L975-L983). After adding
the payment type, Typescript will guide you to update the rest, or most of them.

</aside>

Then we need to update some constants that classify payment methods by behavior

- [`isRedirectionPaymentMethod`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ccf53bbc1ddef20c5089b8401a36a7a6cb02b0b5/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/adyen-platform/helpers.js#L225-L234): add the payment type to this array if the payment is done in an external website
- [`isActionPaymentMethod`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ccf53bbc1ddef20c5089b8401a36a7a6cb02b0b5/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/adyen-platform/helpers.js#L240-L249): add the payment type to this array if the payment requires additional user action (like QR code scanning) without leaving [busbud.com](http://busbud.com/)
- [`isImmediatePaymentMethod`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ccf53bbc1ddef20c5089b8401a36a7a6cb02b0b5/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/adyen-platform/helpers.js#L256-L258): add the payment type to this array if the payment method does not support separate captures
- [`allowsChargebacks`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/f6af73622dc2c107d42f0b0d9a54adf540c2b9e8/apps/bookie/components/payments/domain/model/payment-method.ts#L37-L45): add the payment type to this array if the payment method does not allow chargebacks

<aside>
💡 Answers to these questions can be found in Adyens docs for the speific payment method [https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/mb-way](https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/mb-way)

</aside>

Examples of payment method additions:

https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9581
https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10360/files

### 4. Add a switch

We use an environment variable per payment method to allow enabling / disabling them, except for credit cards. This
allows us to quickly disable payment methods if they don't perform as expected.

In order to do this, we filter the payment methods we receive from Adyen to keep only the ones enabled and available for the selected gateway (`gateways.payment_types`).

So now we can enable or disable the payment method, that's cool, but probably you want to do a progressive rollout and measure it's performance before adopting it. You can refer to [this example](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9581/files#diff-578e22d557c0a181fd7740151e0c08776d047ee9e771ffc1ea82bc3f74fc2a7c) on how to enable a payment method based on a XP.
The logic is quite simple, if the user is under the XP return the new payment method, otherwise hide it. This is just one possible implementation, feel free to do it different of course.

### 5. Update pubweb

In pubweb we may also need to update the payment mapping.

- [`convertToNapiPaymentType`](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/c235f3e3b81c8d45fe8d05e5c763f419e6daea0e/app/modules/checkout/components/drop-in/drop-in.tsx#L436-L448): add mapping here if you've chosen a different internal name for the payment method than Adyen's
- [`no_billing_address_payment_types`](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/c235f3e3b81c8d45fe8d05e5c763f419e6daea0e/app/modules/checkout/hooks/use-dynamic-billing-address.ts#L3-L15): add the payment type here if the payment method does not allow chargebacks

### 6. Test it

Before deploying to production, there's a bit of QA you can do to anticipate issues. The test cases vary on the payment method type: some use redirection, some others a QR code, some support deferred capture, some others don't, some maybe be asynchronous (e.g. they get approved after 48hs).

I'd suggest you to identify the payment method and look for edge cases. But if I had to list a some basic test cases these would be:

1. A successful payment
2. A rejected payment. Adyen usually provides a way of emulating a rejection
3. A self-served cancellation. Check the transaction gets refunded
4. A purchase that fails at book. Check that the payment gets reversed, either voided or refunded.

Most reliable way of testing it is in preview because we have the adyen's notifications webhook already set up.
Still, you can set the webhook locally with `ngrok` to avoid deploying to preview

# Adyen

Adyen is a payment processor but also has the capacity to be “a middleman” (like Spreedly) in some markets where they do not yet process payments directly. This used to be the case for our NN payments in Turkey where they are acting as the middleman for Iyzico (as of Jan 2022, we’re no longer using Iyzico).

We have several different **merchant accounts** with Adyen, by market/region. In Bookie, multiple gateways may exist for a single Merchant Account. This is the case for our `BusbudEurope` account: one gateway for GBP + one for EUR processing.

We do not have a limitation about hitting Adyen’s test environments, unlike Spreedly. Hence, making a purchase through Adyen in Busbud Preview will work as expected, using Adyen’s infrastructure for sure.

## Adyen DropIn component

We’re using the [Adyen DropIn component](https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/cards/web-drop-in), allowing us to integrate new payment methods easily by delegating most of the work to them.

[List of supported payment methods by Adyen DropIn component](https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods#credit-and-debit-cards)

Here’s how the DropIn works:

![adyen-drop-in-workflow.png](Adyen/adyen-drop-in-workflow.png)

Adyen’s [asynchronous notifications](./notification-webhooks) are an important part of dealing with the status of payments.

## **Purchase process**

Adyen flow supports the following payment methods and they have been grouped into different types: direct, redirect, QR action and 3ds action.

| payment method | payment flow |
| --- | --- |
| sofort | redirect |
| klarna | redirect |
| iDeal | redirect |
| trustly | redirect |
| wechat | QR action |
| bancontact mobile | QR action |
| google pay | direct |
| apple pay | direct |
| 3ds 1.0 | redirect |
| 3ds 2.0 | 3ds |
| cards without 3ds | direct |

The description of each payment flow is as follows:

1. `redirect`: a payment method that redirects the user to the bank’s website to complete the payment. When a user opts to use a payment method of this type, the client (e.g. pubweb or mobile app) must provide a [return URL](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/74335126cbdc89ad37ffdd9592ff3c791186c1b5/app/modules/checkout/container/app.js#L1052) at purchase creation endpoint. This return URL is provided to the bank so that when the user finishes an authentication, the bank would use this URL to direct the user back to busbud/neredenereye. Likewise, bookie provides a redirect URL to the client so that [the client would know](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/74335126cbdc89ad37ffdd9592ff3c791186c1b5/app/modules/checkout/container/app.js#L1489-L1493) where to redirect the user.
2. `QR action`: a payment method where a user must be presented with a QR code in the drop-in SDK. The user scan the QR code and complete the payment through an app.
3. `3ds`: the user must authenticate themselves from within the drop-in SDK to complete the payment.
4. `direct`: this is the most basic flow as it doesn’t require any input from the user.

## Support

We have [a good Datadog](https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/xs5-vs5-ctm/adyen) to track Adyen payment-related events, per `MerchantAccount`. Adyen’s console also has a lot of interesting graphs and data.

Our points of contact are our assigned Account Manager, and just [support@adyen.com](mailto:support@adyen.com) for any technical question. Adyen Support is usually pretty good.

## Webhook Notifications

Adyen’s [asynchronous notifications](https://docs.adyen.com/development-resources/notifications#page-introduction) are an important part of dealing with the status of payments.

### How it works

Here's the high-level schema of how it's implemented in Bookie:

![adyen-notifications.png](Adyen/adyen-notifications.png)

👉 [Inaccurate? Here's the source to update!](https://app.diagrams.net/#G17UYXAqBviRI_4ELsZRegWOrGPKuoGf40)

Adyen sends notifications to our system for various reason:

- authorizations
- captures
- refunds
- chargebacks
- reports available
- etc.

We should configure what Adyen can send us on our **Account > Server Communication**. For example, for or *BusbudCanada* account: [https://ca-live.adyen.com/ca/ca/config/showthirdparty.shtml](https://ca-live.adyen.com/ca/ca/config/showthirdparty.shtml)

We have a dedicated endpoint on Bookie for most of these: [`/webhooks/adyen`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/8ddf4c64c10968d3bfcbb76af17599c86eba4518/apps/bookie/routes/webhooks/adyen.ts#L26).

The only Adyen call that synchronously returns the result of the call is `AUTHORIZE` (via calls to `/payments` and `/payment/details` when necessary). For the rest, we should rather trust the notification they send us.

<aside>
💡 **Chargebacks are processed elsewhere.** We don't process the chargebacks notifications here because there's a dedicated application for that: [https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting)

</aside>

### Processing the notifications

First, we log all the notifications we receive into GCS.

Then, we filter the notification types we want to keep/act on and ignore the rest. The endpoint adds the notifications we handle to the `adyen_notifications` queue for actual processing.

We store each notification we process in the `adyen-notifications` table of Bookie DB. We also send them to Datadog under the `adyen.notification.received` event. You can find them in the [Adyen](https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/xs5-vs5-ctm/adyen) dashboard.

[There's a dedicated worker](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/8ddf4c64c10968d3bfcbb76af17599c86eba4518/apps/bookie/workers/adyen-notifications/run.js#L7) for consuming the messages in the queue. It uses our [Adyen Notification processors](https://github.com/busbud/napi/tree/master/apps/bookie/lib/payment-methods/adyen-platform/notification-processors) to process the nofication.

At this point, we mostly do a little bit of alerting and saving of a few `Transaction` properties. We could do more sophisticated things like retry attempts on `CAPTURE` failures for example.

<aside>
⚠️

**We don't handle everything well, yet!** There are different scenarios that we didn't anticipated in the codebase (e.g. we receive a successful authorization notification for a purchase that failed = we should refund). We listed these issues in [https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/7395](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/7395).

</aside>

### The case of CAPTURE and REFUND

Capture and Refund operations are a little particular with regards to notifications. They each have two different notification types that we can receive: `CAPTURE_FAILED` and `CAPTURE`:

- `CAPTURE_FAILED` always indicates failure, even though its contained `success` attribute will be `true`
- `CAPTURE` may indicate a success or failure depending on the `success` boolean attribute

### Security

Notifications are secured by:

1. HTTP Basic Auth that Adyen provides on every webhook call and
2. [HMAC signature verification](https://docs.adyen.com/development-resources/notifications/verify-hmac-signatures) on every notification.

# Spreedly

Spreedly is “the Busbud of payments” in the sense that they are an API middleman allowing merchants to connect to multiple different payment providers by having only a single technical API implementation.

<aside>
💡 **We can forward payments to Adyen through our Spreedly integration.**

</aside>

## Tokenization

Upon the user completing the Spreedly version of the Credit Card form in the Payment section of the Checkout, and the user subsequently submitting the form to confirm his purchase, the following happens:

1. Pubweb communicates with Spreedly directly to send the information entered by the user and to [receive a Token in return](https://docs.spreedly.com/reference/api/v1/#create-credit-card), representing this information. Information aren’t stored in logs on our side, but you can see activity on Spreedly if you need to debug
2. This Token is sent to Bookie from Pubweb as part of the `POST /:cart_id/purchase` call
3. This Token is saved in the Database (both Transaction and Purchase table) and used by Bookie to initiate payment-related calls to Spreedly (specifically the Authorize call)
4. Spreedly response to the Authorize contains another token representing the successful Authorization
5. Bookie continues the payment flow and uses the Authorization token to initiate the Capture call (i.e. Capture the money for this Authorization)
6. If a user submits the same form multiple times, without refreshing the page (for example after running into errors a couple times), the same initial token received by Spreedly is sent to Bookie. When Bookie receives this token multiple times, [there is some logic in place](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/8ddf4c64c10968d3bfcbb76af17599c86eba4518/apps/bookie/models/db/transactions.js#L299) to reuse successful authorization calls and to try to capture that one in retry attempts. This is to avoid freezing large amounts of money on users’ credit cards unnecessarily.

## Transaction Transcripts

These are particularly helpful when debugging Spreedly. They represent the activity that happens between Spreedly and the payment provider (e.g. dLocal).

Nowadays, this can be accessed by logging into the Spreedly web page and navigating to **Dashboard > Transactions**.

All transactions can be searched using the Spreedly token that represents the transaction (authorize operation, capture operation, etc.).

## How to rotate credentials?

Spreedly is enforcing credentials rotation, which is a Good Thing™.

They periodically send us an email to remind us to rotate our secrets.

**1. Connect to Spreedly dashboard**

Go in Busbud’s dashboard in Spreedly: [https://id.spreedly.com/organizations/TGBNlTP7KZjYHaQEy3saccJWtlZ](https://id.spreedly.com/organizations/TGBNlTP7KZjYHaQEy3saccJWtlZ)

Log in if you’re not.

![spreedly-log-in.png](Spreedly/spreedly-log-in.png)

**2. Configure the environment you want to rotate**

Click on “Configure” to open the “Environment Settings”.

You’ll need to rotate both API Access Secrets and Signing Secrets.

![spreedly-configure-env.png](Spreedly/spreedly-configure-env.png)

**Signing secret**

This is the secret Spreedly uses to sign their responses, [so we can verify their identity when using an unsecure channel](https://docs.spreedly.com/guides/offsite-payments/signed-requests/). You can safely generate a new one, there’s nothing configured on our side for that.

**API Access secrets**

![spreedly-api-access-secrets.png](Spreedly/spreedly-api-access-secrets.png)

To rotate these secrets, one by one:

1. **Create a new one** It’s best to use 1 secret / application and suffix with YYYY-MM to ease rotation.
    
    ![spreedly-new-api-access-secret.png](Spreedly/spreedly-new-api-access-secret.png)
    
2. **Change the value of SPREEDLY_ACCESS_KEY in the Bookie app**
    
    👉 For Production, the busbud-bookie-prod app on Heroku
    
    👉 For Preview and local tests, it’s versioned in the Bookie codebase (default config)
    
3. **Delete the old one**

Repeat for each secret.

**What about Pubweb?**

Pubweb is not using API Secrets Key. It uses the environment key, which is not a credential you can rotate (yet).

# Adding a New Payment Processor

<aside>
⚠️ Spreedly is no longer the only way to add new payment processors to the system, since the refactor that was done to accommodate Stitch. This guide should be updated to indicate this.

</aside>

At the time of writing the only payment provider that allow us to effortlessly add a new payment processor is Spreedly thus this guide is specific to Spreedly.

A recent example was the addition of Moka, which required additional work aside from setting up the gateways.
This included

1. Supporting 3DS1 with spreedly. See [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9091](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9091)
2. Making the purchase flow dynamic. See [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9196](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9196)

It can happen that new gateways require new features, but if when they don't these are the overall steps to add a new Gateway via Spreedly.

## 0. Before starting the work

Even though Spreedly provides a common API to interact with different payment processors the behavior can vary across them and we need to make sure we have everything covered to start working and rolling it out.

Checklist:

- [ ]  Review the Gateway Specific Fields and processor's API to ensure that we can provide the required information
- [ ]  Ask for credentials for their test environment
- [ ]  Review how they handle chargeback reporting
- [ ]  Check if deferred capture is supported for all card types
- [ ]  Check if installments are supported
- [ ]  Let Forter know in advance that we are planning to rollout a new payment processor
- [ ]  Anticipate to problems that may affect mobile apps

In detail

### 0.1 Review the Gateway Specific Fields and processor's API to ensure that we can provide the required information

Head to the gateway's documentation Gateway to gather this information. [Example](https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/mercado-pago/#gateway-specific-fields)

Sometimes the description of each field in Spreedly's doc is a bit vague, it's always good to also look at the processor's documentation for additional and up to date information.

What we are looking for at this point is to understand if we already posses all the information required by the processor to process the payment. We usually do, but different processors or countries may require additional data.

Examples:

- A payment processor that requires the billing address and mobile apps don't ask for the billing address. That's a blocker for mobile apps
- Argentina requires the ID Number to be provided for online payments. We need to make sure we are asking that during checkout

### 0.2 Ask for credentials for their test environment

Even though Spreedly provides a test gateway that is ready to use it's much better to use the processor test environment for developing and testing before going live.

### 0.3 Review how they handle chargeback reporting

All Spreedly payments have in common that they are done through credit cards and these are subject to chargebacks. Usually processor provides webhooks to notify these events. We need to make sure that they provide this information in a [compatible way](../Fraud and Chargebacks.md)

### 0.4 Check if deferred capture is supported for all card types

First, [understand what deferred capture means](../Purchase Process.md). In general authorizations on debit cards are not possible, but some payment processors will abstract us from the specifics and allow us to do a authorization + capture without throwing.

Our last two integrations (Moka and Mercado Pago) weren't the case and instead required us to call [`purchase`](https://docs.spreedly.com/reference/api/v1/#purchase) or [`authorize`](https://docs.spreedly.com/reference/api/v1/#authorize) depending on the card type.

Unfortunately Spreedly does not tell us the card type and there's no accurate and centralized data source that can be queried to get this information.
Instead, we expect the payment processor to provide us the information based on the card BIN

Specifics about how we'll consume this data will be covered later in this guide.

### 0.5 Check if instalments are supported

Check if they are supported and how the rates are obtained. Read more [here](notion://www.notion.so/payments/how-it-works/installments/#how-it-works) to catalog them properly and make instalments support a sub task of the issue.

### 0.6 Let Forter know in advance that we are planning to rollout a new payment processor

Last time we added a payment processor Forter was consistently denying all our transactions. This is because they rely on the processor's raw verification response in order to understand the state of the transaction and they weren't prepared to handle the new processor.

In order for our production launch to go smoothly, we let Forter know in advance to make sure everything is prepped on their side.

1. Login to the [Forter Support Portal](https://forter.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/3)
2. Select "Promotion / Drop Sale"
3. Create a ticket providing the new payment gateways name, currency, and if it's being provided through Adyen or Spreedly.
4. After the ticket has been created, hit the share button on the right side and enter `rebecca.bresnahan@forter.com`.

### 0.7 Anticipate to problems that may affect mobile apps

As mentioned above, mobile apps don't provide the same information as the web does and they also don't move as fast.
Just let them know and try to anticipate to issues similar to the following

- [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10846/files](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10846/files)
- [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10781/files](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10781/files)

## 1. Register the gateway in Spreedly

You can follow Spreedly's guide for the gateway you're adding (e.g. [https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/moka/#adding-a-moka-gateway](https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/moka/#adding-a-moka-gateway)) This is something we do once, from your terminal using the credentials for each environment.

Save the tokens from the response (`gateway.token`), you'll use them to set the columns `gateways.development_token` and `gateways.production_token`.

## 2. Add the gateway to Bookie's Database

The first steps are the same as in [Adding a new Gateway](notion://www.notion.so/thebusbudgroup/new-gateway.md), but take a Spreedly gateway as the base example.

For Spreedly, we use additional tables to show the right credit card logos on Pubweb

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5630976/155442721-ecfd94f7-d5ce-4fec-9f93-47091b893696.png)

These tables are

1. `supported_credit_cards`
2. `credit_card_brands`

What you add to `supported_credit_cards` will show up as a logo in the payment form, and `credit_card_brands` is just a reference table containing different card brands, it's likely that you don't have to add anything here

For Spreedly gateways we always do a progressive rollout so take a look at *Darklaunch it* under *Add a new Adyen Gateway*

Example migration file: [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9125/commits/34f0e01772c83ed1b82b1fe0509872c785b5d833](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/9125/commits/34f0e01772c83ed1b82b1fe0509872c785b5d833)

## 3. Implement the `SpreedlyAdapter`

Spreedly is the payment provider, all endpoints are shared across different gateways, but some fields and specially the responses are specific to the gateway. That's why need and Adapter per Gateway

You'll be looking to implement

1. Error mappings
2. Gateway specific fields (aka GFS). Example: [https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/moka/#gateway-specific-fields](https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/moka/#gateway-specific-fields)

And make sure to create the right Adapter based on `gateways.spreedly_gateway_type`

[https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/domain/model/spreedly-adapter.ts#L137-L150](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/domain/model/spreedly-adapter.ts#L137-L150)

```tsx
static createAdapter(client: SpreedlyClient, gateway: SpreedlyGateway) {
    switch (gateway.type) {
        case SpreedlyGatewayType.EBANX:
            return new EbanxAdapter(client, gateway);
        case SpreedlyGatewayType.MOKA:
            return new MokaAdapter(client, gateway);
        case SpreedlyGatewayType.ADYEN:
            return new AdyenAdapter(client, gateway);
        case SpreedlyGatewayType.DLOCAL:
            return new DLocalAdapter(client, gateway);
        default:
            return new SpreedlyAdapter(client, gateway);
    }
}
```

Example adapter: [https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/domain/model/spreedly-adapter.ts#L242-L320](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/c5f8624674772c56e71d77cc5f59c32d0de727cb/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/payment-providers/domain/model/spreedly-adapter.ts#L242-L320)

<aside>
💡 If the payment processor requires special treat for debit cards, the way we do it is to import the credit card information to our `credit_card_bins` table and override the `supportsDeferredCapture` method in the gateway implementation.
Example PR [https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10990](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10990)

</aside>

<aside>
💡 If the gateway supports internal installments plans, the rates can be configured in `config/installments.ts`
If the gateway support external installments plans you'll need to implement a new [`InstallmentsPlanProvider`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/78647d8bac84083c9c6ec5422b81287d9b52ce5a/apps/bookie/components/cart/infrastructure/repository/installments-plans-repository.ts#L141)

</aside>

## 4. Add a new endpoint in `chargeback-reporting`

Add the new endpoint in [chargeback-reporting](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting) to notify chargebacks to bookie.

## 5. Test it

If the gateway has a dev environment you can target that locally, otherwise use the XP on prod.

# Payment Providers

# Overview

Busbud delegates the work of processing payments to **Payment Providers**. There are 2 main benefits of doing that:

1. We can offer more payment methods and features to our end-users. Payment providers usually are the Busbud of banks: they expose an unified API to process many different payments.
2. We don’t have to implement the complex security requirements that are necessary for when you process sensitive data such as credit card information. Sensitive payment details never reach our back-end, so our system is safe.

We mostly use 2 payment providers: Adyen and Spreedly. Although we also delegate some payments to other, custom payment providers (e.g. [UnDosTres](../undostres)).

Adyen’s integration is our preferred integration for both business and technical reasons:

- A single business deal for payment processing.
- Less complexity and edge cases on accounting and tech.
- Support for local payment methods which we do not have with Spreedly.

# Major Payment Providers

[Adyen](Payment Providers/Adyen.md)

[Spreedly](Payment Providers/Spreedly.md)

[Stitch](Payment Providers/Stitch.md)

# Why have both Adyen and Spreedly?

<aside>
💡 Whenever possible, we prefer to use Adyen over Spreedly.

</aside>

Spreedly’s integration gives us the flexibility and possibility of getting payment processing deals with other companies in markets where having a local processing entity with Adyen is not possible or where Adyen has tougher/stricter requirements for doing so than other local companies.

One important example was with Argentina, where we now use [dLocal through Spreedly](https://docs.spreedly.com/payment-gateways/d-local/). However, every such deal means Engineering and Finance needs to deal with that company’s particularities. A big one for Engineering is dealing with [chargeback notifications](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting/tree/master/src/adapters) and of course maintaining the two integrations in parallel.

# Moka

We integrate Moka payment processing API via Spreedly.

## Background

Historically, we used Adyen's Iyzico to do payments on [neredennereye.com](http://neredennereye.com/).

We made the switch to Moka to increase the profit margins in Turkey. The processing fee for Adyen was 3.5%, whereas it is 1.65% for Moka.

## 3DS 1.0

We integrated Spreedly's [Specific Gateway 3DS1 Solution](https://docs.spreedly.com/guides/3dsecure/) as all payments going through Moka must involve 3DS 1.0.

## Debit cards

It should be noted that debit cards are very popular in Turkey. For every credit card, there are [two debit cards](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1099464/credit-card-and-debit-card-number-in-turkey/) in use in Turkey.

### Manual and immediate capture flows

Unlike Iyzico, where we used immediate flow for all payments, we are using both flows for Moka.

We prefer to use manual capture flow as it is less risky and there is also a less chance of taking a user's money without sending them their trip tickets. We use manual flow to process credit card payments and we use immediate capture flow to process both debit and prepaid card payments.

### BIN (Bank Identification Number)

The first four or six digits of a card's number is the BIN. In order for us to know which flow we need to use, we use a card's BIN to find out its card type, such as credit card, debit card and prepaid card.

We are currently getting a list of BIN from Moka, which we then persist in bookie's DB. That is a short-term solution. Eventually, the data in DB will become outdated and we'd need a more robust way of detecting a card type.

More information is also documented [here](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/docs/adrs/0028-use-persisted-data-to-detect-card-type.md).

## Instalments

Instalments are also available with Moka. However, it is only available for credit card payments. The economy in Turkey does not allow instalment payments with debit cards.

Currently, we offer the option to pay in instalments to all users regardless of which cards they are using. This is problematic as there's nothing preventing users from trying to use debit cards. When that happens, then we display an error message to the user that they should either use a credit card or not pay in instalments.

## Refunds

- They are automated, therefore it can be triggered from self-serve cancellation and from `Cancel and Refund` button on Support Tool.
- They are also triggered when the purchase fails after the transaction is either authorized or captured. First we'd try to refund. If it fails, then we'd try to void. One of the reasons that refund could failed is because it shouldn't be done on the same day as the payment.
