# Adding a New Payment Provider

This could be the most complex feature that can be done when it comes to payments because it includes all of its children concepts such as payment processor, gateway and payment method. Not only it may require a considerable amount of backend work, it also depends on clients given support for the payment provider.

It's recommended to read the rest of the "Adding a ..." first (specially the "Before starting to work" section of adding a payment processor) and [this issue](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/9787) that explains what changes we did to ease the addition of new payment providers.

The last payment provider we added was PayU, you can see all related work in the linked PR to [this issue](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/11825)

### 1. Add the payment method and the payment provider type

In case this integration provides a new payment method e.g. "MercadoPago wallet" add it to the `DbModels.PaymentType` type

### 2. [Adding a Gateway](../Checkout/Gateways.md)

That is specific to this payment provider

### 3. Implement the `PaymentProvider` interface

Grab a similar payment provider as an example and create a new implementation, preferably the latest ones (Stitch or MetroTurizm)

<aside>
⚠️ At the time of writing some payment provider implementations write to the `Purchase` or the `Transaction` models. This is not what we want moving forward. Instead we want the payment provider to return a `PaymentUpdate` and let the domain services handle the updates so that they are consistent across payment providers

</aside>

Update `getPaymentProviderForTransaction` to return this new payment provider as well

### 4. Implement notifications and webhooks

Webhooks are specific to the payment provider but we transform their notifications into our own `PaymentUpdate`s. The the updates are published to a queue that will be consumed by the `payment-notifications` worker.

<aside>
⚠️ At the time of writing Adyen has it's own handlers and worker for notifications because we didn't have time to migrate it to the new payment updates. Any new payment provider should reuse the generic payment notifications queues.

</aside>

A good example of this are Stitch webhooks.

Adding a webhook requires Fastly and the dev proxy to be updated to route `/webhooks/my-payment-provider` to bookie ([Fastly example](https://github.com/busbud/fastly-vcl/pull/351)) ([Dev proxy example](https://github.com/busbud/eng-tools/commit/0e9ffd3419078408c04b0017e8a14aa121867eeb))

### 5. Handle risk and chargebacks

If the payment provider allows chargebacks, you’ll need to identify whether the derisk is going to be PRE_AUTH or POST_AUTH. 

`PRE_AUTHORIZATION` means that we derisk before authorizing the payment, this is the case when the payment provider does not allow to perform authorization and capture in two steps.

`POST_AUTHORIZATION` means that we first authorize the payment, derisk it, and the capture it. In this case the result of the [SuccessfulAuthorization](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/bcb4b88c120df2c815c9a53eda79a411c4396965/apps/bookie/components/payments/domain/model/payment-update.ts#L15-L18) event should include `payment_details` 

Then you’ll need to

1. Make some purchases in [localhost](http://localhost) with `FORTER_ENABLED=true` in order to publish examples to Forter’s sandbox. They’ll fail,  contact Forter a `support@forter.com` saying that we are about to add a payment provider and that you published an example purchase to their sandbox environment.
    
    > We're looking to integrate a new payment provider for <country> (<Payment provider name and link>) that works as a <redirect payment method|>. Because of this we will be derisking all orders that go through this gateway as PRE_AUTHORIZATION  ones, and we won't collect the billing address. Let me know if you need more information to set it up on your side
    > 
2. Add a webhook in [chargeback-reporting](https://github.com/busbud/chargeback-reporting) to map the provider’s chargeback to ours and configure the payment provider to send the notifications to it

If the payment provider / payment method does not allow chargebacks there’s no need of derisking and it should be excluded from this processes by adding it [here](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/bcb4b88c120df2c815c9a53eda79a411c4396965/apps/bookie/components/payments/domain/model/payment-method.ts#L47-L61) 

### 6. Integrate the client

Clients will not get any new payment provider until they explicitly opt-in by adding the provider to the `supported_payment_providers` property at cart creation.

Depending on the payment provider, this could either replace or be presented alongside another payment provider. Stitch is an example of an alternative payment provider, because for Adyen provides the option to pay with credit cards and Stitch to pay via ETF. Since the payment methods are different both are returned to clients.

### 8. Test it and document

It's likely that this documentation is missing steps and caveats that will come up during testing and rollout of the new payment provider. Please share the learnings in this section :)

### 9. Add information in ST

We want to add links to the payment provider’s portal so that CX can track the state of the payment directly from the source of truth if needed 

![Untitled](Payment%20Providers/Untitled.png)

### Plans for the future

There some payment providers like Stitch or MercadoPago that work by rendering a button and redirecting the customer. Currently Stitch only supported by the web and the implementation is client specific (the client is responsible for rendering the button alongside the Dropin component).

As described in Option A of [#9787](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/9787) we can consider to implement a custom payment provider that abstracts clients from the underlying payment provider and thus the frontend implementation of it.

This way we could potentially add payment providers without client side code, as long as the behavior is as simple as rending a button and waiting for the redirection.

# Purchase Process

# Overview

When starting a purchase, a few things are happening:

- Create the purchase as well as necessary related models
- Publish the purchase in a queue
- Queue picks up the purchase and runs the relevant purchase flow
- Client (Pubweb, Mobile apps…) poll an API to get the state of the current purchase

# Flows

[TL;DR: Payments](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GOEMLh10SYggp0c9aZr2urINGu2oFgOB6N7IrwjpEXg/edit) that lists our current payments processors and give further links

Here’s the list of all purchase flows we have detailed [here](https://github.com/busbud/napi/tree/master/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/flows).

**There are 4 groups of purchase flows:**

1. Generic purchase flow which supports immediate and deferred captures regardless the payment provider (Adyen, Spreedly, etc …)
    1. includes PMD use case (e.g. retain credit card without an authorization initiated by Busbud)
2. Booking flow for trips with interconnections. Only supports the *Spreedly* payment provider.
3. IOU (I owe you), which are used by partners, including trainline and undostres.
4. Metro Turizm, which is a PMD and is used for that source.

The architectural concept around a booking flow is as follows

- A flow will predetermine a sequence of steps
- The steps are made nearly atomic such that each step can be retried or skipped
- The flow can be suspended at any point between completed steps and later resumed (this allows for continuous deployment assuming graceful shutdowns)
- Typically, each step is managed through a re-entrant queue and state is saved in the database to track progress through the flow sequence.

The specializations allow for adding or removing specific steps.

## Groups of purchase flows

### **IOU**

IOU (I owe you) is generally used with partners that have a full booking integration with the Busbud API. An example would be Trainlines (aka Captain Train). These partners will collect the money from customers using their own website and rely on Busbud to manage the inventory. Periodically, Busbud will invoice the partner for the value of the inventory they booked against the Busbud API.

For IOU (I owe you) groups, we basically skip all the payment method related steps and assume they are properly fulfilled by another party which we will invoice for the full value of the transaction.

Partners are given a part of the revenues, as determined by their revenue share percentage and the revenue made available per [compensation rules](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13NTjRj8XRg7mb-DD0WFmjDezdbdbd6E-qJ3NEopTEn8/edit#heading=h.pn2zusju29e4).

Note that under this payment method, there are NO Transaction DB entries and no payment-related calls from us to our payment or fraud partners of any kind.

### **Generic purchase flow when PMD**

When a purchase is associated with a PMD gateway, the generic purchase flow will take specific decisions accordingly. Indeed, instead of being authorized and captured the payment method will be simply [retained](https://docs.spreedly.com/basics/purchase/#retain) in Spreedly’s vault for future use and the payment method (tokenized credit card) saved in Busbud database.

PMD (Payment Method Distribution) is a feature offered by Spreedly that allows the caller to make an API call that Spreedly will proxy to the original API. In performing the proxying, Spreedly provides the ability to fill in payment method details from a payment method it holds in its secure vault and inject those values into the API request body before sending it to the original API.

This effectively allows Busbud to make API calls, inject credit card details into them securely (and without increasing PCI Compliance scope) and have them sent to third parties like Bestbus that are stubbornly holding on to processing the credit card themselves.

There are a few downsides to this

- The payment methods supported by the supplier are different from Busbud’s and there is no automated mechanism to determine which the supplier supports
- The supplier has no visibility into the fraud risk the given customer exposes them to, and we will not inject scripts into Busbud site to allow the supplier to obtain this visibility
- Busbud loses control over the financial side of the transaction and cannot combine the PMD inventory with other inventory (since CVV data can only be used once per tokenization), or provide discretionary refund capabilities
- This is only supported via the Spreedly integration. It is impossible to do under the Adyen integration or otherwise.
- Complex edge cases may result in user experience glitches or inconsistencies (e.g. Fake roundtrip where one departure is a PMD and the other is a regular departure, resulting in two transactions where one of them is processed by Busbud)

More generally, while allows us to expose customers to potentially more inventory, it does so at the cost of experience inconsistency.

### **Metro Turizm**

This is specific to metro turizm. It is similar to Adyen’s `redirect` payment methods. The users use busbud’s checkout flow. At the `authorize` step of the purchase process, the users are redirected to Metro Turizm where they will perform 3DS 1.0 authentication. Once completed, then the users come back to busbud to complete the payment.

## Steps

### Departure details / Validate

Call GET departure details on the integration.

### Reserve

Reserve bus seat.

### Spreedly Payment Method

Spreedly Credit Card flows only. Get back the PCI-compliant-filtered payment information of the user in Spreedly’s response using the Spreedly Token obtained by Pubweb when Pubweb made the POST /:cart_id/purchase call to Bookie.

### Create Transactions

Create an entry in the Transactions table that will be used to represent the payment for the ongoing purchase.

### Authorize

First of two payment steps. Send the request for payment authorization to the payment provider.

### Verify payment details

Used for payment methods that require user’s input to complete a payment. It is done after the `authorize` step, where a bank requests a user’s verification. Once the user has verified themselves, we submit the result to the bank in this step.

### Verify 3DS2 or 3DS results

It is the same step as verify payment details step, except that it is specific to 3DS 2.0 and Metro Turizm 3DS 1.0.

### Derisk

The derisk step obtains the decision from the fraud risk assessment provider. This work is detailed in [Fraud & Chargebacks](./fraud.md)

### Book

Book a bus seat.

### Capture

Second of two payment steps. Capture the money reserved from the Authorize step.

Capture is an asynchronous process IRL, but we always assume it works because it does about 99.9% of the time. With Adyen’s integration, we are alerted of capture failures.

### Save Credit Card

Only on Spreedly flows, and mostly just for the Mobile Apps nowadays.

### mark transaction captured

This is used for immediate capture flow, where the money is captured at `authorize` step instead of at `capture` step. This step is done near the end of the purchase flow to ensure that all transactions are marked as `captured`, which is the final state for a successful transaction.

### mark purchase completed

This is used for immediate capture flow, where the money is captured at `authorize` step instead of at `capture`. In that case, there is no `capture` step for this flow, which would have marked a purchase as `completed`, which is the final state for a successful purchase. This step is done near the end of the purchase flow to ensure that all successful purchases are marked as `completed`.

### How to find out which flow is used?

We store this information on each purchase, in `details.purchase_flow` 🌟

This will help you understand what were the steps involved in the checkout process!

## Manual Capture vs Immediate Capture

When talking about payment / purchase flows, you’ll often hear us talk about `Immediate` and `Manual` capture, but what does that mean?

### Manual Capture

Let’s take the example of a regular credit card purchase. There are two essential components for a successful payment, which are:

- `authorization`

This operation is meant to ***make sure the customer can afford the purchase***. This is something we ask the bank (through our payment processor, like Adyen or Spreedly). What they do is essentially comparing the balance with the amount requested, do a couple fraud checks on their end, and if everything looks good, they take a *hold* on the money. They lock the amount so that it ***guarantees us that we will be able to capture the money***.

- `capture`

This operation is the confirmation of the `authorization`.

Once we have made sure that everything is in order (we have `derisked` the purchase, `booked` the tickets, etc), we can tell the bank that we want the `authorization` to be `captured` and the money transfered to our bank account.

This step virtually never fails, because of the previous `authorization` step that did all the necessary checks.

We call this flow ***Manual***, meaning we need to manually `capture` the money once it’s authorized.

This is very important to us to be able to do that because it’s easy and fast to cancel an `authorization`. We call that reverse operation a `void`. Customers are able to have access to that money very fast thanks to it.

We need to have this ability because of all the checks we run between the `authorize` and `capture` steps.

That’s when we call our fraud processor (like Forter) to make sure everything is legit, but also when we call the bus operator to `book` the ticket. Both of those steps (especially the `derisk`) will fail regularly and are expected to.

Here are a few examples of payment methods with a `Manual` capture flow:

- Most credit cards (except Metro Turizm)
- Klarna
- Google Pay (except when using debit cards)
- Apple Pay (except when using debit cards)

### Immediate Capture

You might have an idea of where this goes by now, but here’s what an `Immediate` capture is:

This is essentially the combination of the `authorize` and `capture` steps previously described, in one single step.

Certain payment methods or banks impose us this flow. They simply don’t support the `authorization` (taking a temporary hold on the money), so once we send the payment request, we either reject, or `capture` the money right away, no middlegrounds.

As I’ve previously described, the `Manual` flow has the advantage of being able to `void` the `authorization` easily and run steps in the middle.

With the `Immediate` flow, we take the risk that something fails after, and in that case, the reverse operation is a `refund`.

Refunds take much longer to be processed and require more accounting. User experience is worse because it might take days before the money comes back to their account, and some users cannot afford that.

Here are a few examples of payment methods with an `Immediate` capture flow:

- Debit cards (e.g. Moka via Spreedly)
- Credit card with Metro Turizm (They handle the payment on their side and also require immediate capture)
- Most redirect payment methods (e.g. Sofort)
- Most QR payment methods (e.g. weChat)
- Undostres

# What happens when a purchase fails?

[Here’s a detailed presentation on the topic](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wdWRs4hvZ_BvvhbkWCFxHKF56gtxoj9xoF4CbtJ4MOo/edit#slide=id.gbe7850b767_0_0) from Feb. 2021.

TL;DR:

- For most flows, we book tickets before we capture money (except “Immediate Capture” ones)
- When a purchase fails, we rollback and cancel the tickets we eventually booked.
- As of January 2022, we don’t automatically refund money we would have captured.
    - Instead, we have scripts to periodically refund customers in this situation.
    - We used to have a script to periodically void authorized transactions in this situation so that customers would not see pending transactions on their card statements.
- When the UnDosTres integration was introduced in Feb 2021, we started to implement logic to automatically refund the money on rollback.
- For other payment providers, including Adyen and Spreedly, we will automatically void authorized transactions on rollback.

# Purchase States

When polling, different states can be returned, representing how far from completion is the purchase.

Here are the different states, what they represent, as well as what needs to be done in reaction to them.

## no state

If a purchase has no state (aka `null`), then it failed before reaching the first step of the purchase flow, which is to get trip details from an adapter.

### How to handle

Handle the error that should be thrown from the backend.

## `validate`

Validating that everything looks correct by calling the adapter. (`getDepartureDetails` most likely).

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `reserve`

Calling the adapter to try and reserve the bus seat(s).

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `authorize`

Calling the payment processor to try and authorize the amount of the purchase on the customer’s bank account.

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `redirect`

Received during the authorize step, it means that we need to redirect the customer to an external website to continue the payment.

Current use cases are:

- 3DS1
- Bank transfers (e.g. Sofort)

### How to handle

Trigger the redirection using the payload received.

In the first step, bookie provides `redirection_setup` [payload](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/8ddf4c64c10968d3bfcbb76af17599c86eba4518/apps/bookie/types/db-models.d.ts#L1107) to clients, which should then take care of redirecting the user to an external page.

In the second step, where the user finishes their verification, one of two ways happens depending on the type of the redirection:

**HTTP POST Request**:

- Results are automatically submitted by the 3DS platform (e.g. bank website) to Bookie, which responds with a `303 Redirect` to redirect customers to the `return_url`, which was provided at purchase creation endpoint, along with a body payload.

```
POST /purchases/:purchase_id/3ds-results
{ payload: ... }
```

An example of this use case is Metro Turizm

**HTTP GET Request**:

- The external website (e.g. bank) will redirect the user back to a client using the `return_url`, along with a payload. The `return_url` was provided at purchase creation endpoint. For the Web, [the payload is a query param](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/ba362826e512734c6035561b91d914af547d3108/app/controllers/checkout.tsx#L65-L71).
- Send this payload to this API endpoint:

```
POST /purchases/:purchase_id/redirection-completed
{ payload: ... }
```

You can check this [link](https://github.com/busbud/public-website/blob/ba362826e512734c6035561b91d914af547d3108/app/modules/checkout/services/payment-provider-redirection-handler.ts#L5) to see how pubweb handles redirection for each payment provider.

Finally, we resume polling. The previous step should have published the purchase back into the queue and restart the purchase flow.

## `identify`

Received during the `authorize` step, it means that we need to trigger a *3DS2 verification*. This is either a frictionless operation and/or a challenge operation for the end user, but requires some development to trigger it.

We only do this with Adyen: https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/3d-secure/native-3ds2

### How to handle

This is done in two steps:

- Bookie provides `threeds2_setup.action` to the Drop-in. It should take care of running the necessary logic:

```json
{
  "threeds2_setup": {
    "resultCode": "IdentifyShopper",
    "action": {...},
    "paymentData": {...}
  }
}
```

- Get the result of the 3DS 2.0 verification by listening to the Drop-in’s callback. It is platform specific so refer to [Adyen docs](https://docs.adyen.com/checkout) for guidance. This result must be sent to this API endpoint:

```
POST /purchases/:purchase_id/3ds2-results
{
  threeds2_result: {
    threeDSResult: "XXXXXXX"
  }
}
```

Resume polling (the previous step will publish the purchase back into the queue and restart the purchase flow)

## `action_required`

Received during the `authorize` step, it means that we need to present an additional step to be completed by the user. Current use cases for that are QR code based payment methods:

- WeChat
- Bancontact

We present a QR code to the user (in the Drop In), and they need to scan it with their mobile app in order to confirm the payment.

### How to handle

Trigger the action:

- Provide `action_setup` to the Drop In. It should take care of running the necessary logic.
- Get the result of the action by listening the Drop In’s callback (check [Adyen docs](https://docs.adyen.com/checkout), it’s platform specific)
- You need to send this payload to this API endpoint: `POST /purchases/:purchase_id/action-completed` `{ payload: ... }`
- Resume polling (the previous step will publish the purchase back into the queue and restart the purchase flow)

This is the content of the `action` object that we sent in previous 3DS / redirection statuses, so you can directly provide this whole object to the Drop In.

```json
{
  "action_setup": {
    "paymentData": {...}
  }
}
```

## `derisk`

Calling our fraud check providers prevent fraudsters. This step may, and will fail quite often. It’s important not to indicate to the users that they’ve been declined because of fraud, otherwise we essentially give indications to fraudsters that they can use to find a pattern / breach.

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `book`

Calling the adapter to try and book the bus seat(s).

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `capture`

Calling our payment processor to try and capture the previously authorized amount. This is a very high success rate operation, as the authorization essentially guarantees that the money can be captured.

### How to handle

Keep polling.

## `complete`

Everything’s done, you made it!

### How to handle

- Stop polling
- Redirect customers to the confirmation page, providing with a summary of the purchased items as well as their trip tickets.

## `delayed`

Indicates that the `book` cannot be executed just yet. We will try to book it in the following minutes to try and work around bus operators’ APIs temporary failures.

When an adapter or supplier is down temporarily, and a book step fails, we'll keep retrying for a while (1h). We'll let the customer know we're trying to complete the booking.

If we're **successful**, we'll charge them and we'll inform them that their purchase was successful and that their tickets are on their way. Otherwise, we'll let them know it **failed**.

Most of the time, the error is not recoverable and the tickets won't be booked. But in some rare case, when the adapter or supplier is actually down, we are able to book the ticket when it becomes available again, and therefore give the customer their tickets.

### How to handle

- Stop polling
- Redirect customers to a special page, indicating clearly that the tickets **are not booked** just yet, and that we’ll try again and send them a confirmation email with the results.

### Reserve step

We used to use the delayed feature on the reserve step. It had to be removed after we added support to 3DS and redirect payment methods. The reserve step is done before the authorize step. The way the delayed feature works is that it retries to run the purchase flow automatically for some time. The problem is that if we restart it before the `authorize` step, we might need manual intervention from the user (3DS 1.0 or redirection to a bank transfer). Since the user may not in front of their screen at this point, we currently are not able to make those purchase work.

### Technical details

You can see the status of the delayed purchases with this query:

```sql
select delayable, delayed, state, count(1)
from purchases
where created_at > '2020-08-01'
group by rollup(1,2,3)
order by 1,2,3;
```

## `failed` / `error`

The purchase cannot be continued automatically. Could be internal error, derisk failure, cannot authorize, book, etc. Anything that doesn’t follow the happy path.

At this point we try and show the user the clearer explanation on what went wrong, so that they can try again after taking the necessary actions.

### How to handle

- Stop polling
- Present a relevant error message to the user
- Allow them to try again

# Transaction States

Transactions are created when Busbud processes a payment. Transactions can have a number of different states. Some are transitory, some are final and some are for specific use cases.

## `raw`

Transitory state.

This is the Transaction model’s default value of state from the database perspective and the first value of a Transaction’s state upon creation.

Some error scenarios might leave a Transaction in a `raw` state. In this case, the `error` and `details` columns should contain more information.

## `adopted`

Transitory state.

This is the state the Transaction objects will get during the initial parts of the execution of Busbud’s purchase flows if an already existing Transaction with an `authorized` state is found for the purchase being processed.

The point is to re-use a successful Authorization if there are many failed attempts because of a Booking error, for example.

In the purchase flows, it goes like:

- Does a Transaction with `authorized` state already exist, satisfying conditions?
    - If yes:
        - Take it and change the state to `adopted`
        - Clone the adopted Transaction
        - Proceed with the rest of the purchase flow using the cloned Transaction
    - If no:
        - Create a new Transaction with the `raw` state
        - Then, proceed with the rest of the purchase flow using the new Transaction

A Transaction can only change to this state if the previous state was `authorized`.

## `authorized`

Transitory state.

This is the state a Transaction object will get upon a successful Authorization request with the payment processing third party (typically with credit cards).

This represents the verification that the end user actually has the necessary funds available for payment and puts a hold on the amount.

A Transaction can only change to this state if the previous state was `raw`.

If a Purchases’s Capture or Void operation fails, a Transaction might be left in the `authorized` state as a final state. In this case, the `error` and `details` columns should contain more information.

## `captured`

Final state.

This is the state a Transaction object will get upon a successful Capture request with the payment processing third party (typically with credit cards).

This represents the moment when the actual payment is made and the reserved amount from the Authorize step is taken from the end user.

A Transaction can only change to this state if the previous state was `authorized`.

## `error`

Final state.

This state will be set under various error scenarios. Unfortunately, not all error scenarios will result in a Transaction having an `error` state. See transitory states for more info.

## `external_charge`

Final state.

This is used for sources that have explicit gateways (PMD) where the payment is typically handled outside of Busbud for a purchase made on Busbud by end users.

## `voided`

Final state.

This is the Transaction state after an Authorization that had successfully completed was cancelled using a Void request on the payment processing third party. Void requests can also be applied on `captured` Transaction if done quickly enough after the Capture such that the transaction had not yet been settled.

A Transaction can only change to this state if the previous state was `authorized` or `captured`.

## `escrowed`

Legacy state. Not used anymore.

## `credited`

Credited transactions are similar to refunded transactions in the sense that they both set the transaction balance to 0, but the difference is that with refunded transactions, the customer has the money back in their account and with credited transactions, we still own the funds and we credited the customer with either busbud credits or a voucher.

# Overview

Various payment-related subjects that are important to be aware of but not really classifiable in a different section.

# 3DSecure (3DS & 3DS2)

[Quick overview presentation of 3DSecure 2](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1gNJ1-B4msXVR_qKVY0D-yi-kxBjS4WNLE9YbppgrqZ8/edit#slide=id.g3fc08113ff_0_72)

We currently support 3DS and 3DS2 with our Adyen, Spreedly and Metro Turizm integrations.

All of Busbud's clients (except legacy mobile apps) make use of 3DS and 3DS2. For conversion, it is better to not use 3DS or 3DS2 (legacy 3DS especially). But security matters.

Europe, espcially Turkey, is not the only market where 3DS or 3DS2 is possible, but it is the main one where these mechanisms are sort of expected by users.

If a bank requests 3DS and Busbud does not support 3DS integration, then liability will not rest with the bank that authorized the transaction if it turns out that the purchase is fraudulent. Basically, Busbud would be responsible for it (e.g. would have to refund the customer).

## 3DSecure

3DSecure is an additional verification process that happens at credit card authorization time in order for the payment system / bank to decide whether the authorization should be accepted or not. The original 3DSecure is now considered legacy, although still used and likely to be used in Europe for a few years still and unclear how long for some markets.

It is generally accepted that 3DSecure is a conversion killer. 3DSecure redirects the user to a webpage controlled and branded by the credit card company or bank where the user inputs a distinct set of credentials to authenticate himself.

We currently see usage of Legacy 3DS in:

- Europe (until banks there stop using it)
- Turkey
- Brazil

It would be possible to run it in Canada and the US merchant accounts. For Canada, it’s not needed because fraud levels are quite low. For the US, it would be bad for conversion, and fraud levels are nowhere near bad enough.

## 3DSecure 2

3DSecure 2 is the newest iteration of this intent of authenticating the user at credit card authorization time with Europe leading the way in terms of integration and regulation. Relevant keywords related to the regulation are PSD2 and SCA (Strong Customer Authentication).

There are two technical components / steps to 3DSecure 2:

- Device Fingerprinting (transparent to the user)
- Authentication challenge (that the user must succeed)

To have an idea of what challenges can be, have a look at [this Visa documentation](https://developer.visa.com/pages/visa-3d-secure#challenge_methods) meant for banks implementing 3DSecure 2 Challenges.

It is possible for a user to only go through the “fingerprint” step, which is transparent. It is referred to as a “frictionless flow” and is ideal.

To maximize the chances of a frictionless flow and reduce the chances for a challenge to occur, we send [as much information as the payment service provider (Adyen) API requires / supports](https://docs.adyen.com/checkout/3d-secure/api-reference#3d-secure-2-additional-parameters) in relation to 3DS2.

We currently see usage of 3DS2 in:

- Europe
- Brazil (surprisingly enough)

## Adyen

We let Adyen determine the usage of 3DS based on legal requirements, bank requirements and Adyen’s own logic for when it should optimally happen.

We have configured it such that we won't use 3DS on BusbudUSA and BusbudSouthAfrica transactions, unless a bank specifically requests it. It is done on their dashboard and is configured individually for each merchant account:

![adyen-3ds-configuration.png](Varia/adyen-3ds-configuration.png)

The reason is because it has a very negative impact on conversion rate and we're relying on Forter to catch fraudulent purchases.

### In Bookie

<aside>
💡 This part uses Adyen to describe how bookie handles both 3DS and 3DS 2.0. It can be applied to other payment providers (e.g. Spreedly).

</aside>

While the purchase is being processed in the queue, if we encounter an Adyen response during the call to /payments (in the Authorize step) indicating the need to do either 3DS or 3DS2, the flow is interrupted by a specific exception being thrown: [PurchaseActionNeeded](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/lib/payment-methods/adyen-platform/payments-response-strategies/credit-card-authorization-strategy.js#L113). This causes the purchase to exit the processing queue.

We also save some info in the purchase details in the DB relating to the 3DS and 3DS2 process around the same time this “exit” exception is thrown. This allows Bookie to respond with the appropriate and required data in the endpoint that a client is polling (POST [/:purchase_id/status](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/routes/purchases/index.js#L318)).

The client will react accordingly.

In the Legacy 3DS scenario, there are two ways to do it depending on how the 3DS integration is done:

1. **the bank will POST** to Bookie’s [/:purchase_id/3ds-results](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/routes/purchases/index.js#L414) endpoint when the user is done, which will redirect the user back to client to see the result. The endpoint also pushes the purchase back to the Purchase Processing Queue. The client resumes polling.
2. **the bank will GET** to the client's endpoint when the user is done. The client will extract the payload from the query and POST to bookie's `/:purchase_id/redirection-completed` endpoint. This bookie's endpoint will also push the purchase back to the Purchase Processing Queue. The client resumes polling.

In the 3DS2 scenarios, **the client POSTs** the result of the 3DS2 step to Bookie’s [`/:purchase_id/3ds2-results`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/routes/purchases/index.js#L476) endpoint. The endpoint pushes the purchase back to the Purchase Processing Queue. The client resumes polling.

Bookie’s purchase flows’ steps are ordered in such a manner that makes sense and covers all possible scenarios. See the [3DS2 presentation](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1gNJ1-B4msXVR_qKVY0D-yi-kxBjS4WNLE9YbppgrqZ8/edit) or Adyen docs for a clear and illustrated view of possible scenarios. Some important points:

- A purchase cannot go through both Legacy 3DS and 3DS 2 steps.
- A purchase that went through 3DS 2 fingerprint may go through 3DS 2 challenge.
- From Bookie’s perspective, these steps are optional and may appear as [skipped](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/master/apps/bookie/components/purchase-process/flows/credit-card-adyen/one-way.js#L214) in the Support Tool's logs
- The initial authorization attempt (purchase flow ‘authorize’ step) will hit Adyen’s `/payments` endpoint
- Subsequent calls for either 3DS or 3DS2 verification will hit Adyen’s `/payments/details` endpoint

# UnDosTres

<aside>
🧟‍♂️ This integration isn’t really active anymore, though the code is still around. It may come back from the dead at some point, hence why we are keeping these docs.

</aside>

We integrate with a partner named [UnDosTres](https://undostres.com.mx/). It's a platform for Mexican users where they can pay for multiple services.

We went to integrate with them as they were looking for a bus ticket service to propose to their users. For us, it's a way to get exposed to the locals more.

## How it works for the users?

UnDosTres users typically have their mobile app installed. On the app, they have access to a "bus" service that leads them to Busbud.

Busbud is embed as a webview in UnDosTres' app. We show a customized whitelabel version of the website. Users would search and select departures as they'd normally do on our website.

![home-page.png](Varia/home-page.png)

When it comes to paying, the user gets redirected to the UnDosTres payment page they're familiar with. From here, they can use whatever payment method UnDosTres allows to.

![payment-page.png](Varia/payment-page.png)

Finally, users get redirected to Busbud again. We complete the purchase by booking the tickets and showing the thank you page.

### Restricted operators

Because of contracts, we had to restrict the search results. UnDosTres users can't see results from ADO, nor Movelia.

This is [configured in Busplatform](https://busplatform-next-preview.herokuapp.com/main/partner-edit/185), as a denylist of sources available for the UnDosTres partner.

### It works as an IOU provider

UnDosTres plays the role of the Payment Provider here, like Adyen or Spreedly would do. We delegate the payment to their system, then we book the tickets.

UnDosTres has a dedicated purchase flow. We leveraged the logic of IOU providers to do so. This means CX & Finance operations would work similarly as they do for any other IOU partner (e.g. Trainline).

### UnDosTres users are Mexican locals

It's fair to assume they speak Spanish (`es-mx`) and they pay in `MXN`.

## How it works under the hood?

The interaction between our system and UnDosTres is described [in their flowchart](https://app.diagrams.net/#G1MoH0r9RY4ziwOHm4IJB4HD3HuWBU1pDb).

![flowchart-glimpse.png](Varia/flowchart-glimpse.png)

When everything goes fine, we go through these steps:

1. User creates their cart on Busbud and complete the passenger details
2. User clicks on "Pay with UnDosTres"
3. Bookie creates a new Payment on UnDosTres system.
4. The payment needs to be completed on UnDosTres. Hence, Bookie will stop the purchase process and ask the client (Pubweb) to redirect the user to the proper URL.
5. User completes the payment on UnDosTres. Their system sends a notification to Bookie so we know this payment is approved now.
6. User is redirected back to Busbud, the purchase process resumes and we book the tickets.
7. User reaches the "thank you" page and receives their tickets.

### Emails

At this point, we've agreed to NOT send marketing emails to UnDosTres users. Similarly, we can't send emails such as "cart abandonment" since the purchase would need to be completed from the UnDosTres mobile app (otherwise, the redirect wouldn't work).

Hence, we only send UnDosTres users the transactional emails = the email that contains their tickets.

To do so, we had to do a couple of changes:

- In Bookie ([#8141](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/8141), to allow sending these emails
- In Il-Postino ([#581](https://github.com/busbud/il-postino/pull/581) and [#579](https://github.com/busbud/il-postino/pull/579)), to configure the partner so emails are actually sent

### User information encrypted

When users are redirected to Busbud from the UnDosTres mobile app, we receive some encrypted information about them in the `udtref` query parameter.

We decrypt these information on Pubweb. It contains details we could use to prefill passenger information, as well as the user ID. The user ID is required to create the Payment on UnDosTres later. Therefore, we can't move forward if we fail to decrypt user information on Pubweb.

# Cancellation and Refunds

# Discretionary refunds

Sometimes, when something goes wrong, we need to refund customers. Most of the cases it will be because of a bug on our side causing the tickets to not be issued, but we still charged the user.

This will create a `purchase_line_item` called `transaction_refund` with the amount specified by the person issuing the refund.

Sometimes though, because we want to be kind to our customers, we use this feature to refund customers even if the problem is not due to a bug on our side. It means that the problem was on the supplier side, but we didn’t want to wait for them because that’s a bad user experience.

In that case, we’re in debt to the supplier, we still owe them the GMV (minus commission) but we don’t have the money, so we’ll want to make the supplier cancel the purchase so we don’t owe them anymore. Once we convinced them to cancel, we need to register it in our system so that accounting can generate invoices that correctly include those purchases as cancelled. This brings us to our next category of refunds.

# Supplier approved refunds

This category of refund **does not issue a refund to the customer**, this is only used to register the approval of a supplier to cancel the purchase. As explained before, it saves in the system the necessary `purchase_line_item` so that when generating invoices, we don’t include the amount as owed to the partner.

This essentially reverses all line items, as well as registering the cancellation penalty, if applicable. For instance, if we have these line_items:

- `base_price`: $10
- `source_fees`: $1
- `source_taxes`: $1
- `commission`: $1

And the supplier approves an 80% refund, we will issue a refund that includes a 20% cancellation penalty, and register the following line items:

- `base_price_refund`: -$10
- `source_fees_refund`: -$1
- `source_taxes_refund`: -$1
- `commission_refund`: -$1 -> Technically, we could only refund 80% of the commission. See with accounting to make sure, but that would be a great way to cover some of the cost.
- `cancellation_penalty`: $2.4 -> `(base_price + source_fees + source_taxes) * 20%`

# Voucher refunds

In case the supplier allows users to exchange their ticket we support this through self serve cancellation as voucher refunds. In a voucher refund we issue a cancellation to the supplier API with a refund target of type voucher without refunding the ticket price to the customer. The supplier is then responsible for emailing the voucher that the user can use to exchange their tickets.

A couple of decisions were made with this feature:

- We still refund the busbud fee to the customer as we rather respect the configuration that applies to busbud fees globally
- A refund policy of type Voucher will be forced to have no cancellation penalties, despite what’s configure in the terms. This assumes that the terms are incorrectly configured as with an exchange the user is entitled to 100% of the ticket’s value

For more information refer to the issue https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/11521 

# NN

NN purchases work a bit differently currently, because they use an [immediate capture flow](/payments/how-it-works/payment-flows/#immediate), meaning we do not have the possibility to just “cancel” the payment when something goes wrong, like a booking failure.

We have setup a task to refund customers automatically. This is automatically scheduled to run:

- Every hour
- Fetches all purchases older than 10min and more recent than 2 hours
- Issue refunds for all purchases where we captured the money but were not able to issue tickets

Means that in the worst case, people get refunded 1h and 9 minutes after their booking failed, and in the best case, 10 minutes.

# Optimistic Cancellations

When we cancel and refund a purchase, cancelling the tickets may fail for technical reasons (e.g. partner’s API times out temporarily). We don’t want to block the refund in such a situation, so we perform an **optimistic cancellation**.

That is: we’ll refund the user, even if cancelling the tickets fail.

This way, we attempt to cancel the tickets later (automatically or manually by the CX team that would be alerted).

## But sometimes, the tickets can’t be cancelled!

Indeed, sometimes the partner API will fail the cancellation because the user **has no right to cancel the ticket**. For example, some operators won’t allow the user to cancel a ticket after it was modified at the station to avoid fraudsters.

To handle these cases, the refund won’t happen if the adapter throw a specific `PurchaseCancellationDenied` error. This error means “nope, this cancellation can’t happen for a good reason”. That way we can tell the difference between a technical issue and an actual denied cancellation.

You’ll find more context:

- [in the issue that implemented Optimistic Cancellations](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/4673)
- [in the issue that implemented `PurchaseCancellationDenied`](https://github.com/busbud/napi/issues/6285)

# GDPR The GDPR (”**General Data Protection Regulation**”) introduces a right for individuals to have personal data erased known as “the right to be forgotten”. By April 2022, CX was receiving an average of over 1 GDPR delete request per day from automated sources like SayMine.com None of these requests are for high future value customers, so we’d want to minimize the time CX needs to spend on them without reducing quality in favor of more active/promising customers. At a high level, the process follows as illustrated, being **Automation** the part that we built. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Customer participant Zendesk participant Automation participant CX Customer->>+Zendesk: Emails support note right of Customer: Please erase my personal data Automation->>Zendesk: Appends a private note to the ticket note right of Zendesk: This is user XXX, click here to erase personal data CX->>Zendesk: Clicks on link Zendesk->>Automation: Requests an erause for user XXX Automation->>Automation: Processes the request Automation->>Zendesk: Replies to customer Zendesk->>-Customer: Replies to customer note right of Customer: Your data has been erased ``` ## Automation What’s labeled as Automation has actually multiple actors - [Autoresponder](https://github.com/busbud/autoresponder/) (aka Chester) - Github (for the [GDPR customer requests repo](https://github.com/busbud/gdpr-customer-requests)) - Bookie ### Autoresponder Autoresponder is in charge of **adding a private note to the ticket in Zendesk** with a referential link and **creating a GitHub issue** once the link is clicked. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CX participant Autoresponder participant Zendesk Zendesk->>+Autoresponder: Issue created Autoresponder-->>-Zendesk: Append this note note left of Zendesk: Delete user data CX->>+Autoresponder: /gprd?token=abc Autoresponder->>Autoresponder: Create github issue Autoresponder->>CX: github.com/issues/XXX ``` The private note is added after ticket creation along with the rest of the user info that’s useful for CX to have. - [Link to the code](https://github.com/busbud/autoresponder/blob/4aefc1a3bba1380b05421a8b03080a50a0c73018/apps/api/components/private-note/index.js#L7-L30) The anchor link added points to an endpoint in autoresponder, which will create the GitHub issue (if does not exits) and redirect to it. - [Link to the code](https://github.com/busbud/autoresponder/blob/4aefc1a3bba1380b05421a8b03080a50a0c73018/apps/api/routes/gdpr.js#L20-L47) - [Example Github issue](https://github.com/busbud/gdpr-customer-requests/issues/905) ### Bookie With the request being tracked in Github, bookie is responsible of **processing the request**. We do this via a cron job every night, were we loop over opened GitHub issues and process them. Processing a Github issue involves 1. Erasing personal data from the DB: this is replacing personal data with dummy values, we still keep purchase related data. 2. Forgetting users from external services, e.g. Iterable 3. Closing the GitHub issue 4. Informing the customer that the request has been processed, we do this by applying a pre defined macro to the ticket. The macro is managed in Zendesk ### Links - [Link to the cron job definition](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/52d93e8af751e64cd2b203dbe48dffab2bdbae24/apps/bookie/infrastructure/production/main.tf#L412-L421) - [Link to the code](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/52d93e8af751e64cd2b203dbe48dffab2bdbae24/apps/bookie/components/gdpr/application/service/process-gdpr-requests.ts#L17-L48)

## Sharing revenue estimates to Google AdWords

A large portion of our purchases originate from the SEM channel, and it is optimized to maintain a Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) of 100%. Basically at that ROAS, if we pay Google 1$ for ads, we expect to make 1$ in revenue on average.

We currently do not provide the Adwords tracker with the exact revenue we make for each transaction. Originally, this information was considered confidential and sensitive and including it within a webpage would allow our competitors or the curious to find our margins with various suppliers. We've since changed our position on having this information available client-side, the reason being that we value the accuracy of the performance of the SEM channel more than we do the risk of anyone discovering the revenue we might make on a given transaction.

Thus, this is an area we expect to change in the near term. We'd expose the actual revenue, similar to the one we share with systems like Analytics API and Netsuite such that we could accurately represent to the 3rd party SEM systems the true value of completed transactions.

Currently, we use monthly averages to approximate the revenue and represent those in Google Tag Manager (GTM).

# Ticket Generation

# Generated Tickets

After user paid and we booked the trip, we generate tickets and send them to the user.

Some tickets might be generated by the partners. We receive that from the integration adapters.

If they don’t, we are able to generate tickets ourselves with a determined template approved by the supplier, in Hodor. We render them as web pages and save them as PDF byte streams.

We can also render Apple Wallet tickets and we handle Google Pay tickets. For the latter, we publish the ticket metadata to Google and provide a UI affordance (Pubweb or Ticket Confirmation Email) to link it to your Google Pay account. From there, you use a dedicated application (Google Pay) to access the tickets.

The overall process for generating tickets post-purchase looks like this:

1. We retrieve the tickets from the partners or generate them ourselves
2. We validate that they look good
3. We store them, so we can retrieve it later (e.g. in the Support Tool)
4. We send them to the purchaser’s email

## What if something goes wrong?

We try harder. Things can go wrong for multiple reasons (e.g. operator API fails temporarily). So we try again multiple times.

If we still can’t get it work, then we notify CX about it in Slack.

![failed-ticket-generation.png](Ticket%20Generation/failed-ticket-generation.png)

## Ticket validation

This is necessary because tickets we get from the partner might be broken.

First, we verify nothing is *obviously* broken:

- We check if the ticket is empty, which we can infer from the file size
- We check if the ticket file is corrupted and fails to open

Then, we compare it with similar tickets that we edited in the past and we know are valid. For example we compare:

- the number of pages,
- the file size with the average file size,
- the ticket with a valid ticket using an image analysis library,
- etc.

Our validation strategy isn’t perfect. Sometimes we have false positive because the 2nd step isn’t very reliable. That’s why we send the tickets anyway if they are not obviously broken!

If we think the ticket isn’t valid but we’re not sure, we log that information internally so we can investigate and refine our strategy.

## When are they generated?

### **Apple Wallet**

**Apple Wallet** tickets are generated when ([code](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ee5e237092e4dff07618e7a29be6f2f5310c5a25/apps/bookie/components/ticket-generation/index.ts#L283-L308)):

1. `PKPASS_ENABLED` is enabled on Bookie (which is enabled) AND
2. Source has `pkpass_template` AND
3. the trip's ticket_types is one of `["print", "eticket", "voucher"]` ([array](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ee5e237092e4dff07618e7a29be6f2f5310c5a25/apps/bookie/components/core/domain/model/ticket-type.ts#L3C41-L3C73)) AND
4. the ticket has `fields` and a “barcode” (`ticket.fields?.barcode` )

**Google Wallet** Tickets are generated when ([code](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ee5e237092e4dff07618e7a29be6f2f5310c5a25/apps/bookie/components/ticket-generation/get-google-pass-jwt.ts#L10-L34)):

1. `GOOGLE_PAY_PASSES_ENABLED` is enabled on Bookie (which is enabled) AND
2. The trip's ticket_types is one of `["print", "eticket", "voucher"]` ([array](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/ee5e237092e4dff07618e7a29be6f2f5310c5a25/apps/bookie/components/core/domain/model/ticket-type.ts#L3C41-L3C73)) AND
3. The ticket includes a “barcode” (`ticket_data.ticket.fields?.barcode` )

# Autocomplete

As explained in the [Flex section](./flex.md), Flex is responsible for returning suggestions for the autocomplete search form on the website. In this section, we will see what actually happens in the background.

### 1. User types on the search form

When the user types on the search form, it sends a request to Flex. However, Fastly will receive the request first since Flex is running behind Fastly. For example, typing `london` will send a GET request to `https://www.busbud.com/napi/flex/suggestions/places?q=london`.

### 2. If there is a cache hit in Fastly, Fastly responds with cache

Fastly will receive the request and check cache for that query. If it is a cache hit, Fastly responds immediately from cache without propogating the request to Flex.

![autocomplete-cache-hit.png](Autocomplete/autocomplete-cache-hit.png)

### 3. If there is a cache miss in Fastly, Flex processes the request

If Fastly doesn’t have cache for that query, it will pass the request on to Flex. Once Flex queries the database to get suggestions, the response from Flex is:

1. returned to the client
2. cached in Fastly for subsequent requests

![autocomplete-cache-miss.png](Autocomplete/autocomplete-cache-miss.png)

Flex consists of dialect providers that are responsible for resolving data for each dialect type. In this case, the `places provider` is used to process the suggestions request. `places` is a dialect that combines both `cities` and `locations`. Therefore, the suggestions returned to the user will contain both city and location suggestions. Not all autocomplete suggestions are resolved by the `places provider`. Consumers such as NN and mobile apps uses the `cities provider` to process the suggestions request. As suggested by its name, the suggestions will only contain cities.

**Suggestions returned by places provider (cities + locations)**

![places-provider.png](Autocomplete/places-provider.png)

A location is analogous to a bus stop (e.g. Port Authority in NYC).

**Suggestions returned by cities provider (only cities)**

![cities-provider.png](Autocomplete/cities-provider.png)

# Interconnections # Introduction Interconnection flow allows quick search of interconnecting trips. The major part of trip construction is done by interconnection worker and cronjob.
💡 Note: Interconnection trip search is only available if trip legs are available in cache.
- **Example:** 1) New search metadata cache entry for Montreal -> Toronto 2) Search metadata cache already holds trips: Quebec -> Montreal Toronto -> London Toronto -> Niagara 3) Interconnection flow will store information regarding possible interconnection trips in Redis: Quebec -> Toronto: { Quebec -> Montreal, Montreal -> Toronto } Montreal -> London: { Montreal -> Toronto, Toronto -> London } Montreal -> Niagara: { Montreal -> Toronto, Toronto -> Niagara } 4) During search, Poll Service flow will pull trips based on the stored interconnection information. **Interconnections legs must have the following requirements:** - Transfers are not allowed between 12am and 5am if the transfer time exceeds 2 hours. - Transfers at the same station must have a transfer window greater than 30 minutes. - For transfers at different stations: - The transfer window must be at least 120 minutes. - The transfer station must be within 25 kilometers of the previous station. - Passengers must be able to reach the transfer station before the next bus departs, assuming a travel speed of at least 450 meters per minute. - Transfers must have a total window of less than 21 hours. - Only valid ticket types and boarding requirements that support interconnections are allowed. - Interconnections through a second country are not allowed if the origin and destination are in the same country. After the trip legs are approved, we select the best ones based on the following conditions, where tie breakers move to the next condition: - Earliest next leg (shortest transfer within requirements) - Cheapest - Same Operator - Same Class For instant interconnections (Tier 1), we pick the top 5 from the lists above: - **North America / LATAM** - For North/Central/South America routes we build interconnections only on routes which match following conditions: - routes that have direct bus supply, and had more than 2000 searches in the previous year, and the routes are not already covered by Flixbus to avoid pollution. - routes that do not have direct bus supply, and had more than 500 searches in the previous year - **South Africa** - For South Africa routes we build interconnections only on routes which match following conditions: - routes that do not have direct bus supply, and had more than 200 searches in the previous year - **Europe** - Europe is very heavy to fully support interconnections. To support instant interconnections on popular routes in Europe we have added a possibility to selectively add specific routes. - only routes which are part of [this](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/master/tools/user-searches/query.sql#L112) query will be open to build interconnections. Once routes has been added to the query, the query should be rerun (see [readme](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/master/tools/user-searches/README.md)) **Point Of Interest Interconnections** The general rule for interconnections is that the connecting city must be different from both the origin and destination. However, we allow manually unlocking specific cities that support Point Of Interest (POI) interconnections. For example: **Windsor → Toronto Union Station → Toronto Airport** Currently, POI interconnections are only supported in **Toronto**. - To enable additional cities, update [this list](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/7122794eb9764adbba683a1a90c67a4e4da73c02/src/route-resolver/resolver.ts#L17) in **Flex**. While making changes, ensure the new city is not filtered out in **user_searches** by checking [this query](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/7122794eb9764adbba683a1a90c67a4e4da73c02/tools/user-searches/query.sql#L39). Since we have a limit on the number of interconnections that can be generated, priority will be given to trips connecting to **airport locations**.
💡 A supplier (source) must have their `interconnection_enabled` flag set to `true` for it to be eligible for interconnection, meaning we can manually validate what sources to interconnect beforehand.
# Technical details Interconnection flow consists of the following parts: 1. [Search Metadata Cache worker](Interconnections.md) 2. [Interconnection Departure Results queue](Interconnections.md) 3. [Interconnection cronjob](Interconnections.md) 4. [Interconnection Combinations queue](Interconnections.md) 5. [Interconnection poll](Interconnections.md) ## **Search Metadata Cache worker** For each new entry to search metadata cache, a message is submitted to **ps_interconnection_departure_results** queue consisting of *origin_city_id*, *destination_city_id*, *outbound_date and passenger_counts.* ```mermaid flowchart LR getDepartures((live.getDepartures.results))-->|Listen|QCCD[\ps_city_cache_departure_results\] QCCD-->PC{passenger
count?} PC-->|More than one adult|Submit1[Submit]-->|origin_city_id, destination_city_id,\noutbound_date, passenger_counts|QIDR[\ps_interconnection_departure_results\] PC-->|One adult|Submit2[Submit]-->|debounce-sm-city-cache debounce key|L2[(L2Redis)] ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR getDepartures((live.search.resultsUpdated))-->|Listen|QCCT[\ps_city_cache_tasks\] QCCT-->Poll[Poll Trips] Poll-->PC{passenger
count?} PC-->|One adult|Submit[Submit]-->|origin_city_id, destination_city_id,\noutbound_date, passenger_counts|QIDR[\ps_interconnection_departure_results\] Poll-->|Update redis with trips information|L2[(L2Redis)] ``` ## **Interconnection Departure Results queue** ### Summary: **ps_interconnection_departure_results** queue is responsible for submitting interconnection debounce keys to redis for one-way searches. ![Untitled](Interconnections/Untitled.png) ### Flow: 1. For each one-way message received from search metadata cache create a debounce key and store it in redis ## **Interconnection cronjob** ### Summary: Interconnection cronjob is responsible for finding possible interconnection combination keys: For each debounce key, build possible interconnection combination keys based on information stored in search metadata cache and submit them to **ps_interconnection_combinations** queue - **Interconnection key example:** Debounce key: city_a -> city_b Interconnection combinations: city_c -> city_b (possible interconnection through city_a) city_a -> city_d (possible interconnection through city_b) ![Untitled](Interconnections/Untitled%201.png) ### Flow: 1. Pull and delete entries from *debounce-ic* key in Redis (submitted by Interconnection Departure Results queue) 2. Find all cities which can be used as first/second leg of debounce key (flex call) - **Example:** Debounce key: **city_a -> city_b** First leg city city_c (route **city_c -> city_a -> city_b**) Second leg city city_d (route **city_a -> city_b -> city_d**) 3. Build all possible search metadata Redis cache keys based on found cities: - **First leg city_c example:** **sm-city_c-city_a-yesterday** **sm-city_c-city_a-today** - **Second leg city_d example:** **sm-city_b-city_d-today** **sm-city_b-city_d-tomorrow** 4. Use built search metadata cache keys to verify if trips exist in redis 5. For each key which exists, build an interconnection key - **Example:** Debounce key: city_a -> city_b Interconnection keys: city_a-city_d-today city_c-city_b-yesterday city_c-city_b-today 6. Submit each possible interconnection key with passenger counts to **ps_interconnection_combinations** queue ## **Interconnection Combinations queue** ### Summary: Interconnection combinations queue is responsible for polling trips for each interconnection key and store trip hashes of corresponding trips in Redis in following format: Interconnection key: { all possible hashed trip keys } Interconnection key looks like: **ic_origin-city-id_destination-city-id_outbound-date_passenger-counts** ![Untitled](Interconnections/Untitled%202.png) ### Flow: 1. Poll trips for each interconnection key 2. Build trip hash for each trip and build a **hashed trip key**: route_ids-date-trip_hash 3. Store interconnection keys and corresponding **hashed trip keys** in redis Interconnection key: { all possible hashed trip keys } ## **Interconnection poll** ### Summary: During the search, poll interconnection trips consist of pulling hashed trip keys for corresponding poll and building interconnection trips based on the data. ![Untitled](Interconnections/Untitled%203.png) ### Flow: 1. Retrieve hashed trip keys for corresponding search from redis 2. Pull routes from flex and match them with routes from redis hashed trip keys 3. Build search requests for matching flex routes and pull trips from Inventory Service 4. Filter pulled trips by matching pulled trip hash with trip hashes from hashed trip keys and add them to trip maps 5. Build trip pairs by finding interconnectable trips from trip maps 6. Generate public trips from trip pairs

# Supply Rules

Supply rules are a system designed to control the availability of supply by enforcing restrictions based on a set of conditions, such as sources, partners, operators, channels. The goal is to replace rigid, hardcoded logic with a flexible, centralized, and easily configurable solution that business can manage through the [Backoffice](https://backoffice.busbud-int.com/dashboard/bus-company/supply-rules).

These rules can be created or edited to control specific routes, operators, currencies, and other trip or route details. But their primary use is to define which sources are accessible to each demand partner or whitelabel.

<aside>
ℹ️

Supply rules are inherently restrictive. Whenever the conditions of a rule match, the corresponding trip, route, and any other record being evaluated should be invalidated.

</aside>

## Application

Supply rules are stored in the Grand-Central (GC) database. A dedicated [integration package](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/tree/master/packages/supply-rules) provides a unified framework for evaluating records such as trips, routes, and more to come. This package not only determines whether a record should be invalidated but also identifies the specific supply rules responsible for the decision.

They are currently applied during searches in Poll-Service, ensuring that restricted supply is filtered out before reaching partners or users. Supply rules are also used in the Flex routes resolver to reduce the number of routes based on demand partner (or whitelabel) and source restrictions.

<aside>
ℹ️

Any service still relying on the `partner_sources` table should transition to the Supply Rules system.

</aside>

### Trips evaluation

Trip evaluation is conducted **per-segment**, meaning that if any segment is considered invalid, the entire trip will be invalidated.

## Disabling rules

Rules **must not be deleted** for auditing purposes. If a rule is no longer applicable, it should be disabled.

<aside>
⚠️

Rules **must not be reused or repurposed**! Modifying a rule that previously defined sources for demand partner A to now apply to partner B makes auditing difficult and affects the clarity of historical records.

</aside>

## Auditing

Every modification to a supply rule is logged in the `supply_rule_edits` table for audit purposes. Each entry records the previous values of the rule, allowing for comparisons with the current or subsequent versions. While the Backoffice interface only displays the author and timestamp of edits, full details can be accessed directly from the database.

```sql
SELECT * FROM supply_rule_edits sre
WHERE sre.rule_id = :id
ORDER BY sre.updated_at DESC
```

# The Search Flow

In this section, we will explain the search flow by going through the work carried out by each of the services in the stack. As seen below, `Grand Central`, `Poll Service`, `Flex`, `Inventory Service` are involved in the backend to complete a successful search.

![search-stack.png](The%20Search%20Flow/search-stack.png)

## 1. Initiate search

![search-form-complete.png](The%20Search%20Flow/search-form-complete.png)

When a user clicks on the search button after completing the search form, a request is sent to our Search V2 stack. First, the request from `Pubweb` reaches `Poll Service` through `Grand Central` (Although the objective of Search V2 is to migrate all search logic out of Grand Central, we are still sending requests to Grand Central because we are relying on it to handle some of the tasks yet to be migrated). After the initial request, `Pubweb` will periodically poll the backend until the search request is complete.

## 2. Process search request and delegate tasks

Once `Poll Service` receives the search request, it needs to perform and delegate the following tasks:

### 1. Get all the routes that connect from origin to destination from `Flex`

First, Poll Service needs to get all the routes for the given origin/destination pair from Flex. The cities provider in Flex resolves the routes by querying the database. The response is cached in Fastly.

![resolve-routes.png](The%20Search%20Flow/resolve-routes.png)

### 2. For each route, request departures from `Inventory Service`

Using the routes data, `Poll Service` requests departures for each route from `Inventory Service`. `Inventory Service` is responsible for retrieving departures either from cache or the supplier’s API. When it receives a request for departures, there are three possible scenarios:

1. Cache hit
    
    ![cache-hit.png](The%20Search%20Flow/cache-hit.png)
    
2. Cache hit but the cache entry is deemed stale by the caching policies
    
    ![cache-hit-stale.png](The%20Search%20Flow/cache-hit-stale.png)
    
3. Cache miss
    
    ![cache-miss.png](The%20Search%20Flow/cache-miss.png)
    

### 3. Assemble the departures

Once Poll Service receives departures from `Inventory Service`, it assembles the departures before returning them to `Grand Central` with a `complete` flag to tell the client whether to keep polling or not. The `complete` flag will be set to true when departures for all the routes are returned.

Please note that if there was a cache miss, departures for that route will not be available immediately because `Inventory Service` is fetching the data in the background from the supplier’s API. It will be available only after when the departures are fetched and written to the cache. Therefore, in the case of a cache miss, the `complete` flag will be set to false to tell `Pubweb` to continue polling. Those departures will be made available on subsequent polls.

`Poll Service` uses `Redis` in order to keep track of the status of each route for a given search request. This allows `Poll Service` to determine whether departures for all routes have been returned or not. If the search for all routes are complete, the `complete` flag will be set to true.

![poll-state.png](The%20Search%20Flow/poll-state.png)

image

## 3. Filter departures

The assembled departures are processed in `Grand Central` before they are returned to `Pubweb`. `Grand Central` is responsible for filtering out departures that do not meet the quality bar. For example, departures with invalid date, malformed prices, incorrect cities will be filtered out because we do not want to show them to our users.

![filter-departures.png](The%20Search%20Flow/filter-departures.png)

image

## 4. Polling

`Pubweb` will keep polling until the `complete` flag is set to true.

# Maintenance

## Logs

Logs for integrations are currently stored on Google Cloud Storage. We do this in order to have a cheap logging solution for the gigabytes of logs we push from the integrations per hour. The logs are queryable through a VM that can be accessed with `bb gcs-logs`. You’ll find all integrations in paths `/gcs/INTEGRATION/DATE/DATE-TIME.log` on the host. You can query through the logs using traditional Unix tooling (`cat *.log | grep PURCHASE_ID`), Node, or [Tidalwave](https://github.com/dustinblackman/tidalwave/tree/1.0.0).

### Tail Live Logs

To tail the logs of your adapter in real time, you can use `bb logs -a my-integration -f`.

By default, [`busbud-requester`](https://github.com/busbud/busbud-requester) and [BELa](https://github.com/busbud/integration-bela) logs are recorded. This is usually enough for most purposes. However, if you need to send custom logs you can use [`busbud-logger`](https://github.com/busbud/busbud-logger).

### BELa and Requester

Two types of requests are made to and from the adapter. Logs with `{"name": "bela"}` are requests being made to the adapter itself from our consuming services, and `{"name": "requester"}` are requests being made from the adapter to the partners API.

### Purchase Logs

We also have a tool to simplify gathering logs for purchases with gist creation support called `bb purchase-logs`. See `bb help` for more details on usage. Example:

```bash
# Downloads all the logs for purchase ID 1679911, formats them with gisterator, and then uploads them to gist.
bb purchase-logs 1679911 --gist
```

### Request and Purchase ID

Every log line contains an identifier supplied by NAPI to track the calls made for a single request. Each call to BELa and outbound calls to the partners API’s will contain `{"request_id": "IDHERE"}` at the root of the log line, making it easy to grep for logs for a specific request.

For purchase, the `purchase_id` is passed along for all purchase related request with `{"purchase_id": "IDHERE"}` at the root of the log. This is how tools such as `bb purchase-logs` find and returns log lines for you.

### jq / Parsing logs

`jq` is a really handy tool to keep in mind when processing logs as it makes life much easier to minimize the amount of data you want to read. A fun example is getting `origin_xid`, `destination_xid`, and `date` used in `getDepartures` for BlackHills on a single days worth of logs, and how often we see that combination sorted by most searched.

```bash
cat /gcs/transcor/2018-09-01/* | grep blackhills | grep bela | grep getDepartures | jq -r -c '{"origin_xid": .jsonPayload.request.body.origin_xid, "destination_xid": .jsonPayload.request.body.destination_xid, "date": .jsonPayload.request.body.date}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -n -r

      5 {"origin_xid":"830357","destination_xid":"580294","date":"2018-10-01"}
      5 {"origin_xid":"830126","destination_xid":"581350","date":"2018-10-01"}
      5 {"origin_xid":"830126","destination_xid":"580393","date":"2018-10-01"}
      5 {"origin_xid":"820028","destination_xid":"580305","date":"2018-10-01"}
      5 {"origin_xid":"581185","destination_xid":"580294","date":"2018-10-01"}
      4 {"origin_xid":"831237","destination_xid":"830126","date":"2018-09-01"}
      ...
```

To break down this command pipe:

- `cat /gcs/transcor/2018-09-01/*` prints all the logs for Transcor made on 2018-09-01, which is the adapter the BlackHills source runs on.
- `grep blackhills` filters all lines that do not contain the word `blackhills`. All our logs for the BlackHills source will have `{"source": "blackhills"}` at the root of the log.
- `grep bela` will filter all lines that do not contain the word `bela`. All the request/responses made to the HTTP layer for an integration have `{"name": "bela"}` at the root of the log.
- `grep getDepartures` will filter all lines that do not contain the word `getDepartures`. Any log outputed from an integration will contain the method that’s being called, in our case `{"method": "getDepartures"}` lives at the root of the log.
- `jq -r -c '{"origin_xid": .jsonPayload.request.body.origin_xid, "destination_xid": .jsonPayload.request.body.destination_xid, "date": .jsonPayload.request.body.date}'` parses each log line and creates a new object only containing `origin_xid`, `destination_xid`, and `date` by setting the keys and paths to the values in the log line.
- `sort` will sort all our newly created JSON lines alphabetically in order for the next command to work correctly.
- `uniq -c` will remove any duplications outputted from the previous comamnds, and count how many duplicates there were, allowing us to see how often our combindation came up.
- `sort -n -r` sorts the output from `uniq -c` by number, putting the highest seen entry at the top.
