# **FAQ**

## **Why are modifiers and conditions separated?**

Conditions are used to select which Interconnections we are applying the rule to. Either to block, allow, prioritize or modify.

Modifiers are the values that will modify the default value from the configuration of each PS filter.

For example: imagine a rule that says that the maximum transfer time for VIARail trips is 60 mins. In this case, a VIARail interconnection is a condition (which interconnections the rule is applied to), and the maximum transfer time of 60min is a modifier that changes the default value.

This is also useful for the default filter values. As described above, we’ll add all current default values as modifiers rules with priority 1000 (lowest possible priority) without any conditions (meaning they apply to all interconnections; unless a rule with a higher priority is available).

## **Why not use supply rules?**

Supply rules are designed to handle filtering out inventory based on the search context (given a search, which inventory from cache can we sell?) while interconnection rules control which interconnections can be generated to be saved on cache.

## **Can we use supply rules to filter out interconnections before applying interconnection rules?**

Not really. Most of the current supply rules have conditions related to search parameters - as they are designed to control which inventory is going to be returned for a given search. This means that we cannot use them to control which inventory can be used for interconnections - we generate interconnections and cache them for use in every channel. We can use supply rules to control which of the cached interconnections can be returned on the given search (which we already do), but not to control how they are generated.

# Overview

---

Our import process needs to start hitting the gym. It tends to run into memory issues and troubleshooting is a pain. This spec is proposing the following to achieve a more resilient, debuggable and extendable import:

- distinguishing an export process from the import
- imports as isolated and ephemeral processes using cron jobs
- use of external storage and queues for better importer-service load management and improved troubleshooting

![Diag. 1 - System view of the proposal. Arrows represent direction of communication.](Stronger%20Partner%20Data%20Imports/Untitled.png)

Diag. 1 - System view of the proposal. Arrows represent direction of communication.

# Context

---

Our import process exports location and route data from our inventory partners (aka sources). These location and route exports contain the relevant information for performing trip origin/destination searches against the source APIs. 

The import process is triggered in two ways:

- A source import job schedule within the Postgres database `importer` used by the `importer-service`.
- An API endpoint trigger on the importer-service.

Once a source import job is triggered, the service proceeds to make HTTP requests to our source integration API, through the `/import` endpoints. Depending on the amount of data exported from our partners, the import data is processed in batches through several HTTP calls and a property within responses indicates if data remains to be retrieved.

![Diag. 2 - Current system view of import process. Arrows represent direction of communication.](Stronger%20Partner%20Data%20Imports/Untitled%201.png)

Diag. 2 - Current system view of import process. Arrows represent direction of communication.

This process is currently leading to the following issues:

- Overloading integration memory and CPU resources due to their import process (increasing infrastructure costs)
- Creating sudden load onto running integration instances and risking their availability

# Proposal

---

## Key components

### Distinguishing between partner exports and imports

Our current import process can be viewed in three main phases: data export from partner systems, partner data import, and subsequent import processes. This is mainly wording but it allows us to view our import into 3 composable steps that can be troubleshooted accordingly. This proposal puts its main focus on the partner export phase.

### Isolated and ephemeral

Running the partner data export (aka the integration import flow) process within its own resource limited context makes a lot of sense: it is short-lived and it typically requires more resources than its other integration flows (search, booking). Kubernetes CronJobs are a great tool (that is familiar to our team) which can be used in this way. Consequently, using cron jobs will also reduce infrastructure related costs due to its short-lived nature + reducing the main integration service’s reserved resources. Using k8s CronJobs also enables us to easily trigger the export process manually with the `kubectl` CLI.

### External storage

Partner export data will be stored in Google Cloud Storage (GCS). The GCS document URLs will then be given to the importer-service via an HTTP call and will make the data available at the convenience of the importer; the importer-service will have control over when it wants to proceed with an import.

The exported data will be stored as JSON formatted files. This is a tradeoff on slower transfer speeds and larger file sizes for human readable data and a familiar data format. Storage costs on GCS are relatively low, and imports are not time sensitive processes.

The current format for object paths would be as follows for location and route export data types:

- Locations: `gs://exports/locations/:source_slug/:export_date/{export_job_timestamp}_{file_idx}.json`
- Routes: `gs://exports/routes/:source_slug/:export_date/{export_job_timestamp}_{file_idx}.json`

Structure is: some export root path, export data type, source, export date, export job timestamp (start) with a file index. The timestamp with a file index should be a sufficient identifier; I don’t expect more than one export-job per day for the same data type and if it does occur, grouping them will be straightforward.

### Queues

The use of queues will be put in place for processing successful export jobs. A queue will give some additional processing control to the importer-service and a simple mechanism for reprocessing exports if errors were to occur during the import process.

Concretely, once the importer-service completes persisting the export-job related data provided by the cron job, it will publish a message to a remote queue including the export-job identifier that is ready for processing. An importer-service process will be listening to this queue and consuming messages to process exports. Other than downloading the exports from GCS, the processing logic will remain the same.

## Architecture

### Technologies

- Cron job: Kubernetes CronJob (with Terraform)
- External Storage: GCS
- Database: PostgreSQL (existing `importer` db)
- Message-broker/Queue: RabbitMQ

### Happy path flow

The following is the happy path flow:

1. Cronjob initiates and starts running the export.
2. Exported data is gradually uploaded to GCS. GCS URLs are accumulated.
3. Once all export data is uploaded to GCS, cronjob calls the importer-service to create an export-job with the export details (source, versions, export types, export URLs).
4. Importer-service creates database entries for the export-job and its exports.
5. Importer-service publishes message to remote queue for upcoming export-job processing.
6. Cronjob gracefully ends.
7. Importer-service consumes the export-job “ready” message, and proceeds with import.

![Diag. 3 - Sequence model of export process.](Stronger%20Partner%20Data%20Imports/Untitled%202.png)

Diag. 3 - Sequence model of export process.

With this design, a single HTTP call between the export cronjob and the importer-service is required for the export, reducing possible failure scenarios. Plus, the importer-service may then make the necessary assumptions regarding the “completeness” (all of the export data is available) of an export-job without validating state-related properties. 

```json
// Example importer-service POST "/export-jobs" body
{
	"source_slug": "my-source", // to link source
	"tracing_id": "asdfuioasdfuoi-asdufioasudiof-7asdf4564asdf", // for searching logs, debugging
	"versions": { 
		"int-a": "asfuio13", // should be git hash; gives us a reference to export source code
		"export-cron": "jfkdl123"
	},
	"export_types": ["location", "route"],
	"exports": [
		{
			"url": "gs://exports/locations/:source_slug/:export_date/{export_job_timestamp}_{file_idx}.json",
			"type": "location"
		},
		{
			"url": "gs://exports/routes/:source_slug/:export_date/{export_job_timestamp}_{file_idx}.json",
			"type": "route"
		}
	]
}
```

Following the HTTP call, the importer-service will persist the export-job and its exports to two new tables within the importer-db: the `ExportJob` table and the `Export` table. The next section goes into their details.

```json
{
	"id": "uiouiouoouisdf-12346asdf-fasdjfklsjadkf",
	"creation_date": "1715347976", 
	"url": "gs://exports/raw/locations/:source/:export-date/{timestamp}.json",
	"type": "location",
	"export_job": "1231asdasd213-uasdoifuasdf-uoasdfosd"
}
```

These models are to be immutable and are created following the HTTP `POST /export-jobs` call. They allow the importer-service to decide, at its convenience, when to process exports from an export-job. This model also keeps in mind the “completeness” requirement for our import deprecation process; an export-job represents a list of exports that need to be considered as a group, and cannot be processed partially.

## Job Triggers

### Manual (Engineering)

```bash
kubectl create job --from=cronjob/<cronjob-name> <job-name> -n <namespace-name>
```

### Schedule

Integration Terraform module will have a set schedule for the export job to run automatically.

## Alerts and monitoring

The export process should send the following Datadog metrics:

- k8s resource monitoring for cron job
- export-job failure (int-framework): $E_f$
- export-job completion (int-framework): $E_c$
- export-job duration (for completion) (int-framework)
- export-job processed (importer-service)
- queue related monitoring metrics (e.g. number of messages in queue)

Coverage SLI: $E_c/(E_c+E_f) \times 100$ over a weekly period per source.

# Implementation Strategy

---

Implementing these changes needs to be incremental without impact or minimally impacting the existing process until migration is complete. We should be able to use the existing integration's import logic.

The current idea is to have us modify the existing integration Terraform module and the integration framework. The Terraform module will have the cron job creation details (resource requests + limits with good defaults, cronjob schedule).

## Development tasks + timeline

These should be the relevant (somewhat ordered) tasks for implementing the spec:

1. creating new database tables in the `importer` database
2. create new RabbitMQ queue
3. create cronjob service account that has access to GCS
4. create new endpoint `/export-jobs` for the `importer-service`
5. create new export processing logic from published export-job messages
6. create new export-cron logic in the `integration-framework` package
    1. add/use existing metric for datadog monitoring and alerting
7. update integration terraform module for cronjob
8. create new Datadog export dashboard + alerts
9. migrate 3 (max) integrations and observe for a week (minimum)
10. migrate all integrations gradually to new export process
    1. use new int-framework + upgrade terraform module version and define new export related details within it
    2. deploy
    3. delete/deactivate deprecated importer-service import schedule for associated sources.
11. Clean up of deprecated importer-service endpoints.

Considering this, I believe it should take around 2-3 weeks to go through with these changes.

# Future Considerations

---

## Accessible logging information

Logging will be similar to existing workers in other deployments. Depending on how easy log retrieval is for specific export jobs, there could be room for improvement here. 

## Lifespan for exports within GCS and DB

Assuming that most exports occur weekly and that their exported data tend to be unchanged, there shouldn’t be much value in keeping them indefinitely. We could introduce an archival mechanism (batch, compress and store in archive storage class or even deletion) similar to what we do for our service log data.

GCS does have a TTL on objects if we’d like, which would require no JS/TS.

As for the DB export entries (depending on what the sentiment is regarding how long we should keep these), we could implement a cleanup mechanism as well (e.g. a clean-up cronjob).

## Other types of partner exports

Some partner systems have more than just location and route data available for our consumption (e.g. schedules, operators) before initiating searches and completing bookings. This specification tries to keep this in mind by keeping the model extensible for other possible uses.

## Hash calculation of exports

We could eventually calculate the hash of exported data to avoid unnecessary processing of exports. 

## TypeScript migration

The importer-service is currently still in JS. It would be worthwhile to migrate over to TypeScript (i.e. for the devx).

# Resources and Links

- Importer-service: [https://github.com/busbud/integration-importer](https://github.com/busbud/integration-importer)
- Integration-framework: [https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/tree/master/packages/integration-framework](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/tree/master/packages/integration-framework)
- Integration Terraform module: [https://github.com/busbud/terraform-modules/tree/master/v2/modules/integration](https://github.com/busbud/terraform-modules/tree/master/v2/modules/integration)

# Supply rules partner x source restriction

| Reviewer | Status | Date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @Dustin Blackman  | Complete | 2025-02-03 |
| @Lisa Zhao  | Complete | 2025-02-06 |
| @Muhammad Aqsam  | Complete | February 6, 2025  |
| @Paulo Moreno  | Complete | February 6, 2025  |

## 1. Introduction

This specification provides context and proposes an approach to address the current challenge of implementing efficient solutions for services that are more database-oriented and have a stricter set of requirements.

## 2. Background & Motivation

### 2.1 Context

Supply rules are a series of rules stored in our Grand-Central database, and are easily managed through Backoffice. With their dedicated package, we can evaluate records (such as trips) to determine whether supply should be invalidated.

Poll-Service has been working well with a moderate-complexity implementation of the Supply rules evaluation, and now other services need to start consuming them as well to get up-to-date data that used to be supplied by other ways.

### 2.2 Problem Statement

Unfortunately, we couldn't find a way to apply the supply rules logic in certain database-oriented scenarios mainly due to it's weakness of hard implementation on the database level - each supply rule currently has its conditions in two separated *JSONB* columns (`triggers` and `criterias`). Not only these columns are **not indexed** but each condition may use **different properties** (source, demand partner, operator, and many others) and **different evaluations** (is exactly, is in, is not in, starts with and ends with), making it tediously complex to fully implement in a SQL statement.

The cases we aim to address with this specification include the Flex route resolver implementation and other logics spread across our services dependent on the old `partners_sources` table. Another case we can patch to make sure we fully use supply rules filtering capabilities is the whitelabel cities sync.

### 2.3 Goals

- Provide a simple and fast access to a list of **partner x source** restriction.
- (nice to have) Keep the ease of use for the rules management (Backoffice).
- (nice to have) Keep the efficiency of trips evaluation (used in Poll-Service).
- (nice to have) Avoid spreading evaluation logic across different services or tools.
- (nice to have) Simplify and make the rules less confusing.

## 3. Proposed Solution

### 3.1 High-Level Approach

We should create a new table similar to the `partners_sources` and regularly populate it with up-to-date data in order to have a partner x sources restriction easily available. This table will provide the relation needed on Flex route resolver to filter out routes and a similar data to any logic consuming the old table.

### 3.2 Detailed Implementation

### 3.2.1 Supply rules package

Let's start by adapting the Supply rules evaluation in the [Supply rules package](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/tree/master/packages/supply-rules) to evaluate any record, so we can properly evaluate the partners x sources relationship regardless of other rule conditions. At the moment we can only evaluate specific types, like some variations of trips (adapter, public and domain) and routes:

```tsx
interface AdapterTripSegmentProperties {
  type: "adapter";
  source_name: string;
  operator_xid?: string;
  partner_id?: number | null;
  channel?: SearchInfo.Client | null;
  search_currency?: string | null;
  PoSe?: string | null;
}

interface PartnerXRouteProperties {
  partner_id: string;
  source_name: string;
  origin_operator_xids: string[] | null;
  destination_operator_xids: string[] | null;
}
```

This is an example of a model we'd like to work with in order to make flexible evaluations possible:

```tsx
export interface Properties {
  source_name?: string;
  operator_xid?: string;
  partner_id?: number | null;
  channel?: SearchInfo.Client | null;
  search_currency?: string | null;
  origin_city_id?: string;
  origin_country_code?: string;
  destination_city_id?: string;
  destination_country_code?: string;
  route_ids?: number[];
  PoSe?: string | null;
  PoSu?: string;
  origin_operator_xids?: string[] | null;
  destination_operator_xids?: string[] | null;
}
```

Whenever evaluating a property with value `undefined`, we must skip it and not use it to filter out the record. Example: if a rule has conditions to filter out supply with `partner A`, `source B` and `operator C`, and we're evaluating a record with only `partner A` and `source B`, we should not filter it out, as any other operator would be valid.

### 3.2.2 Grand-Central

**Database changes**

Now we create the new table in Grand-Central. Using cascade rules for update and delete actions will help during ID patches or removal of sources and demand partners, which are rare but do happen. The `created_at` column will help us check the last time we populated the table.

```sql
CREATE TABLE supply_rules_partners_sources (
  partner_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES partners(id)
    ON UPDATE CASCADE 
    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  source_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES sources(id)
    ON UPDATE CASCADE 
    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  created_at timestamp NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (partner_id, source_id)
)
```

**Worker**

Next, we should create the worker to populate the new table. We'll retrieve every partner, non-disabled source and active supply rule from the database, use the [Supply rules package](https://github.com/busbud/integration-packages/tree/master/packages/supply-rules) to execute the evaluation of each pair of partner and source, clean the table and repopulate it with fresh data.

[Example and performance results](Supply rules partner x source restriction/Example and performance results.md)

The worker will [listen](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-listen.html) to GC database for [notifications](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-notify.html) of changes on the partners, sources and supply rules tables. It might be a good idea to restrict which changes will trigger the repopulation of the table to avoid consuming resources for no reason. [Here](https://github.com/busbud/napi/pull/10999)'s a good implementation example for the notify + listen feature on a worker.

A manual way to trigger it could be useful in case we have unexpected cases or issues on the worker. After populating the table, trigger the Whitelabel cities sync ([code](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/0551e995bf24a394b16e00b953814748a537d9ee/src/workers/stream-insert/grand-central-sync/sync-whitelabel-cities.ts#L19-L47)), so we get the latest restrictions on Flex search.

The worker must be monitored and well documented.

~~We should find a good balance between the cronjob execution interval and the resources it consumes to run. Instead of populating the table every time the cronjob is executed, we can survey the rows of related tables (`partners`, `sources` and `supply_rules`) and check if there was any change since the last execution. If there were any changes, we simply delete all the table content and recreate it. If not, we simply skip the execution.~~

### 3.2.3 Implement the changes

<aside>
ℹ️

Create a feature flag, giving us an easy rollback mechanism. As this will touch multiple projects, it might be necessary to create more than one.

</aside>

Now it's time to migrate every code that is still using `partners_sources` table. Different from the previous version, the new table is only meant to be read as "**allowed** sources per demand partner”. So places that implement the table data should be adapted to use the list properly, no longer relying on the partner `sources_restriction` column.

We should also replace the existing Supply rules implementation on Flex route resolver and whitelabel cities sync ([code](https://github.com/busbud/flex/blob/0551e995bf24a394b16e00b953814748a537d9ee/src/workers/stream-insert/grand-central-sync/sync-whitelabel-cities.ts#L19-L47)) with the new table.

### 3.3 Tradeoffs

These changes are creating an extension of the supply rules features, making sure the most used supply restriction in our services is available, fast and simple to consume.

The performance for existing logic that consumes the old version of this restriction should be untouched while adding a light-weight worker. Although this will introduce a new moving part that orbits Grand-Central, its code will be easy to maintain, as the evaluation complexity will remain contained inside the dedicated package.

This implementation is not a future-proof solution for other restrictions (e.g., operator, currency), but it ensures that everything currently working relying on the old table will get the latest data from the new feature at no extra cost per request. If more elegant and robust solutions are needed, we'll still support the full evaluation, which will remain unchanged.

The data will be consistent and we'll be able to keep it updated. Depending on the increase of partners and sources, we can consider improvements on the worker script to instead of repopulating the whole table, make more precise operations.

### 3.4 Clean up and Next Steps

### 3.4.1 Merging triggers and criteria

There are some rough edges that could be polished in Supply rules, especially on it's data model and UI presentation. Merging triggers and criteria under a new property can simplify and make the rules less confusing. Having both give us no benefits on the user experience in Backoffice - we try to explain them as two separate things, when in fact they have the exact same role -, and in the evaluation having both don't add any feature:

```tsx
// integration-packages/packages/supply-rules/src/services/evaluator/segment-properties.ts
const triggered = rule.triggers.every((trigger) => this.isCriteriaTruthy(trigger, properties));
if (!triggered) {
  return false;
}

return rule.criterias.every((criteria) => this.isCriteriaTruthy(criteria, properties));
```

- Implementation steps
    - Add the new property `conditions` in `core-types`, `supply-rules` and `test-database` packages
    - Grand-Central
        - Create new column `conditions` in the `supply_rules` table
        - Implement the new property in supply rules endpoints as optional (use `triggers` + `criteria` when it's not provided)
    - Populate `conditions` column with the `triggers` + `criterias` data.
    - Update the script that manipulates database data during preview restore to also copy and manipulate `conditions` column ([code](https://github.com/busbud/napi/blob/1b80139ff8f3edc87495673ed09ff2530a2251c9/apps/grand-central/scripts/transform-partner-sources-into-supply-rules/index.ts#L132-L154))
    
    From now on we have all the data up-to-date on both use cases: `conditions` and `triggers + criterias` 
    
    - Remove `triggers` and `criterias` properties from Supply rules types in `core-types`, `supply-rules` and `test-database` packages
    - Update int-packages and remove `triggers` and `criterias` in favor of `conditions` on Poll-Service
        - Need to be careful because of the cached search context
    - (we should not need to update Flex as it's supposed to be already using the new table at this point)
    - Remove `triggers` and `criterias` in favor of `conditions` on Betterez Service ([PR](https://github.com/busbud/betterez-service/pull/60))
    - Make `triggers` and `criterias` optional in Grand-Central endpoints
    - Remove `triggers` and `criterias` in favor of `conditions` on Backoffice
    - Remove `triggers` and `criterias` from Grand-Central endpoint
    - Update the script that manipulates database data during preview restore removing the `triggers` and `criterias` columns
    - (not sure if we would want to keep them) Remove `triggers` and `criterias` columns from table via migration

### 3.4.2 Backoffice improvements

**Merge triggers and criteria**

By merging triggers and criteria conditions into a single list we can make it simpler and less confusing:

Before

![image.png](Supply%20rules%20partner%20x%20source%20restriction/image.png)

After

![image.png](Supply%20rules%20partner%20x%20source%20restriction/image%201.png)

**Provide visual examples**

Instead of giving a simple descriptive example, create a help button that opens a modal with some visual examples combining the description + UI elements.

The following one is an example of how to use the `list excludes` evaluation.

![image.png](Supply%20rules%20partner%20x%20source%20restriction/image%202.png)

### 3.4.3 Clean up

Remove the feature flag implementation and the old version of the code from every project affected. After that, remove the feature flag.

---

### Appendix

**`partners_sources` table**

The main feature under deprecation in favor of Supply rules. It can still be managed in Backoffice on the [Partners page](https://backoffice.busbud-int.com/dashboard/partners), and consists of a list that will either behave as an *allowlist* or *blocklist* depending on the option chosen for the partner (`sources_restriction` in the `partners` table).

**Flex route resolver**

It's responsible to provide all the possible routes between an origin and a destination, and should invalidate any routes not allowed to the requesting partner. This invalidation is currently only applied by partner x source, using the `partners_sources` table.

# Supply rules repository on Poll Service

## Introduction

Create a **repository** to handle the **Supply rules** on Poll Service with the intention of serving `SearchContext` instances and reduce drastically the database access.

## Glossary

- Repository: class used to temporarily store and manage data, allowing fast, easy and centralized access.

## What is this going to fix or improve?

1. (important improvement) Allow `SearchContext` objects built from cache to have access to up to date supply rules.
    - Currently: supply rules are only fetched during the initialization of the `SearchContext` or when there are routes missing when it is built from cache or has the `build` method called. This can lead to cases an incorrect change on a supply rule takes up to 15 minutes to be fixed in already instantiated searches.
2. (improvement) Remove complex SQL SELECT statement to retrieve partially matching supply rules ([code](https://github.com/busbud/poll-service/blob/9c9025f3a468d6d4678396b502be648744d3a915/src/models/supply-rule.ts#L66-L83)) and turn it into proper readable code in the supply rules package.
3. (improvement) Reduce drastically database readings and improve performance
As the SELECT statement is built depending on the search context properties, we ended up with 27 different queries from [July 31st - Aug 1st](https://app.datadoghq.com/apm/services/poll_service-postgres/operations/pg.query/resources?query=env%3Apreview%20operation_name%3Apg.query%20service%3Apoll_service-postgres&dependencyMap=qson%3A%28data%3A%28telemetrySelection%3Aall_sources%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&deployments=qson%3A%28data%3A%28hits%3A%28selected%3Aversion_count%29%2Cerrors%3A%28selected%3Aversion_count%29%2Clatency%3A%2195%2CtopN%3A%215%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&env=production&errors=qson%3A%28data%3A%28issueSort%3ATOTAL_COUNT%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&fromUser=true&groupMapByOperation=null&infrastructure=qson%3A%28data%3A%28viewType%3Apods%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&logs=qson%3A%28data%3A%28indexes%3A%5B%5D%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&panels=qson%3A%28data%3A%28%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&resources=qson%3A%28data%3A%28visible%3A%21t%2Chits%3A%28selected%3Atotal%29%2Cerrors%3A%28selected%3Atotal%29%2Clatency%3A%28selected%3Ap95%29%2CtopN%3A%2110%2Csearch%3Asupply%29%2Cversion%3A%211%29&sort=p95%2Cdesc&summary=qson%3A%28data%3A%28visible%3A%21t%2Cerrors%3A%28selected%3Acount%29%2Chits%3A%28selected%3Acount%29%2Clatency%3A%28selected%3Alatency%2Cslot%3A%28agg%3A95%29%2Cdistribution%3A%28isLogScale%3A%21f%29%2CshowTraceOutliers%3A%21t%29%2Csublayer%3A%28slot%3A%28layers%3Aservice%29%2Cselected%3Apercentage%29%2ClagMetrics%3A%28selectedMetric%3A%21s%2CselectedGroupBy%3A%21s%29%29%2Cversion%3A%211%29&traces=qson%3A%28data%3A%28%29%2Cversion%3A%210%29&view=spans&start=1722394800000&end=1722567540000&paused=true).
    
    ![image.png](Supply%20rules%20repository%20on%20Poll%20Service/image.png)
    
    The amount of requests is not high when compared to other items in the list (~2.7KK) but their total duration surpasses the routes query duration (~4h01), guaranteeing it's place on the **top 3**. Currently we **only have 35 active rules** - and this number should increase significantly during the next months.
    
    ![image.png](Supply%20rules%20repository%20on%20Poll%20Service/image%201.png)
    
    The query is currently filtering the supply rules by using some key properties (source and partner being the main ones). This guarantees our search contexts end up carrying only 1~2 rules from the 35.
    
4. (small improvement) Unifies the loading of supply rules in one spot. Currently it's being loaded on the `init`, and on `getFromcacheAndUpdate` and `build` when there are missing routes. This proposal aims to only load supply rules in the `build` method, no matter there are missing routes or not.

## Implementation

### `SearchContext`

1. Supply rules list would still live in the `SearchContext` objects
    1. They will **not be cached anymore**
    2. The current supply rules map can be converted into an array - it won't be cached anymore and it's not accessed by any key like the other records (sources, operators…) - at the moment every time we want to use the supply rules we need to use `Object.values()`
2. Execute a partial matching filter during the `build` method to load the supply rules
    1. The filter will work like the SQL SELECT statement currently filters the rows
    2. We can implement it in the `@busbud/supply-rules` package as a new static function

### The repository

> The initial idea was using a Redis database published by GC, so any time a rule was created, updated or removed we'd have the change reflected instantaneously in the search results. Although this would be a nice trait for the supply rules, specially when we talk about quickly addressing incorrect changes, situations like this should not be common. In order to create less "moving parts" I'm now proposing a SQL repository + recycler repository (in-memory repository with TTL).
> 
1. It will consist of a recycler repository that will fetch the data from a SQL repository.
2. A nice TTL for the recycler repository could be 30~60 seconds.
3. It should load all the **active** (`state` = `active`) supply rules (currently 35, but this number could increase a lot depending on new business approaches). This is really hard to predict, but we were working with 100~200 rules earlier.
4. It will handle millions of requests a day, always returning all it's records each time. The current SQL query is executed ~1.3KK times a day, so I'd expect the repository being accessed a similar amount of times, or maybe even more as we'll always load fresh supply rules from the repository, regardless of missing routes.
Updating the supply rules every 30 seconds would result in up to 2,880 database readings per day per pod.

## Complexity

This repository should be of small complexity just as it's SQL statement, and the fact it won't be cached anymore and there will be only one point of loading supply rules should remove complexity that was recently implemented.

The only challenge in this case should be the code to filter out supply rules by exclusion in the `supply-rules` int-package. But in the end it will be reproducing what the SQL statement that we aim to remove currently does, but it'll be readable.

Supply rules have a different role compared to other `SearchContext` entities (sources, routes, operators, etc), they can't be fetched by any specific ID in this context and their criteria (which we use to filter out in a first moment) can have include many different properties, evaluations and values, making it a pain to filter using SQL statements.
filename: Supply rules repository on Poll Service.md

# Currencies: billed vs source vs partner’s

- **Source Currency:** in which currency does Busbud pay the supplier? There can be multiple suppliers involved in a purchase so there can be multiple source currencies. Amounts that don't have a supplier, for example interests or discretionary refunds don't have supplier amounts or a supplier currency.
- **Billed Currency**: in which currency does Busbud receive the payment from the customer? A purchase has a single billed currency. This isn't the currency that is displayed on the website during the purchase but the currency in which the customer was actually charged. For IOU partners like Trainline, the billed currency is always the partner currency.
- **Partner Currency**: is the currency of the settlement between Busbud and the Partner.

# Email Proxy Service (EPS)

The service uses an [XP Flag(called purchase-mask-email)](https://growthbook.busbud-int.com/features/purchase-mask-email) to disable using the EPS for upcoming purchase and to block forward to some email providers(aka Microsoft).

## Troubleshooting

### IP Reputation alert

When you get an alert for IP Reputation it means a provider is banning our IP causing messages sent to a given domain to bounce and therefore the customer not receiving the message.

To mitigate, the number of people impacted by this, we:

1. Check what is/are the domain(s) causing issue by running

```sql
SELECT split_part("CustomerEmailProxy".original, '@', 2) AS domain, count(*) as nb_bans
FROM "Message"
INNER JOIN "EmailProxyMapping" ON "Message".email_proxy_mapping_id = "EmailProxyMapping".id
INNER JOIN "CustomerEmailProxy" ON "EmailProxyMapping".customer_email_proxy = "CustomerEmailProxy".proxy
INNER JOIN "DeliveryAttempt" ON "DeliveryAttempt".message_id = "Message".id
INNER JOIN "DeliveryAttemptStatus" ON "DeliveryAttemptStatus".delivery_attempt_id = "DeliveryAttempt".id
WHERE "DeliveryAttemptStatus".status = 'bounce'
AND ((status_details::jsonb #>> '{}')::jsonb) ->> 'bounce_classification' = 'Reputation'
AND "DeliveryAttemptStatus".created_at >= '2025-12-05' -- UPDATE THE DATE HERE
GROUP BY domain
ORDER BY nb_bans DESC;
```

This will list all the domains that have been banned since the date you provided

2. Add the domain to the list of banned domains in the [purchase-mask-email XP](https://growthbook.busbud-int.com/features/purchase-mask-email)

# How we work

# **Before coding**

- Kick-off meeting
- Create a main issue
    - labeled as **Epic** in the repository [team-personalization](https://github.com/busbud/personalization-team) (or directly in the corresponding repository)
    - It will help to structure and organize the work among the team
    - Break down the epic into sub-issues
        - Each sub-issue to include **acceptance criteria** which need to be ensured to match what is expected from a product standpoint
    - Each bet needs to get its Epic issue.

# **Review process**

- Tests needs to be performed by the issue owner
- The PR should be first open in a draft to make sure CI is green before assigning reviewers (as a red CI might impact consequent code changes)
- If a comment is opened, the comment’s author is the only one who shall close it
- Enforce 1 approval per PR (to be done in the wallet [@Amélie](https://busbud.slack.com/team/UTCF3HEKD))
    - Except for revert branches ([@Amélie](https://busbud.slack.com/team/UTCF3HEKD) to override in the config)
- QA Acceptance criteria to be added in a Github template
- Demo Video can be a great bonus - depending on the feature’s complexity to test.

# **After it’s shipped**

- **ADR** should be merged before the feature gets started as much as possible
- **Monitoring** should be implemented alongside with the feature
    - Once feature is merged, it gets in prod so it’s already too late
- Manual QA once feature is shipped in production
    - Feature flag to be used for demo / testing / hand-off purposes
    - Add a **“personalization”** tag and a description on ALL the feature flag we introduce
- Systematic Hand-off meetings
- Columns to be followed in the Project to reflect the progress state of the issue
    - Preview
    - Documentation
    - QA
    - Hand-off
- Write a runbook for alerting in Notion when needed
    - Add the link of the runback in the feature flag description and / or in the alert

# Jan 1st: Update tier list

# Details

This script is ran every year on January 1st and update all Loyalty profiles with their new computed Tier Status. The Tier Status depends currently only on the number of rewarded tickets purchased the previous year from the 1st January to the 31st December.

It is safe to rerun this script since updated profiles won't be updated again.

Commands to run in the terminal for local and production:

```bash
DATABASE_URL=$(yarn -s get-envs:production DATABASE_URL) yarn do:loyalty:update-tier-status-profiles
```

# Finance Data

When a customer buys RFAR, a **CFAR** `line_item`  will be added to their purchase. The amount of the item is currently set at 10% of the ticket value. 

If the customer cancels their trip and ask for a refund, a `base_price_refund` and a `transaction_credit` will be added to the purchase line items.

# Queries

### accounts with a reserve balance over 0

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM (
    SELECT account_id
    FROM transactions
    GROUP BY account_id
    HAVING SUM(CASE  
          WHEN transaction_type = 'RESERVE' THEN amount
          WHEN transaction_type = 'RELEASE' THEN -amount
          ELSE 0
    END) > 0
) AS result;
```

### 15 accounts with most transactions

```sql
SELECT
	count(*) AS transaction_count,
	account_id
FROM
	transactions
GROUP BY
	account_id
ORDER BY
	transaction_count DESC
LIMIT 15;
```

### consumed deposit states for a specific account

```sql
SELECT
	d.id AS deposit_id,
	d.amount AS original_amount,
	d.created_at,
	COALESCE(SUM(
			CASE WHEN t.transaction_type = 'RELEASE' THEN
				- r.amount
			ELSE
				r.amount
			END), 0) AS matching_transactions_sum,
	CASE WHEN d.amount = COALESCE(SUM(
			CASE WHEN t.transaction_type = 'RELEASE' THEN
				- r.amount
			ELSE
				r.amount
			END), 0) THEN
		'YES'
	ELSE
		'NO'
	END AS IS_FULLY_CONSUMED
FROM
	transactions d
	LEFT JOIN transaction_to_deposit_relations r ON d.id = r.deposit_id
	LEFT JOIN transactions t ON r.transaction_id = t.id
WHERE
	d.transaction_type = 'DEPOSIT'
	AND d.account_id='9df5de0f-acb8-4823-bb9e-3f4d7386ff3d'
GROUP BY
	d.id,
	d.amount,
	d.created_at
ORDER BY
	d.created_at DESC;
```

### account balance from transactions relations

```sql
SELECT 
    d.account_id,
    SUM(d.amount - COALESCE(mt.matching_transactions_sum, 0)) AS remaining_amount
FROM 
    transactions d
LEFT JOIN 
    (
        SELECT 
            r.deposit_id,
            SUM(
                CASE 
                    WHEN t.transaction_type = 'RELEASE' THEN -r.amount
                    ELSE r.amount
                END
            ) AS matching_transactions_sum
        FROM 
            transaction_to_deposit_relations r
        JOIN 
            transactions t ON r.transaction_id = t.id
        GROUP BY 
            r.deposit_id
    ) mt ON d.id = mt.deposit_id
WHERE 
    d.transaction_type = 'DEPOSIT'
	AND d.account_id='faf3fe1f-8635-49f2-81bc-3d887c3c7a85'
GROUP BY 
    d.account_id;
```
